# Coleman llms.txt

> Generated file. Do not edit manually.
> Source: scripts/generate_llms_txt.py

## Project

Coleman is a framework for test-case prioritization in CI using multi-armed bandits,
with typed YAML configuration, deterministic run identifiers, sweep orchestration,
parallel execution, and extensibility via hooks and namespaced custom config.

# Coleman

[![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docs-Coleman%20Site-3D9970?style=flat-square)](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/)
![](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.14+-blue.svg)
[![Vulnerabilities](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=jacksonpradolima_coleman4hcs&metric=vulnerabilities)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/new_code?id=jacksonpradolima_coleman4hcs)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/github/jacksonpradolima/coleman4hcs/branch/main/graph/badge.svg?token=BW04LB0B5Y)](https://codecov.io/github/jacksonpradolima/coleman4hcs)


**Adaptive test prioritization for continuous integration. Reproducible experiments from source data to results.**

COLEMAN learns from test outcomes to prioritize CI suites under an execution budget.
Compare classical, contextual and non-stationary bandit policies, run experiments
across seeds and budgets, and resume interrupted work with the same configuration
and checkpoint. Inspect the inputs, decisions and evidence behind each result.

[**Run real CI data**](#start-with-real-ci-data) · [**Explore benchmarks**](#datasets) ·
[**Library and CLI**](#quick-start) · [**Documentation**](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/) ·
[**4.10 release**](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/tag/v4.10.0) · [**Cite COLEMAN**](#citation)

## What you can build with COLEMAN

| Your goal | Available workflow |
| --- | --- |
| Compare adaptive CI prioritization policies | Native TCPCI runner, configurable policies/rewards, contextual inputs and [parameter sweeps](#sweep-engine) |
| Evaluate configurable software | Dune examples and [whole/variant test-set strategies](#running-for-an-hcs-system) |
| Collect real-fault observations | [Controlled Java matrix](docs/java-fault-matrix.md): three curated fixes, frozen source/runtime recipes, raw evidence and offline recovery |
| Reproduce and inspect an experiment | Typed RunSpec, deterministic run identity, [provenance](#provenance), Parquet results and resumable checkpoints |
| Check a CI decision before adoption | [Independent mathematical benchmarks](docs/decision-benchmarks.md), [protected comparisons](docs/protected-evaluation.md) and [operational accounting](docs/operational-pilot.md) |
| Extend or integrate the platform | [Library API](#library-api), [application API and optional MCP](docs/application-api.md), [versioned domain results](docs/domain-results.md) and runner extensions |

Use the [resource replay](docs/resource-replay.md),
[point-in-time observations](docs/point-in-time-observations.md) and
[frozen shadow evaluation](docs/prospective-shadow.md) workflows to distinguish
modeled costs, observed execution and evidence available at decision time.
Negative and inconclusive results remain visible in their reports.

## Start with real CI data

With Python 3.14+ in an activated environment, install the published wheel and run
the complete LRTS workflow. Use cache/output directories outside Git:

```bash
python -m pip install "https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"
python -m coleman.transports.lrts_etl \
  --cache /tmp/coleman-lrts-source-cache \
  --output /tmp/coleman-lrts-data --fetch --run

# Continue the same experiment from the verified cache, offline:
python -m coleman.transports.lrts_etl \
  --cache /tmp/coleman-lrts-source-cache \
  --output /tmp/coleman-lrts-data --run
```

This downloads pinned public reports for **eight Karaf builds**, preserves
**6,876 observations** in analytical Parquet and projects **6,567 compatible
executions** into native input. **309 not-run cases** stay visible as exclusions.
Random and UCB produce **16 native result rows** across eight modeled rounds;
repeating the command resumes the same run. The JSON summary gives the data,
completion receipt and native-result paths. The [complete guide](docs/lrts-parquet-etl.md)
explains schemas, provenance, attribution and resource limits. Docker and MCP are
optional for other integrations and are unnecessary for this workflow.

The replay declares serial costs, assumed label correspondence and budget-censored
RNFail feedback. Source temporal admission remains blocked; this run demonstrates
a usable data pipeline and simulation. Policy efficacy and prospective savings
require their own eligible observations and comparisons.

The same **4.10 wheel** also provides
[RTPTorrent → analytical/native Parquet → checkpointed replay](docs/rtptorrent-parquet-etl.md).
Its complete HikariCP raw member preserves **46,995 class executions across 1,662
source jobs**. The declared eight-job preset projects **18 executions** and
produces **16 Random/UCB result rows**, with the other **46,977 records** retained
analytically. The guide includes a resumable download of the approximately 5 GB
source, full ZIP64 verification and an owned offline example. Method observations
from LRTS and class observations from RTPTorrent retain their distinct units.
Both workflows are explicit post-hoc simulations; the admission and comparison
gates remain visible in the [benchmark readiness table](#datasets).

For larger method histories, the **published 4.10 wheel** includes
[ActiveMQ and separate Log4j stage views](docs/lrts-stage-views.md). ActiveMQ
preserves **18,901 method observations / 18,668 native cases**. Log4j preserves
**30,066 observations**, with **14,957 Ubuntu / 14,906 Windows native cases**.
Each view runs two policies over four modeled rounds and resumes from checkpoint.
The Log4j views share source build groups; their observations are correlated.
The guide includes explicit archive acquisition, exact raw-node bindings and
the temporal evidence still missing for protected evaluation.

Reproduce upstream Java faults with the [controlled CLI/Codec matrix](docs/java-fault-matrix.md),
also included in **4.10**. One frozen plan collects three curated fixes across two
codebases, retaining all **714 role observations / 357 same-test pairs** from the
initial qualification, including both-fail and inconclusive outcomes. Typed indices
verify source, context and raw packets; interrupted collection remains incomplete,
and completed evidence reopens offline. This optional workflow requires the pinned
native arm64 Docker runtime. These constructed functional observations retain
separate admission and generalization limits.

# Quick start

Coleman ships a **typed, library-first experiment system** with
YAML configs, composable config packs, a sweep engine, and deterministic
`run_id` hashing.  External projects can install the [release wheel](#installation) and
drive experiments programmatically **or** via the `coleman` CLI — no repo
checkout required.

The library namespace is now `coleman`.

> **Breaking change** — the `CONFIG_FILE` environment variable, raw TOML
> dict workflow, and `main.py` entry-point are removed.  Configuration is now
> handled via YAML configs, typed Pydantic v2 models, config packs, and
> the `coleman` CLI.

## Library API

```python
from coleman.spec import RunSpec, SweepSpec, SweepAxis, compute_run_id
from coleman.api import run, run_many, sweep

# 1. Define a spec
spec = RunSpec(
    experiment={"datasets": ["alibaba@druid"], "policies": ["UCB"], "rewards": ["RNFail"]},
    results={"out_dir": "./runs"},
)

# 2. Deterministic run_id — same config always produces the same ID
assert compute_run_id(spec) == compute_run_id(spec)

# 3. Single run
result = run(spec)
print(result.run_id, result.artifacts_dir)

# 4. Parameter sweep (grid × seeds)
specs = sweep(spec, SweepSpec(
    axes=[SweepAxis(mode="grid", params={"algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c": [0.1, 0.3, 0.5]})],
    seeds=[0, 1, 2],
))  # 3 values × 3 seeds = 9 specs

results = run_many(specs, max_workers=4)
```

| Function | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `run(spec)` | Execute a single experiment from a resolved `RunSpec` |
| `run_many(specs, max_workers=)` | Execute multiple specs, optionally in parallel |
| `sweep(base, sweep_spec)` | Expand a base spec × sweep definition into concrete specs |
| `load_spec(path)` | Load and validate a `RunSpec` from YAML (with pack resolution) |
| `save_resolved(spec, path)` | Persist a resolved spec as canonical JSON |

## CLI

The `coleman` console script is installed automatically with the package:

```bash
# Execute a single run
coleman run --config run.yaml

# Parameter sweep (grid mode)
coleman sweep --config base.yaml \
    --grid algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c=0.1,0.3,0.5 \
    --grid execution.seed=range(0,20) \
    --workers 4

# Parameter sweep declared in YAML (no --grid needed)
coleman sweep --config base.yaml --workers 4

# Dry-run — print generated specs without executing
coleman sweep --config base.yaml --grid execution.seed=range(0,5) --dry-run


You can now define a top-level `sweep:` section in the YAML config used by
`coleman sweep`; CLI `--grid` values are merged on top.
# Validate a config and optionally write the resolved spec
coleman validate --config base.yaml --resolve resolved.json
```

## Config packs

Config packs are composable YAML fragments under `packs/`.  Reference them
with the `packs` key in your config and inline overrides win:

```yaml
# my-experiment.yaml
packs:
  - policy/linucb
  - reward/rnfail
  - results/parquet
  - telemetry/off

experiment:
  datasets: ["alibaba@druid"]
  policies: ["LinUCB"]

execution:
  independent_executions: 30

hooks:
  fail_fast: false
  plugins:
    - my_project.hooks.ForecastHook

extensions:
  my_domain:
    forecast_selection:
      policy: ThompsonSampling
      reward: Binary
```

Shipped starter packs:

| Pack | Category | Contents |
|------|----------|----------|
| `policy/linucb` | Policy | LinUCB with default alpha values |
| `reward/rnfail` | Reward | RNFail reward function |
| `runtime/local` | Runtime | Single-process local execution |
| `results/parquet` | Results | Parquet sink with defaults |
| `results/duckdb` | Results | DuckDB sink with consolidated files |
| `telemetry/off` | Telemetry | Telemetry disabled |

## Sweep engine

The sweep engine supports **grid** (Cartesian product) and **zip** (paired)
modes, with optional seed replication:

```python
from coleman.spec import SweepSpec, SweepAxis, expand_sweep, RunSpec

base = RunSpec()
sweep_spec = SweepSpec(
    axes=[
        SweepAxis(mode="grid", params={
            "algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c": [0.1, 0.3, 0.5],
            "execution.parallel_pool_size": [1, 4],
        }),
    ],
    seeds=[0, 1, 2],
)
specs = expand_sweep(base, sweep_spec)
# 3 × 2 × 3 seeds = 18 specs, deterministic order
```

- **Grid mode** — Cartesian product of all parameter lists
- **Zip mode** — paired lists (must have equal length, raises `ValueError` otherwise)
- **Seeds** — each base spec is replicated per seed; the seed is stored on `ExecutionSpec.seed` and affects `run_id`
- **CLI + YAML composition** — `coleman sweep` reads top-level `sweep:` from YAML and combines it with `--grid`

## Runner extensibility

Coleman supports extensibility without replacing the native runner:

1. `extensions` for namespaced custom domain config.
2. `hooks` for lifecycle plugins (`on_run_start`, `on_dataset_start`,
   `on_execution_start`, `on_execution_end`, `on_dataset_end`, `on_run_end`,
   `on_error`).

Execution-level hooks are process-local in worker context and remain
parallel-safe when `parallel_pool_size > 1`.

## Deterministic run_id

Every `RunSpec` hashes to a deterministic 12-character identifier:

```
run_id = sha256(canonical_json(resolved_spec))[:12]
```

- **Canonical JSON**: sorted keys, compact separators (`json.dumps(sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))`)
- **Same config → same `run_id` → same output directory**
- Provenance files and artifacts are written to `<out_dir>/<run_id>/`

## Provenance

Each run persists:

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `spec.resolved.json` | The fully resolved `RunSpec` as canonical JSON |
| `provenance.json` | Git commit, dirty flag, Python version, `uv.lock` hash |

# Installation

## As a library (recommended for new projects)

Requires Python 3.14 or later in an activated virtual environment. Install the
wheel published in this repository’s GitHub releases. These examples pin version
4.10.0 and its published SHA-256. Pip verifies the wheel before installation:

```bash
python -m pip install "https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"
```

Or with optional extras:

```bash
# OpenTelemetry SDK
python -m pip install "coleman[telemetry] @ https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"
# ClickHouse results sink
python -m pip install "coleman[clickhouse] @ https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"
```

Then use the [Library API](#library-api) or the [`coleman` CLI](#cli) to
drive experiments — no repo checkout required.

## From source (for development)

To develop or modify the tool, follow these steps:

1. Clone the repository:

```shell
git clone git@github.com:jacksonpradolima/coleman.git
cd coleman
```

2. Install [UV](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) – a fast Python package manager.

3. Install dependencies:

```shell
uv sync
```

4. Install the project locally in editable mode:

```shell
uv pip install -e .
```

5. Create a YAML config file (see [Quick start](#quick-start) for
   the config format) and run with the `coleman` CLI:

```bash
coleman run --config my-experiment.yaml
```

This project uses a `Makefile` to streamline common development tasks. Run `make help` to see all available commands.

| Command                  | Description                          |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `make install`           | Full dev setup (all extras + editable install) |
| `make pre-commit-install`| Install pre-commit hooks             |
| `make test`              | Run tests with pytest                |
| `make lint`              | Run the ruff linter                  |
| `make format`            | Run the ruff formatter               |
| `make docs`              | Build documentation with Zensical    |
| `make cost-structural`   | Run all structural cost checks (CC + MI + Xenon) |
| `make cost-energy`       | Estimate energy/carbon for a workload |
| `make help`              | Show all available Make targets      |

## Code Cost Evaluation

Coleman enforces code quality through a **multi-dimensional cost scorecard**
covering structural complexity, runtime profiling, and energy estimation.

**CI gates** run automatically on every pull request:

- **Xenon complexity gate** — fails if any block exceeds C, any module average exceeds B,
  or the project average exceeds A.
- **Radon maintainability index** — fails if any module scores below A (MI < 20).

**Local evaluation commands:**

```bash
make cost-structural        # all structural checks (CC + MI + Xenon)
make cost-complexity        # radon cyclomatic complexity
make cost-maintainability   # radon MI gate (fails if any module < 20)
make cost-xenon             # xenon complexity gate
make cost-wily              # wily trend analysis
make cost-profile-scalene   # scalene CPU/memory profiling
make cost-energy            # codecarbon energy estimation
```

See [Code Cost Evaluation](docs/code-cost.md) for full documentation.

## DevContainer (recommended)

The fastest way to start developing is with a [DevContainer](https://containers.dev/). Open the repo in VS Code or any DevContainer-compatible editor and select **"Reopen in Container"** — **everything works out of the box**, including the full observability stack.

**What happens automatically:**

1. Python 3.14 + uv + all dependencies (including telemetry & ClickHouse extras) are installed *(on create)*
2. Pre-commit hooks are configured *(on create)*
3. The **observability stack** (OTel Collector + Prometheus + Grafana + ClickHouse) starts via Docker-in-Docker *(on every start)*
4. **Telemetry** can be enabled via the `telemetry/local` pack *(swap `telemetry/off` for `telemetry/local` in `run.yaml`)*

After the container builds, just run your experiment:

```bash
coleman run --config run.yaml
```

Grafana is already live at http://localhost:3000 — open it in your browser to see metrics in real-time.

**Other useful commands:**

```bash
make test           # run the test suite
make lint           # lint with ruff
make docs-serve     # preview docs locally
```

**What's included in the DevContainer:**

| What | Why |
|------|-----|
| Python 3.14 + [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) | The project's package manager |
| Docker-in-Docker | Runs the observability stack automatically |
| VS Code extensions | Ruff, Pylance, Pyright, Copilot, TOML, Jupyter, etc. |
| Telemetry + ClickHouse extras | Pre-installed — no extra `pip install` needed |
| OTel Collector + Prometheus + Grafana + ClickHouse | Started automatically on container start |
| Port forwarding | All service ports mapped to your host (see table below) |

**Forwarded ports (all accessible from your host browser):**

| Port | Service | URL |
|------|---------|-----|
| 3000 | Grafana | http://localhost:3000 |
| 9090 | Prometheus | http://localhost:9090 |
| 4317 | OTel Collector (gRPC) | — (used by the framework) |
| 4318 | OTel Collector (HTTP) | — (used by the framework) |
| 8889 | Prometheus metrics | http://localhost:8889/metrics |
| 8123 | ClickHouse (HTTP) | http://localhost:8123 |
| 9000 | ClickHouse (native) | — |

> **ClickHouse sink remains optional.** The service is running in DevContainer,
> but you still need `sink: "clickhouse"` in your results config or use
> a ClickHouse results pack if you want results persisted to ClickHouse instead of Parquet.

# Architecture: Results, Checkpoints & Telemetry

Coleman is **framework-first**: `coleman run --config run.yaml` works with zero external
services.  All monitoring is split into three independent layers that can be
enabled or disabled individually:

| Layer | Purpose | Default | Optional |
|-------|---------|---------|----------|
| **Results** | Persist experiment facts (NAPFD, APFDc, …) | Partitioned Parquet (zstd) | ClickHouse sink |
| **Checkpoints** | Crash-safe resume | Local filesystem (pickle + `progress.json`) | — |
| **Telemetry** | Observability (latency, throughput) | Disabled (NoOp) | OpenTelemetry + Collector |

When a layer is disabled its module resolves to a **null implementation** with
near-zero overhead (`NullSink`, `NullCheckpointStore`, `NoOpTelemetry`).

## Configuration

All settings live in `run.yaml` and composable config packs under `packs/`.
See [Configuration](docs/configuration.md) for the full YAML schema reference.

```yaml
# run.yaml — default configuration using packs
packs:
  - execution/default        # parallel_pool_size: 10, independent_executions: 10
  - experiment/alibaba_druid # datasets, rewards, policies
  - algorithm/defaults       # baseline defaults (UCB/FRRMAB/EpsilonGreedy/LinUCB/SWLinUCB)
  - results/parquet          # Parquet sink with default settings
  - checkpoint/default       # checkpoint enabled, interval: 50000
  - telemetry/off            # telemetry disabled (swap for telemetry/local to enable)

# Inline overrides (applied on top of packs):
# execution:
#   parallel_pool_size: 4
```

## Optional extras

```bash
# Telemetry (OpenTelemetry SDK)
python -m pip install "coleman[telemetry] @ https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"

# ClickHouse results sink
python -m pip install "coleman[clickhouse] @ https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"
```

## Querying results

Results are written as Hive-partitioned Parquet files under `./runs/`.  You
can query them directly with DuckDB (already a project dependency):

For a guided end-to-end example covering configuration, observability,
resume/recovery, export, and final analysis, see [docs/workflow.py](docs/workflow.py).

```sql
-- Average NAPFD per policy
SELECT policy, AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd
FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
GROUP BY policy
ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC;

-- Cost distribution per reward function
SELECT reward_function,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY cost) AS median_cost
FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
GROUP BY reward_function;
```

# Observability

> **Framework-first guarantee:** `coleman run --config run.yaml` works without Docker or
> any of these services.  The observability stack is **optional** for local
> installs, but **enabled automatically** in the DevContainer.

Coleman ships with a local observability stack (OTel Collector + Prometheus + Grafana)
for real-time metrics and traces during experiments.

## Using the DevContainer (zero-step setup)

If you develop inside the DevContainer, **everything is already running**.
The post-start hook automatically:

1. Starts the OTel Collector + Prometheus + Grafana + ClickHouse via Docker Compose
2. Telemetry can be enabled via the `telemetry/local` pack in `run.yaml`

The `telemetry` and `clickhouse` pip extras are installed during container creation.

Just run your experiment and open Grafana:

```bash
coleman run --config run.yaml
# Open http://localhost:3000 → metrics appear in real-time
```

No manual steps required.

## Local setup (without DevContainer)

If you're **not** using the DevContainer, follow these steps:

```bash
# 1. Start the observability stack
cd examples/observability
docker compose up -d

# 2. Install telemetry extras
uv pip install "coleman[telemetry] @ https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"

# 3. Enable telemetry in your run.yaml:
#    Replace telemetry/off with telemetry/local in the packs list

# 4. Run experiments — metrics flow to Grafana
coleman run --config run.yaml
```

## Port reference

| Port | Service | URL |
|------|---------|-----|
| **3000** | Grafana | http://localhost:3000 |
| **4317** | OTel Collector (gRPC) | — (used by the framework) |
| **4318** | OTel Collector (HTTP) | — (used by the framework, default endpoint) |
| **8889** | Prometheus metrics | http://localhost:8889/metrics |
| **8123** | ClickHouse (HTTP) | http://localhost:8123 *(auto-started in DevContainer; local: `--profile clickhouse`)* |
| **9000** | ClickHouse (native) | — *(auto-started in DevContainer; local: `--profile clickhouse`)* |

## Metric names

| Metric | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `coleman.cycles_total` | Counter | Total experiment cycles processed |
| `coleman.bandit_update_latency` | Histogram (s) | Bandit arm-update latency |
| `coleman.prioritization_latency` | Histogram (s) | Test-case prioritization latency |
| `coleman.evaluation_latency` | Histogram (s) | Evaluation step latency |
| `coleman.napfd` | Histogram | NAPFD score distribution |
| `coleman.apfdc` | Histogram | APFDc score distribution |

### Cardinality rules

- **No `step` label** in metrics (would create unbounded cardinality).
- `run_id` is a resource attribute, not a metric label.
- Per-step detail is available in **traces** (span attributes).

## Adding ClickHouse (optional)

In the DevContainer, ClickHouse is already started by the post-start hook.
For local setups, start ClickHouse alongside the existing stack:

```bash
cd examples/observability
docker compose --profile clickhouse up -d
```

Then switch the results sink in your `run.yaml`:

```yaml
results:
  sink: clickhouse
```

```bash
# Run experiments — results go to the coleman_results table
coleman run --config run.yaml
```

The ClickHouse extras are already installed in the DevContainer.  For local
installs, follow the [optional extras](#optional-extras) instructions first.

## Tear down

```bash
cd examples/observability
docker compose --profile clickhouse down -v
```

# Datasets

## Available today

Choose a workflow by the evidence you need. Runnable examples, source readers,
controlled reproductions and empirical benchmark corpora have different roles:

| Dataset or benchmark | What you can use now | Scope and readiness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **LRTS / Karaf real CI reports** | [Pinned download → analytical/native Parquet → Random/UCB → checkpoint recovery](docs/lrts-parquet-etl.md) | Complete eight-build preset; explicit post-hoc serial simulation. Protected historical admission remains blocked. |
| **LRTS / ActiveMQ and Log4j stage views** | [Published 4.10 wheel → explicit local archive → analytical/native Parquet → checkpoint recovery](docs/lrts-stage-views.md) | Four-build profiles; exact context/node bindings. All raw stages retained; Log4j views share source observations. Temporal admission remains blocked. |
| **Druid and Retrofit** | Bundled native/contextual Parquet examples, native runner and [descriptive profiles](docs/benchmark-corpus.md#local-profiles-and-the-first-diversity-matrix-44) | Runnable legacy experiments. Source terms, duration units and outcome availability still need corpus admission evidence. |
| **Dune and its variants** | Bundled native Parquet, WTS/VTS workflows and [variant-aware inventory](docs/benchmark-corpus.md) | Runnable HCS examples. Variants/context files may share executions; broad HCS benchmark admission remains unfinished. |
| **RTPTorrent / HikariCP** | [Verified ZIP64 → full analytical history → native-compatible Parquet → replay/recovery](docs/rtptorrent-parquet-etl.md) | Available in 4.8: 46,995 class executions / 1,662 jobs retained; eight declared jobs provide the bounded native preset. Explicit post-hoc assumptions; temporal admission remains blocked. |
| **Controlled Java real-fault sources** | Published 4.10 wheel: [CLI-13 producer](docs/junit-source-capture.md) and [three-fix CLI/Codec matrix](docs/java-fault-matrix.md) with typed indices and offline recovery | Two codebases, explicit common fixtures, 357 same-test pairs in the initial qualification. Docker/arm64; negative and inconclusive results remain visible. Controlled evidence, not historical CI or full Defects4J reconstruction. |
| **Owned CI correctness fixtures** | Two tiny [serial/parallel corpus fixtures](docs/benchmark-corpus.md), validation and native integration examples | Available without network. One constructed family for contract/metric checks; no independent-project diversity. |
| **Coverage and scenario-allocation microbenchmarks** | [Correctness and performance profiles](docs/decision-benchmarks.md), independent exhaustive references and JSON/Markdown reports | Runnable finite-model benchmarks with runtime/memory observations; separate from empirical CI-policy comparisons. |
| **Pilot, resource and shadow examples** | [Operational accounting](docs/operational-pilot.md), [resource replay](docs/resource-replay.md) and [shadow recovery](docs/prospective-shadow.md) | Runnable synthetic demonstrations of accounting/recovery. Collected prospective evidence remains insufficient. |

The ten inventoried legacy Parquet artifacts contain **1,386,730 raw rows**,
including contextual files, shared variants and a synthetic example. Their row
count is an inventory fact; shared executions do not become independent projects
or faults. Third-party data terms remain separate from COLEMAN's MIT code license.
See the [source cards and diversity inventory](docs/benchmark-corpus.md) for the
actual identities, counts, missing semantics and admission blockers.

From an installed package, in your chosen workspace:

```bash
# Inspect registered corpus metadata and explicit blockers:
python -m coleman.corpus list
python -m coleman.corpus validate ci-serial-boundary-v1 --output corpus-artifacts
python -m coleman.corpus validate ci-parallel-occupancy-v1 --output corpus-artifacts

# Run independent decision mathematics; reports are written below this workspace:
python -m coleman.benchmarks --profile correctness --output benchmark-artifacts
```

The corpus registry contains **12 registrations: two owned fixtures and ten
legacy artifacts**. Source-specific LRTS/RTPTorrent readers and controlled-source
recipes are separate workflows, linked above; `corpus list` is not a catalog of
every executable example. Registration and successful source conversion each
retain their own validation gates.

## What remains in the benchmark roadmap

[#261](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/issues/261) remains open.
Broader controlled Java and non-Java fault corpora (including the investigated
Defects4J/BugsInPy paths), seeded-fault objects such as SIR, further source ETLs,
additional HCS topologies and the interaction-covering synthetic stress laboratory
remain work. External baseline reproduction, including investigated DANTE methods,
also requires its own verified integration and comparable protocol.

Completing the issue additionally requires the predeclared baseline matrix,
eligible temporal/statistical comparisons, production-reality/diversity coverage,
a frozen confirmatory run and the per-project/cross-corpus report. All seven
required diversity regimes remain uncovered in the registry. Existing source
readers and a working real-data slice support that program without claiming it
has already finished. Follow the [public roadmap](docs/roadmap.md).

Existing dataset discovery links remain available at the
[Harvard Dataverse collection](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataverse/gres-ufpr).
The [GitLab CI extraction tool](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/gitlabci-torrent),
adapted [TravisTorrent tool](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/travistorrent-tools)
and [dataset utilities](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/tcpci-dataset-utils)
are separate projects; review each source's terms and semantics before use.

# About the files input

**COLEMAN** now uses Parquet files (`features-engineered.parquet` and
`data-variants.parquet`) as the primary scenario input format. CSV inputs are
still accepted for compatibility, but they are deprecated and emit warnings.

The second file, **data-variants** (Parquet/CSV), is used by the HCS, and it represents all results from all variants.
The information is organized by commit and variant.

- **features-engineered.parquet** (or legacy `features-engineered.csv`) contains the following information:
  - **Id**: unique numeric identifier of the test execution;
  - **Name**: unique numeric identifier of the test case;
  - **BuildId**: a value uniquely identifying the build;
  - **Duration**: approximated runtime of the test case;
  - **LastRun**: previous last execution of the test case as *DateTime*;
  - **Verdict**: test verdict of this test execution (Failed: 1, Passed: 0).

- **data-variants.parquet** (or legacy `data-variants.csv`) contains all information that **features-engineered.parquet** has, and in addition the following information:
  - **Variant**: variant name.

In this way, **features-engineered** organizes the information for a single system or variant, and
**data-variants** tracks the information for all variants used during the software life-cycle (for each commit).

During the **COLEMAN**'s execution, we use **data-variants** to identify the variants used in a current commit and apply the **WTS** strategy.

For **CONSTANTINE**, additional columns can be used and represents a contextual information. In this way, you define
what kind of information can be used!

#  Using the tool

## How data flows through Coleman

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[YAML config + packs: run.yaml] --> B[coleman CLI / library API]
    R[Pinned LRTS reports + metadata] --> S[Verified external source cache]
    V[Pinned RTPTorrent ZIP64 + raw class history] --> S
    S --> T[Source-specific typed ETL and explicit serial model]
    T --> U[Analytical Parquet + completion provenance]
    T --> C["Native Parquet / legacy CSV; variant input for HCS"]
    C --> D[Scenario Provider]
    B --> D

    D --> E["Virtual Scenarios (CI cycles with test cases)"]
    E --> F[Environment]

    G["Policy (Random, UCB, FRRMAB, LinUCB, etc.)"] --> H[Agent]
    I["Reward Function: (RNFail, TimeRank)"] --> H
    H --> F

    F --> J[Test prioritization per cycle]
    J --> K["Test execution outcomes (verdict, duration, rank)"]
    K --> L["Evaluation Metrics (e.g., NAPFD)"]
    L --> M["Results Sink (Parquet / ClickHouse)"]
    L --> P["Telemetry (OTel → Collector → Grafana, optional)"]

    F --> Q["Checkpoint Store (local, crash-safe resume)"]

    K --> O[Feedback loop]
    O --> I
    O --> G
```

Define experiments through the library's typed RunSpec or a YAML configuration.
Create your own `run.yaml`, or edit the repository's example when working from a checkout.
The file uses composable config packs for a clean, modular setup — each pack provides
defaults for one concern.  Add inline overrides below the `packs:` list to customise settings.

Here's an example `run.yaml` file:

```yaml
# run.yaml — Default Run Configuration
packs:
  - execution/default        # parallel_pool_size: 10, independent_executions: 10
  - experiment/alibaba_druid # datasets, rewards, policies
  - algorithm/defaults       # FRRMAB, UCB, EpsilonGreedy, LinUCB, SWLinUCB params
  - results/parquet          # Parquet sink
  - checkpoint/default       # checkpoint enabled
  - telemetry/off            # telemetry disabled
  - reward/rnfail            # RNFail reward
  - hcs/off                  # HCS disabled
  - contextual/default       # contextual information defaults

# Inline overrides (applied on top of packs):
execution:
  parallel_pool_size: 4
experiment:
  datasets:
    - square@retrofit
```

**where:**
- Execution Configuration:
  - `parallel_pool_size` is the number of worker processes to run **COLEMAN** in parallel.
  - `independent_executions` is the number of independent experiments we desire to run.
  - `force_sequential_under_scalene` forces sequential execution while Scalene is active to improve profiling stability and avoid missing per-thread attribution issues.
  - Parallelism has two layers:
    - inside a run: `execution.parallel_pool_size` controls process-pool workers for independent executions;
    - across many specs: `coleman sweep --workers` (or API `run_many(..., max_workers=...)`) controls concurrent spec execution.
- Experiment Configuration:
  - `scheduled_time_ratio` represents the Schedule Time Ratio, that is, time constraints that represents the time available to run the tests. **Default**: 0.1 (10%), 0.5 (50%), and 0.8 (80%) of the time available.
  - `datasets_dir` is the directory that contains your system. For instance, we desire to run the algorithm for the systems that are inside the directory **data**.
  - `datasets` is an array that represents the datasets to analyse. It's the folder name inside `datasets_dir` which contains the required file inputs.
  - `experiment_dir` is the directory where we will save the results.
  - `rewards` defines the reward functions to be used, available RNFailReward and TimeRankReward (See **Ref1** in [References](#references)).
  - `policies` selects the Policies available on **COLEMAN** (classic + extended), including greedy, UCB, contextual, and non-stationary/sliding-window variants.
- Algorithm Configuration: each algorithm has its own individual configuration. Next, we present some of them:
  - FRRAB:
    - `window_sizes` is an array that contains the sliding window sizes
    - `c` is the scaling factor. It's defined for each reward function used.
  - UCB:
    - `c` is the scaling factor. It's defined for each reward function used.
  - Epsilon-Greedy:
    - `epsilon` is the epsilon value. It's defined for each reward function used.
- HCS Configuration:
  - `wts_strategy` represents the usage of Whole Test Set (WTS) Strategy for a system HCS (See [Whole Test Set Strategy](#whole-test-set-strategy)).
- Contextual Information:
  - Config
    - `previous_build` what kind of information we obtain from previous build and not in the current one. For
      instance, the test case duration (`Duration`) will _know_ only after the test execution.
  - Feature Group
    - `feature_group_name` represent the name of a feature group. We can create different groups of feature to
      evaluate the influence of each one.
    - `feature_group_values` represent the features selected to be used by the Contextual MAB.


##  MAB Policies Available

The following policies are available on **COLEMAN**.

Baseline and classical policies:
- Random
- Greedy
- EpsilonGreedy
- UCB
- UCB1
- SlMAB
- FRRMAB

Greedy variants:
- DecayEpsilonGreedy
- OptimisticGreedy

UCB variants:
- UCB2
- SlidingWindowUCB
- KLUCB
- UCBTuned
- UCBV
- MOSSUCB

Bayesian/stochastic/adversarial variants:
- ThompsonSampling
- BayesianUCB
- Softmax
- Pursuit
- EpsilonDecreasing
- BootstrappedThompson
- PHE
- EXP3
- EXP3IX
- DiscountedUCB
- ChangeDetectionUCB

Combinatorial variants:
- CombinatorialUCB
- CombinatorialThompson

Dueling / ranking variants:
- DuelingUCB
- PairwiseThompsonRanking

Portfolio meta-policy:
- PortfolioUCB

Contextual variants:
- LinUCB
- SWLinUCB
- LinTS
- ContextualEpsilonGreedy
- SWLinTS
- SWContextualEpsilonGreedy

## Running for Non-HCS System

To execute **COLEMAN** for a non-HCS system, first update the experiment settings in your `run.yaml` (or override inline):

- `datasets_dir: examples`
- `datasets: [fakedata]`

Subsequently, you can run the program with the following command:

```
coleman run --config run.yaml
```

## Running for an HCS system

For HCS systems, we provide two distinct strategies to determine optimal solutions for variants:
**WTS** (Whole Test Set Strategy) and **VTS** (Variant Test Set Strategy).
You can learn more about these in **Ref2** under the [References](#references) section.

When employing the **WTS** and **VTS** strategies, regard `datasets_dir` as the directory housing your system.
For the **WTS** approach, variants of a system are discerned from subfolders within the `datasets_dir` directory.
Essentially, `datasets_dir` symbolizes the project name.
This differentiation in execution methodology between HCS and non-HCS systems is crucial,
alongside the `wts_strategy` variable. For clarity, please inspect our example directory.

### Whole Test Set Strategy

The **WTS** strategy prioritizes the test set composed by the union of the test cases of all variants.
To employ this strategy, set in your `run.yaml`:

- `hcs_configuration.wts_strategy: true`

For a practical demonstration, set `datasets = ["dune@total"]`
(a dataset amalgamating test cases from all variants)
and `datasets_dir = "examples/core@dune-common"`.
This provides a concise example using the Dune dataset.
More details on the dataset are available under [Datasets](#datasets).

### Variant Test Set Strategy

Contrastingly, the **VTS** approach evaluates each variant as an isolated system.
To harness this strategy, set in your `run.yaml`:

- `hcs_configuration.wts_strategy: false`

As example, use `datasets = ["dune@debian_10 clang-7-libcpp-17", "dune@debian_11 gcc-10-20",
"dune@ubuntu_20_04 clang-10-20"]` and `datasets_dir = "examples/core@dune-common"`
to run one small example using Dune dataset (See [Datasets](#datasets)).
Now, we consider each variant as single system.

As a hands-on example, set `datasets =
["dune@debian_10 clang-7-libcpp-17", "dune@debian_11 gcc-10-20", "dune@ubuntu_20_04 clang-10-20"]`
and `datasets_dir = "examples/core@dune-common"`.
This offers a succinct example using the Dune dataset, treating each variant as a unique system.
Further insights into the dataset are available in the [Datasets](#datasets) section.

# Analysis of COLEMAN Performance

As part of our ongoing effort to provide the state-of-the-art tool, Coleman, for TCPCI, we've created examples to guide any researcher to understand the performance, effectiveness, and adaptability of our tool. The analysis, available in our [marimo notebook](notebooks/analysis.py) (and the original [Jupyter notebook](notebooks/analysis.ipynb)), leverages various libraries such as DuckDB, Pandas, Seaborn, and Matplotlib to process data and visualize the results.

## Performance Metrics

The notebook has examples including but not limited to test case execution times, prioritization effectiveness, and algorithm efficiency under different configurations and environments.

## Methodologies

The notebook employs SQL queries for data manipulation and leverages Python's data analysis and visualization libraries to derive meaningful insights from historical test data. Our methodology ensures a robust analysis framework capable of handling large datasets and producing actionable intelligence.

## Visualizations

Data visualizations play a key role in our analysis, offering intuitive understanding of complex data patterns and algorithm performance. The notebook includes various charts and graphs that elucidate the trade-offs between different prioritization strategies and their impact on test cycle times and failure detection rates.

<a id="solving-the-test-case-prioritization-using-multi-armed-bandit-algorithms"></a>

# Research background

**COLEMAN** (_**C**ombinatorial V**O**lati**LE** **M**ulti-Armed B**AN**dit_)
originated as a multi-armed bandit approach to Test Case Prioritization in
Continuous Integration (TCPCI). Its research lineage includes adaptive ranking,
Highly Configurable Systems (HCS), and contextual prioritization under the name
**CONSTANTINE** (_**CON**textual te**S**t priori**T**iz**A**tion for co**NT**inuous
**INE**gration_). See [References](#references) for the original publications.

HCS experiments support **Whole Test Set (WTS)**, which prioritizes the union of
tests across variants, and **Variant Test Set (VTS)**, which prioritizes the test
set for each variant. Contextual policies such as LinUCB and SWLinUCB consume
configured features, including historical duration, executed/failed method counts,
test age, change type, complexity and size when supplied by the dataset. Features
used for a decision must have been available before that decision; the current
execution's duration and verdict become feedback afterward.

The experiment interface accepts test-execution data independently of the subject's
implementation language. Each source producer has its own supported language,
runtime and evidence limits, documented in the [benchmark inventory](#datasets).

### FILE: docs/analysis-playbook.md

# Analysis Playbook

This guide is a complete reference for post-run analysis in Coleman, focused on
decision-quality, cost, stability, and extensibility impact.

Use this after one or more experiment runs have produced Parquet data under
your configured results directory.

## Protected comparisons

The summaries below are descriptive. For chronological eligibility, frozen
candidates, durable holdout access, paired independent-unit inference and
insufficient-evidence reports, use [protected evaluation](protected-evaluation.md).
Repeated seeds/worker executions do not increase the number of independent units.

## Data Access Patterns

### DuckDB (recommended)

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect("analysis.duckdb")
con.execute(
	"""
	CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW experiment_results AS
	SELECT *
	FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
	"""
)
```

### Basic sanity checks

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_total FROM experiment_results;

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT execution_id) AS executions,
	   COUNT(DISTINCT policy) AS policies,
	   COUNT(DISTINCT reward_function) AS rewards
FROM experiment_results;
```

## Core Comparisons

### 1. Quality ranking (NAPFD)

```sql
SELECT policy,
	   reward_function,
	   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
	   STDDEV_SAMP(fitness) AS std_napfd,
	   COUNT(*) AS n
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY policy, reward_function
ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC;
```

### 2. Cost-aware quality ranking (APFDc)

```sql
SELECT policy,
	   reward_function,
	   AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc,
	   STDDEV_SAMP(cost) AS std_apfdc,
	   COUNT(*) AS n
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY policy, reward_function
ORDER BY avg_apfdc DESC;
```

### 3. Stability (coefficient of variation)

```sql
SELECT policy,
	   reward_function,
	   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
	   STDDEV_SAMP(fitness) AS std_napfd,
	   CASE
		 WHEN AVG(fitness) = 0 THEN NULL
		 ELSE STDDEV_SAMP(fitness) / AVG(fitness)
	   END AS cv_napfd
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY policy, reward_function
ORDER BY cv_napfd ASC NULLS LAST;
```

## Budget and Scenario Sensitivity

Use scenario/time-ratio segmentation to find robust policies.

```sql
SELECT scenario,
	   policy,
	   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
	   AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc,
	   AVG(prioritization_time) AS avg_prioritization_time
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY scenario, policy
ORDER BY scenario, avg_napfd DESC;
```

If your scenario naming encodes time ratio, normalize it once and persist a
derived table for repeated analyses.

## Quality vs Cost Frontier (Pareto)

Goal: maximize NAPFD and APFDc. The legacy `cost` column contains an APFDc
quality score; it is not execution expense in seconds or money.

```python
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

df = duckdb.sql(
	"""
	SELECT policy,
		   reward_function,
		   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
		   AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc
	FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
	GROUP BY policy, reward_function
	"""
).df()

def pareto_frontier(data: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
	pts = data.sort_values(["avg_apfdc", "avg_napfd"], ascending=[False, False]).reset_index(drop=True)
	keep = []
	best_napfd = float("-inf")
	for _, row in pts.iterrows():
		if row["avg_napfd"] > best_napfd:
			keep.append(True)
			best_napfd = row["avg_napfd"]
		else:
			keep.append(False)
	return pts.loc[keep].copy()

front = pareto_frontier(df)
print(front)
```

Interpretation:

1. Points on the frontier are non-dominated trade-offs.
2. Off-frontier points are strictly worse in both metrics than at least one alternative.

## Win Rate Analysis (Pairwise)

Compare how often one policy beats another on the same execution slice.

```python
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

base = duckdb.sql(
	"""
	SELECT scenario,
		   execution_id,
		   policy,
		   AVG(fitness) AS score
	FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
	GROUP BY scenario, execution_id, policy
	"""
).df()

pivot = base.pivot_table(index=["scenario", "execution_id"], columns="policy", values="score")
policies = list(pivot.columns)

rows = []
for a in policies:
	for b in policies:
		if a == b:
			continue
		valid = pivot[[a, b]].dropna()
		wins = (valid[a] > valid[b]).sum()
		total = len(valid)
		rows.append({"policy_a": a, "policy_b": b, "win_rate": wins / total if total else None, "n": total})

win_rate_df = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values(["policy_a", "win_rate"], ascending=[True, False])
print(win_rate_df.head(30))
```

## Runtime and Resource Footprint

```sql
SELECT policy,
	   AVG(prioritization_time) AS avg_prioritization_time,
	   AVG(process_memory_rss_mib) AS avg_rss_mib,
	   AVG(process_cpu_utilization_percent) AS avg_cpu_pct,
	   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY policy
ORDER BY avg_prioritization_time ASC;
```

Use this to identify policies that are fast enough for CI budget constraints.

## Extensions and Hook Artifacts

When using runner hooks and extensions, persist additional artifacts under the
run folder (for example, JSON/CSV derived from custom domain logic).

Recommended pattern:

1. Write one artifact per execution_id.
2. Include run_id, dataset_id, execution_id, and worker_id in each record.
3. Join artifact rows with experiment results in DuckDB for impact analysis.

Example join pattern (adapt paths to your artifact layout):

```sql
WITH base AS (
  SELECT run_id, execution_id, policy, fitness, cost
  FROM experiment_results
),
ext AS (
  SELECT run_id, execution_id, custom_signal, custom_bucket
  FROM read_json_auto('./runs/**/artifacts/*.json')
)
SELECT b.policy,
	   e.custom_bucket,
	   AVG(b.fitness) AS avg_napfd,
	   AVG(b.cost) AS avg_apfdc
FROM base b
JOIN ext e
  ON b.run_id = e.run_id AND b.execution_id = e.execution_id
GROUP BY b.policy, e.custom_bucket
ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC;
```

## Reproducibility Checklist

1. Keep spec.resolved.json and provenance.json for every run.
2. Compare only runs with consistent datasets and time-ratio sets.
3. Report both central tendency and variance.
4. Track run_id and execution_id in every exported table/chart.
5. Version-control analysis scripts and generated figures metadata.

## Suggested Reporting Bundle

For each experiment campaign, export:

1. Overall ranking by NAPFD and APFDc.
2. Pareto frontier table and scatter chart.
3. Stability table (std and CV).
4. Scenario sensitivity matrix.
5. Runtime/resource table.
6. Hook/extension impact table (if enabled).

### FILE: docs/api/evaluation.md

# Evaluation

Coleman includes classic TCP/IR-aligned metrics:

- NAPFD and NAPFD-Verdict
- APFDc
- Precision@k
- Recall@k
- AveragePrecision@k (AP@k)
- ReciprocalRank@k (RR@k, equivalent to MRR for a single ranked suite)
- NDCG@k (normalized discounted gain at top-k)

Literature references:

- Rothermel, G.; Untch, R. H.; Chu, C.; Harrold, M. J. (2001). Prioritizing test cases for regression testing. IEEE TSE.
- Elbaum, S.; Malishevsky, A. G.; Rothermel, G. (2002). Test case prioritization: a family of empirical studies. IEEE TSE.
- Catal, C.; Mishra, D.; Tufekci, S.; Cagiltay, N. E. (2011). Mapping study of software test case prioritization. Software Quality Journal.
- Manning, C. D.; Raghavan, P.; Schutze, H. (2008). Introduction to Information Retrieval. Cambridge University Press.
- Baeza-Yates, R.; Ribeiro-Neto, B. (2011). Modern Information Retrieval (2nd ed.). Addison-Wesley.
- Thakur, N.; Reimers, N.; Ruckle, A.; et al. (2021). BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models. NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks.
- Muennighoff, N.; Tazi, N.; Magne, L.; Reimers, N. (2023). MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark. EACL.

::: coleman.evaluation

### FILE: docs/api/reward.md

# Reward

Coleman supports reward formulations inspired by TCP, ranking, and cost-aware literature:

- RNFail (binary fault signal)
- TimeRank (failure-aware order-sensitive reward)
- ReciprocalRank (inverse-rank gain)
- TopKRNFail (prefix-constrained binary reward; precision-style)
- DiscountedFailure (DCG-like logarithmic discount)
- APFDc (cost-aware reward using execution time and detected failure positions)

Literature references:

- Spieker, H.; Gotlieb, A.; Marijan, D.; Mossige, M. (2017). Reinforcement Learning for Automatic Test Case Prioritization and Selection in Continuous Integration. ISSTA.
- Jarvelin, K.; Kekalainen, J. (2002). Cumulated gain-based evaluation of IR techniques. ACM TOIS.
- Rothermel, G.; Untch, R. H.; Chu, C.; Harrold, M. J. (2001). Prioritizing test cases for regression testing. IEEE TSE.
- Elbaum, S.; Malishevsky, A. G.; Rothermel, G. (2002). Test case prioritization: a family of empirical studies. IEEE TSE.
- Manning, C. D.; Raghavan, P.; Schutze, H. (2008). Introduction to Information Retrieval. Cambridge University Press.

::: coleman.reward

### FILE: docs/application-api.md

# Bounded CI application API and optional MCP

COLEMAN 4.0 provides a bounded application API while remaining a CI test
prioritization and selection platform. The application layer makes its existing
native services available through reusable, bounded commands. It does not introduce a new runner,
an LLM decision algorithm, or a hosted service.

## Install the release

Use Python 3.14 or later on Linux or macOS in an activated virtual environment:

```bash
python -m pip install 'https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29'
```

For optional tools, install the same GitHub wheel with its extra:

```bash
python -m pip install 'coleman[mcp] @ https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29'
```

Use this repository's release assets and verify their published digest and
attestations. The bare PyPI name belongs to a different project. Base CLI/library
execution requires no MCP dependency, model, credentials, network service, or
client. The optional adapter is tested against the pinned MCP Python SDK 2.3.0
and its negotiated MCP protocol; the independent COLEMAN application contract is
`coleman-application-v1`.
Contributor `make install` includes the optional SDK to exercise its tests and
type annotations; installing the base release wheel still excludes it.

## Architecture and ownership

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Library[Typed library commands] --> Service[ApplicationService]
    CLI[coleman application] --> Commands[Versioned command boundary]
    MCP[Optional local MCP stdio tools] --> Commands
    Commands --> Service
    Registry[Host-approved immutable registry] --> Service
    Identity[Trusted caller context] --> Service
    Service --> Queue[Bounded queue and lifecycle supervisor]
    Queue --> Worker[Owned subprocess with deadline and resource guards]
    Worker --> Coverage[Native finite coverage solver]
    Worker --> Allocation[Native scenario allocation service]
    Worker --> Runner[Existing api.run and TCPCI runner]
    Coverage --> Publish[Existing ArtifactWriter: complete immutable JSON]
    Allocation --> Publish
    Runner --> Publish
    Publish --> Receipt[Schema-validated caller-owned result handle]
    Receipt --> Portable[Explicit portable export and import]
```

Domain packages never import CLI or MCP. Native `run`, sweeps, extensions, sinks,
checkpoints and unrestricted library APIs retain their existing behavior. The
application service owns a unique private session directory under a trusted
host-selected root. Clients select registered IDs; they cannot send a RunSpec,
plugin import, path, shell command, dataset URL or exporter endpoint.

The packaged registry contains three **synthetic smoke fixtures**:

| Spec ID | Native service | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `weighted-overlap-3` | Finite coverage | Overlapping A/B/C capabilities, modeled duration in seconds |
| `signed-ci-resource-3` | Scenario allocation | Declared joint scenario model with conservative evidence handling |
| `native-ci-smoke-v1` | TCPCI runner | Two synthetic builds, Random baseline, RNFail, seed 42, fixed-time budget 3 s |

These fixtures validate integration and mathematics; they are not independent
CI observations or evidence of practical time savings. Seeds do not create
independent observations. Native allocation retains its insufficient-evidence
and conservative fallback semantics.

## Complete library example

Run from outside the checkout after installing the wheel:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from coleman.application import (
    ApplicationService, Caller, Parameters, ResultBundle, Submit, default_registry,
)
from coleman.selection import CoverageResult

caller = Caller(subject="local-analysis")  # supplied by trusted host code
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    with ApplicationService(default_registry(), root=Path(directory)) as service:
        print(service.capabilities().to_json())
        request = Submit(
            schema_version=1,
            request_id="ci-budget-3",
            spec_id="weighted-overlap-3",
            parameters=Parameters(budget=3),
        )
        initial = service.submit(request, caller=caller)
        final = service.wait(initial.job_id, caller=caller)
        assert final.state == "completed" and final.handle is not None
        bundle = service.result(final.handle, caller=caller)
        assert isinstance(bundle.result, CoverageResult)
        assert bundle.result.selected_ids == ("A", "C")
        assert bundle.result.cost.value == 3
        assert bundle.result.objective.value == 1
        assert service.submit(request, caller=caller).job_id == final.job_id
        exported = service.export_result(final.handle, caller=caller)
        Path(directory, "portable.json").write_text(exported, encoding="utf-8")
        assert ResultBundle.from_json(exported) == bundle
        imported = service.import_result(exported, caller=caller)
        assert imported.handle is not None
        assert imported.handle.digest == final.handle.digest
```

Save the export outside a temporary directory to retain it after shutdown.
Coverage budget overrides are exact nonnegative decimals, at most twelve decimal
places, in the registered cost unit and meaning. JSON serializes them as decimal
strings. Zero is valid; null means **no override**. Negative budgets, non-finite
values, unknown keys and implicit unit conversions are rejected. Allocation and
experiment parameters are frozen in their registrations in v1.
Application JSON readers preserve decimal number literals before precision
validation, so extra digits cannot disappear through intermediate binary64
rounding. Existing native readers retain their original compatibility behavior.

One-shot CLI execution uses the same command and services:

```bash
coleman application --request '{"schema_version":1,"request_id":"ci-budget-3","spec_id":"weighted-overlap-3","parameters":{"budget":3}}'
coleman application --request '{"schema_version":1,"request_id":"native-ci","spec_id":"native-ci-smoke-v1"}'
```

CLI output is a canonical JSON envelope. Success contains `ok: true` and `data`;
errors contain `ok: false`, a stable `error` and safe human `message`. A failed or
expired one-shot job returns the same error envelope, includes its typed state
in `data`, and exits with status 2. Existing
`coleman run --config ...` remains available.

## Native experiment registration by trusted hosts

For your own approved local dataset, create a normal RunSpec in host code, set
one sequential worker, one to sixteen executions and an explicit seed; use the
Random baseline, one or two RNFail/TimeRank rewards, and one to eight budgets.
Disable checkpoints, telemetry, hooks and extensions; use the local Parquet sink.
Call `register_experiment("approved-ci", spec)` and pass the returned immutable
`Configuration` to `ApplicationService`. Registration snapshots up to eight
`<datasets_dir>/<dataset>/features-engineered.parquet` files, totaling 1 MiB, with
at most 10,000 rows per dataset and 1,000 candidates per build. Dataset IDs use
the conservative application ID alphabet. This bounded adapter deliberately
supports a smaller surface than unrestricted native RunSpec execution.
The seed and every repetition offset (`seed + iteration_index`) must fit the
unsigned 64-bit range shared by the native NumPy/Polars execution path. Negative
seeds and overflowing repetition ranges are rejected during registration.

Inputs are copied into an owned worker directory; original files are never
reread during execution. Normalized relative input/output paths make the native
resolved run ID independent of temporary directories. Configuration fingerprints
bind complete input bytes and normalized RunSpec. Work units are total builds ×
executions × rewards × budget values. An over-limit experiment is rejected before
queue admission; work-limited decisions can return an explicitly limited native
result. V1 does not resume application jobs through native checkpoints. Existing
direct checkpoint APIs remain available separately.

Registration recomputes build/candidate dimensions from the snapshotted bytes.
The bounded adapter requires integer build IDs and binary verdicts, unique
testcase names per build, numeric finite nonnegative durations in seconds and
non-null native required columns. Invalid rows are rejected; this adapter never
invokes the legacy loader's null-duration-to-zero coercion. The direct legacy
loader remains compatible with its existing callers. Algorithm overrides are
outside the approved Random baseline registration surface in v1.
Build IDs must also survive the native loader's signed Int64 conversion; values
outside that range are rejected before execution.
Registration also checks the actual native duration conversion (Float64 loader
then the bandit's Float32 schema): overflow and positive-to-zero underflow are
rejected. Genuine zero and representable subnormal durations remain valid;
ordinary native rounding is preserved and native result bytes keep that meaning.
Budget values must produce unique native directory segments of at most 255 UTF-8
bytes. This also rejects different ratio budgets rounded to the same native label;
existing unrestricted native naming remains unchanged.
`CalcPrio` must be an integer column fitting the bandit's signed Int32 schema.
`LastRun` must survive the existing string conversion; unsupported nested values
are refused. Duration validation applies the loader's Float64 conversion first,
so supported decimal/integer source columns retain their native behavior.

Experiment bundles contain original resolved-specification and native result
bytes with logical filenames, byte counts, SHA-256 and canonical base64.
`provenance.json` in a produced bundle is explicitly a
`portable-native-provenance-v1` derivative: it records schema version, COLEMAN
producer/version, Python/platform runtime facts, the original local file's
SHA-256, and the redacted field names `cwd`, `git`, `uv_lock_hash`. Ambient host
directories, Git context and lock-file context are not exported. The original
native provenance file remains unchanged inside the worker until cleanup;
the source digest permits host-side audit and does not authenticate a producer.
Import preserves supplied evidence and never extracts files. Existing Parquet fields retain their
legacy meanings; unavailable metrics are not invented or converted to zero.
Runtime observations, timestamps and native shard filenames can differ across
equivalent executions. Mathematical results and approved-source provenance are
compared separately from runtime metadata and complete artifact digests.

## Limits, states and failures

`Limits` requests are reduced componentwise by `ServerPolicy.caps` before work.
Default caps are 30 elapsed seconds including queue/startup, 10,000 native work
units, 100 candidates, 512 MiB worker peak RSS/solver allocation ceiling and
256 KiB combined native output files plus portable result JSON. Native solver working-memory estimates cap at
1 GiB even if a host permits larger worker RSS. Native proof/dimension ceilings
still apply. The service defaults to one active worker, eight pending jobs,
64 retained job identities, 16 MiB reserved results and 2 GiB reserved active
worker memory. Limits count bytes, seconds and documented native work units;
they are not calibrated probabilities or scientific quality guarantees.

Admission reserves each job's maximum output until expiry and sums admitted
worker memory before starting processes. Registry snapshots are bounded to 32
configurations of 1.5 MiB each. Parent/interpreter overhead, input snapshots,
protocol frames and temporary serialization buffers add bounded local overhead
outside worker RSS. Linux worker peak RSS uses the current executable's kernel
`VmHWM`, because `getrusage` can include the parent's footprint before `exec`.
Other platforms retain the existing sampler; historical general telemetry and
stored artifacts keep their existing meaning. The memory ceiling is unchanged.
Worker RSS and native-file output are checked before/after
calculation and sampled every 20 ms; transient overshoot is possible. Unsupported
RSS measurement fails closed. This is a guard for trusted local native code,
not a hard memory allocator or hostile-code sandbox. The underlying SDK stdio
framing is for a trusted local client and is not an untrusted network ingress
limit. Hosted deployment needs its own authenticated, size/concurrency-limited
gateway and process/resource isolation; v1 provides none.
Pending admission counts actual capacity after active memory reservations:
unused concurrency slots do not expand the pending queue when memory prevents
their use. Jobs that fit an available slot start before `submit` returns;
otherwise the finite pending-queue cap applies. A zero queue cap permits only
immediate starts. Portable evidence imports require storage, not a worker slot.

Completion retains only the validated portable JSON bundle. Native work files,
input copies and private request files are removed after the worker exits, before
the completed receipt is issued; the bundle preserves native result/specification
bytes and the explicit redacted provenance derivative. Retained output reservations therefore cover the entire completed job
directory. Before final publication, the combined native-file and bundle byte
count must also fit the admitted output cap.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued: validated and admitted
    queued --> running: worker and memory slot
    queued --> cancelled: cancel wins
    queued --> failed: worker startup fails
    queued --> expired: elapsed deadline
    running --> completed: exit zero and validated immutable JSON
    running --> failed: native error or resource refusal
    running --> cancelled: cancel wins
    running --> expired: elapsed deadline
    completed --> expired: retention TTL
    failed --> expired: retention TTL
    cancelled --> expired: retention TTL
```

Cancellation and completion commit under the same lock: the first terminal state
wins. Cancelling a completed job returns completion unchanged; cancelling queued
or running work terminates/reaps its worker and exposes no partial result. A
complete native incumbent with a work-limit status is valid evidence, not an
optimality claim. Native failures never become fabricated negative scientific
results. Only exit zero plus valid, matching native result JSON permits completion.

Retention starts at a terminal state, defaults to one hour, and deletes result
bytes on expiry. Status retains an `expired` tombstone; retrieval returns the
stable expiry error. Request IDs are scoped by trusted caller: identical retries
reuse the same job, changed commands conflict, and expired IDs never silently
start new work. Tombstones count toward the finite session job limit. After that
limit, start a new service session deliberately. `close()` cancels work and removes
session files. Restart loses job handles; orphaned crash directories require
trusted operator cleanup. Export/import is the explicit portable continuation,
not a claim to resume an interrupted native calculation.

| Error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `invalid_input` | Invalid schema/version/parameter, changed request ID or wrong issued digest |
| `unknown_spec` | No such approved configuration |
| `not_found` | Job absent from this service session |
| `forbidden` | Existing job belongs to a different trusted caller |
| `expired` | Deadline or result retention expired |
| `resource_limit` | Input, native workload, queue, job, output or memory limit |
| `unavailable_result` | No completed result, corrupted artifact, worker failure or closed session |

Status is inspectable before a handle exists. A handle includes schema version,
job ID and content digest. Ownership is checked independently **before** exposing
its result. A digest proves integrity, not producer identity or authorization.
Imports recheck decision mathematics and opaque experiment-file hashes, then issue a fresh local
handle to the importing caller; they do not attest the claimed producer or run
any imported content. Imported experiment observations remain producer claims,
not independently rerun evidence. Bundle v1 requires integer version 1; missing, future and
unknown versions fail closed. Legacy native artifacts keep their existing readers;
there is no automatic migration or reinterpretation.

## Configure MCP once, then use tools

After installing the optional wheel extra, point an MCP-capable local client at
the absolute executable `/tmp/coleman-application-env/bin/coleman-mcp`, with no
arguments. This starts a local stdio server with the packaged registry. A trusted
custom host can instead call `create_server(service, caller=...)` with its own
approved registry. Each process has one host-owned local principal; caller fields
inside requests are rejected. There is no HTTP listener or hosted authentication.

Once configured, the client can discover configurations, submit a bounded CI
request, poll status, cancel, retrieve and export/import results through tools.
The user does not run a shell command for each request. No model is required to
exercise these operations; a natural-language client is only another consumer.

| Tool | Argument | Response |
|---|---|---|
| `discover` | none | IDs, kinds, fingerprints, budget units/meaning, policy and submit JSON schema |
| `submit` | `request_json` | Versioned `JobView` in success envelope |
| `status` / `cancel` | `command_json`: `{"schema_version":1,"job_id":"..."}` | Job state |
| `result` / `export_result` | `handle_json`: exact issued handle | Portable bundle in `data` |
| `import_result` | `bundle_json`: serialized exported `data` | New local completed job and handle |

Commands have a 16 KiB cap before JSON parsing; imports use the server output
cap. MCP JSON framing and escaping add overhead to the bundle byte cap. Unknown
fields, duplicate JSON keys, traversal/import/URL attempts and future versions
fail before execution. Standard SDK protocol/schema failures remain MCP errors;
valid tool invocations return the versioned COLEMAN success/error envelope.

The no-model tests use the actual optional SDK client both in process and over
stdio, then repeat the stdio lifecycle from an installed noneditable wheel outside
the checkout. They also verify base installation without MCP, real two-build
native execution, CLI/library/tool mathematics, caller isolation, races, immutable
publication, golden fixtures, portability, expiry, malicious inputs and saturation.



### FILE: docs/benchmark-corpus.md

# Versioned CI benchmark corpus: foundation and local profiles

This is the first implementation slice of
[#261](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/issues/261), introduced in
**COLEMAN 4.2**. It implements source manifests, a typed registry and data
cards, bounded independent correctness references, local validation and native
integration. COLEMAN **4.4** adds bounded local native-Parquet profiles, a reproducible diversity
inventory and [licensed source-package materialization](corpus-materialization.md).
The diversified benchmark program remains open.

For the separate source-specific ETL workflows, see [Karaf](lrts-parquet-etl.md),
[RTPTorrent](rtptorrent-parquet-etl.md) and the published 4.10 [ActiveMQ/Log4j stage
views](lrts-stage-views.md). Those exports preserve their own provenance and
admission blockers; they do not silently add admitted registrations to this registry.

For controlled Java sources, the published 4.10 wheel includes a separate [CLI/Codec
matrix](java-fault-matrix.md) using the existing controlled/JUnit producer.
Its typed index preserves all selected outcomes and incomplete evidence. It does
not silently change this registry's admission or diversity coverage.

The registry contains two small repository-authored MIT-licensed CI fixtures and
an inventory of ten existing public example Parquet artifacts. Historical sources
remain **blocked for evaluation** until their data-specific terms, duration units,
availability semantics, adapter and conversion evidence are verified. The code
repository's license is never inferred to license third-party datasets.

Both tiny sources share one constructed build/test family. They are not independent
CI observations. All seven required diversity regimes remain uncovered, including
the broad adversarial simulation regime: a three-test fixture is not a stress lab.
No policy effectiveness, state-of-the-art, production savings or commercial claim
follows from passing these checks.

## Installed commands

Install the wheel attached to [COLEMAN 4.10](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/tag/v4.10.0)
in a Python 3.14+ environment, or build a development wheel from the reviewed source.
Copy examples to a directory outside the checkout. Once installed, these local
operations need no optional dependency, provider subscription, credential or
network access.

```bash
python -m coleman.corpus list
python -m coleman.corpus show ci-serial-boundary-v1
python -m coleman.corpus schema
python -m coleman.corpus validate ci-serial-boundary-v1 --output corpus-artifacts
python -m coleman.corpus validate ci-parallel-occupancy-v1 --output corpus-artifacts
```

`list` returns registered IDs, explicit blocked reasons, verified fixture IDs
(empty until validation evidence is supplied), and all missing minimum regimes.
`show` returns the complete typed card. `schema` emits the manifest's structural
JSON schema; semantic cross-field checks still require the library validator.
`validate` writes a deterministic immutable report and returns its path/source
digest. Exit 0 means the requested metadata or tiny correctness operation passed;
it does not mean corpus diversity is satisfied. Invalid/blocked sources, unknown
IDs, future schemas, unsupported adapters, bad bytes or output failures return 2.
CLI output must remain within the current workspace; existing symlinked report
parents are resolved and checked before publication. This local path check assumes
no concurrent hostile filesystem mutation; it is not an OS sandbox. Library callers
supply their own trusted `ArtifactWriter` root, independently of CLI/MCP transports.

The profile commands below and [source-package fetch/cache/validation](corpus-materialization.md)
are also available in 4.4. Source-specific conversion, large stress generation,
baseline matrices, dependence-aware statistical profiles and confirmatory run/report
commands remain subsequent slices of #261.

## Source contract and admission

The [RTPTorrent source assessment](rtptorrent.md) in COLEMAN 4.5 adds a
bounded raw-class reader and an owned isolated native replay. It preserves repeated
class executions and missing CI clocks; it does not admit an external source or
change the registry's diversity inventory.

The [LRTS source assessment](lrts.md) preserves processed metadata alongside raw
Jenkins method/suite/node identities. Its bounded owned replay checks native
compatibility; missing availability, stage mapping and expected-suite evidence
keep real-source temporal evaluation blocked.

`CorpusManifest` schema v1 binds:

- source URI/version/citation, SHA-256, byte count and verified local availability;
- specific data license ID, terms URI/digest/review time and redistribution rule;
- adapter/version and its actual implementation state;
- logical observation/group dimensions and shared source dependence group;
- event, outcome and feature availability fields, timestamp origin and timezone;
- explicit verdict mapping, failing-test versus genuinely mapped fault unit,
  duration units/meaning and unknown-outcome policy;
- intended evaluation purpose, temporal boundaries when available, budget units,
  budgets, seed labels, metrics and source resource limits;
- input/output row counts and unique primary exclusion reasons with conservation;
- validity limitations that remain visible in human and machine reports.

Registration is not admission. `blocking_reasons` exposes unresolved prerequisites;
`require_ready()` checks metadata only. `validate_fixture_source()` additionally
checks real bytes, canonical source grammar, actual row counts, declared field
semantics and native correctness. A metadata declaration is a producer attestation,
not cryptographic proof of legal rights, completeness or statistical independence.

Fixture reports embed their parsed source data. Their validation, reads and
publication therefore require `redistribution="permitted"`. Verified `recipe_only`
terms can support metadata registration or future download recipes, but cannot
authorize an embedded-source fixture report through the library API.

The phase-one adapter supports only `ci-fixture-json`, version `1`, for constructed
synthetic correctness inputs. It never imports an adapter from a user-provided
name or follows its URI. Other formats remain visible registrations with planned
adapters. In particular, native Parquet inputs are not silently routed through
legacy missing-value coercions: the new admission gate must establish semantics
before those inputs can enter a corpus evaluation. Direct native behavior is
unchanged.

Data cards retain facts separately from claims: observed footer row counts and
source byte counts are available in the inventory; unverified duration profiles
are unavailable. Null language/execution axes are unverified; empty axes are
explicitly inapplicable to a purely numerical fixture. Constructed/control
histories cannot be labeled observed CI, and synthetic fixtures cannot be labeled
real faults. Seeded-fault and controlled-real-fault layers must retain matching
seeded/real origins or explicitly unverified origin; contradictory classifications
fail when registering or serializing cards. Context/variant artifacts retain shared
dependence groups rather than becoming additional independent projects.

The initial inventory pins the exact public source revision
`b743f51d5ba444410b32f2c0e318b2587b882c43`; every file's SHA-256, byte size and Parquet
footer row count were checked against that Git object. It contains 1,386,730
source rows across ten artifacts, **not** that many independent observations.
Physical duration/churn/availability/provider semantics remain unverified, not zero.
The local profiling recipe below describes raw fields without resolving those gates.

## Local profiles and the first diversity matrix (4.4)

These additions are available in the 4.4 wheel; 4.3 and older wheels retain their
previous commands. The profiler is a separate descriptive recipe, **not** an implemented corpus evaluation adapter.
It does not change registry v1, cards, fixture/readiness v1, old native result
rows, source licenses or admission blockers.

```bash
# SOURCE is a local copy of the exact registered file, not a download URL.
python -m coleman.corpus profile native-example-e970afe1686d7fe6 source.parquet --output profiles
# Copy examples/corpus-profiles/inventory.py outside the checkout first.
python inventory.py /absolute/path/to/coleman corpus-inventory
```

The inventory example reads the ten existing files from the explicit checkout,
checks every frozen digest/size, and publishes ten profiles plus one complete
inventory. It fetches nothing, copies no source data and runs no evaluation.
A missing, changed or oversized source prevents publication of a complete new
inventory. Existing completed inventories remain content-addressed evidence of
their original inputs; failed later invocations do not erase them.

The pinned source snapshot produces this matrix. Contextual files and separately
