stored variants can share the same executions; these rows must not be added as
independent projects. Execution groups retain `Variant` when present, whereas
logical builds count `BuildId` among rows with complete group identity.

| Registered artifact | Raw rows | Logical builds | Execution groups | Repeated identity rows | Conflicting identities | Failed rows | Raw Duration median |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Druid | 308998 | 168 | 168 | 0 | 0 | 237 | 0.002 |
| Druid contextual | 308998 | 168 | 168 | 0 | 0 | 237 | 0.002 |
| Retrofit | 71238 | 2711 | 2711 | 0 | 0 | 161 | 0.196 |
| Retrofit contextual | 71238 | 2711 | 2711 | 0 | 0 | 161 | 0.196 |
| Dune Debian 10 | 119316 | 1029 | 1029 | 4433 | 3237 | 1417 | 0.07 |
| Dune Ubuntu 20.04 | 44052 | 367 | 367 | 1408 | 1031 | 532 | 0.09 |
| Dune Debian 11 | 35140 | 290 | 290 | 1291 | 886 | 193 | 0.03 |
| Dune total | 229213 | 2186 | 2186 | 6689 | 4858 | 3094 | 0.3 |
| Dune variants | 198508 | 1036 | 1686 | 7132 | 5154 | 2142 | 0.07 |
| Synthetic example | 29 | 5 | 5 | 0 | 0 | 14 | 0.134 |

Raw `Duration` medians have **unverified source units**, not seconds. They are not
comparable across sources and cannot be used to infer runner work, parallel wall
time or savings. Failed rows use only the explicitly declared binary failing-test
mapping with exact native-type comparisons, without rounding decimal labels to
binary64; they are not unique faults. Repeated identity rows count rows beyond
the first complete declared observation key. A conflicting identity has multiple
`(Duration, Verdict)` pairs. These are integrity findings, not deduplicated or
resolved outcomes. Different context values alone are outside that conflict test.

Every profile includes all source column names/null counts, raw duration finite,
null, nonfinite, negative and zero counts, min/median/p95/max, raw verdict categories,
missing identity/group counts, and the distribution of raw rows per execution
group. The latter includes duplicates and is not a count of distinct runnable
tests. Quantiles use the inverse empirical CDF `ceil(p*n)-1`, without interpolation,
over finite binary64 values. Quantile ranks use integer arithmetic; signed zeros
normalize to positive zero in statistical projections while source bytes/digests
remain unchanged. All-null/nonfinite or empty distributions have null
quantiles and unavailable measurements; observed zero stays zero. Negative raw
numbers remain visible and do not certify valid physical execution durations.
A declared duration unit/meaning is retained when supplied; it is never guessed.

Chronology is explicitly **not evaluated** by this recipe. `LastRun`, numeric
`BuildId`, file order and repeated seeds cannot establish event order, UTC,
feature/outcome availability, time span, adjacent-build churn, flakiness, retries
or independent observations. These facts and provider/language axes remain
unverified where their original cards lack evidence. All **seven regimes remain
uncovered**; profiles cannot promote a source or weaken that diversity matrix.

This complete library example uses the same exact local synthetic file as the CLI:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from coleman.artifacts import ArtifactWriter
from coleman.corpus import (
    CorpusProfileInventory, NativeSourceProfile, load_registry,
    profile_native_source, publish_profile_inventory, publish_source_profile,
)

registry = load_registry()
card = registry.card("native-example-e970afe1686d7fe6")
profile = profile_native_source(card, Path("source.parquet"))
assert profile.rows == 29 and profile.logical_builds == 5
assert profile.raw_duration.zero_count == 3
assert profile.duration_median.unit == "source-unit-unverified"
assert profile.card == card  # No admission metadata is rewritten.
writer = ArtifactWriter("library-profiles")
path = publish_source_profile(profile, writer)
assert NativeSourceProfile.from_json(path.read_bytes()) == profile
inventory = CorpusProfileInventory(
    schema_version=1, registry=registry, profiles=(profile, profile),
    uncovered_required_regimes=registry.required_regimes,
)
assert len(inventory.profiles) == 1  # Identical retries are idempotent.
assert len(inventory.uncovered_required_regimes) == 7
publish_profile_inventory(inventory, writer)
```

The default ceiling is 16 MiB compressed input, two million rows, 64 columns and
256 MiB declared uncompressed row-group bytes; tighter manifest bounds also apply.
One bounded byte snapshot is hashed before decoding. Footer limits precede native
Parquet decoding, but are not measured peak-memory guarantees or a sandbox for
malicious codecs. Inputs are explicit trusted local files. Source URI strings
never trigger downloads or dynamic imports. Numeric summaries are descriptive
producer attestations: reading validates conservation, membership, sign counts
against inverse-CDF quantile ranks, equality at shared ranks, and integral
group-count quantiles consistent with the total rows. Nonempty complete group
rows require logical builds and execution groups. Key-column null counts bound
missing identities/groups, and
duplicates require original identities covering the known build/group grain.
Observed source-row/byte declarations must agree with the profile; the declared
row/source-byte resource ceilings also apply on reads. Without `Variant`, logical
builds and execution groups are equal. Missing group/observation identities retain
their subset relationships and extra-column null bounds. Reproducing the
producer's observations still requires the matching source and recipe.

New `NativeSourceProfile` and `CorpusProfileInventory` schema-v1 artifacts use
`corpus-profiles/` and `corpus-profile-inventories/`; native manifests discover both.
Missing, duplicate-key, future or unknown versions fail closed. There is no implicit
migration from old native artifacts/cards into profile evidence. Recompute from
reviewed source bytes and preserve the old artifact alongside the new family.
Identical publication and interrupted retry reuse existing immutable artifacts;
a completed profile is published only after its complete source scan. Profiling
has no incremental learning state and needs no second checkpoint store.

## Independent known answers

The serial source has t1=1 s/pass, t2=2 s/fail, t3=4 s/fail, base order t1/t2/t3.
Every excluded known failing test stays in the denominator.

| Budget | Selected | Failing-test recall | NAPFD | APFDc | First failure | Runner work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 runner-s | t1, t2 | 1/2 | 1/4 | 5/14 | 3 elapsed-s | 3 runner-s |
| 7 runner-s | t1, t2, t3 | 1 | 1/3 (full-suite APFD) | 1/2 | 3 elapsed-s | 7 runner-s |

APFDc here names the native **full-universe cost** convention, including excluded
failures and full-suite duration. It is a normalized ordering/selection measure,
not financial cost. It cannot be substituted for an unrelated selected-only cost
formula. No unique-fault recall is inferred from binary test verdicts.

The parallel fixture dispatches all three tests at zero on three distinct workers:
**7 runner-seconds, 4 elapsed-seconds, first failure at 2 seconds**. No serial
APFD/APFDc value is inferred for that schedule. Queue, shared setup and overhead
are not modeled or claimed saved.

Hand-declared source answers are checked against separate exact `Fraction`/tick
references, then the real native `NAPFDVerdictMetric` or existing event replay is
checked against those answers. The exact oracle imports no production metric or
scheduler. Its scope is at most 16 complete binary tests. The native fixture
projection uses integer seconds <=1,000,000 to preserve exact input costs in
Float32/Float64; this is a fixture restriction, not a generic unit conversion.
Actual scalar checking declares binary64 absolute tolerance `1e-12`, with zero
relative tolerance. Exact rational answers remain authoritative in the source.

Zero is real. No failure detected gives null/right-censored time; a failure at
time zero remains 0/detected. No failing tests makes recall/ranking ratios
inapplicable, without rewriting native legacy default rows. Unknown/timeout
outcomes cannot enter the complete-binary oracle. A zero-work failing serial suite
is explicitly unsupported by the legacy native APFDc checker, rather than receiving
a fabricated finite score. Nonfinite quantities/ratios and incompatible units fail.
Rational text has <=128 characters, no exponent, and numerator/denominator <=256
bits; decimal precision/scale are bounded to 64 before conversion, preventing tiny
exponent strings from triggering unbounded integer allocation.

## Complete library workflow

```python
from pathlib import Path

from coleman.artifacts import ArtifactWriter
from coleman.corpus import (
    CorpusFixtureReport, fixture_readiness, load_registry,
    publish_fixture_report, publish_fixture_readiness, validate_bundled_source,
)

registry = load_registry()
reports = tuple(
    validate_bundled_source(source_id, registry)
    for source_id in ("ci-serial-boundary-v1", "ci-parallel-occupancy-v1")
)
writer = ArtifactWriter("corpus-library-artifacts")
for report in reports:
    path = publish_fixture_report(report, writer)
    assert CorpusFixtureReport.from_json(path.read_bytes()) == report
readiness = fixture_readiness(registry, reports)
assert len(readiness.validated_fixture_sources) == 2
assert len(readiness.fixture_dependence_groups) == 1
assert len(readiness.uncovered_required_regimes) == 7
assert readiness.evidence_status == "insufficient_diversity"
publish_fixture_readiness(readiness, writer)
```

Readiness artifacts embed the frozen registry and verified fixture reports. Reads
and publication rederive registered/blocked source IDs, validated sources and
actual dependence-group identities from that evidence. A fabricated summary cannot
turn the two related fixtures into independent groups. Reordered identical retries
canonicalize to the same identity; conflicting reports for one source fail.

To author a derived owned fixture without touching the runner, obtain its typed
`CIReferenceFixture`, change its explicit fixture identity/cases, serialize with
`fixture_bytes()`, and create a new reviewed `CorpusManifest`. Update the source
URI/version/SHA-256/byte count, intended budgets/metrics and actual conversion
counts. Supply data-specific license evidence; keep the history constructed and
related dependence group intact. Call `validate_fixture_source(manifest, payload)`
before publishing. A changed reference, swapped verdict mapping, false timestamp
field, unsupported metric, broken row conservation or mismatched source fails.
A real provider needs a separately implemented/verified adapter; marking it
“implemented” in JSON cannot make the fixture-only validator execute it.

## Real native execution and artifact recovery

Copy [`ci.py`](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/v4.4.0/examples/corpus-foundation/ci.py)
and run `python ci.py native-output` from the installed 4.4 wheel or a source build. It uses
`api.run()` with native Random/RNFail and a full seven-second budget, verifies each
actual native ranking's NAPFD/APFDc against the independent oracle, and publishes
both source checks plus the insufficient-diversity inventory through existing
artifacts/manifests. Two explicitly constructed copies exercise the runner's
initial shuffle and next-build path; neither real CI history nor independence is
claimed. The example requires a fresh output directory for each complete native
invocation and rejects an existing directory before writing, including pre-existing
symlinked input/native descendants. Direct native runs retain their existing append
behavior. The 4.4 example sets a checkpoint interval of one build and reopens the
same run before validating that exactly two native rows remain. It profiles the
exact constructed native input, preserving fixture lineage, declared seconds and
the constructed-history label, then publishes both new artifact families. Native
learning checkpoints remain the runner's responsibility; this adds no second runner/checkpoint store.

Corpus validation/readiness publication is deterministic and idempotent for the
same input. Concurrent identical retries share the same content address. Existing
`ArtifactWriter` hard-link/fsync publication prevents partial completed JSON;
conflicts and I/O failures propagate. The same existing local filesystem and
power-loss limits apply. Native manifests discover these corpus artifacts and
pilot reports; no source archive or large generated experiment result is committed.

Unknown/future/missing schema versions, duplicate JSON keys and incompatible
protocols fail closed. Unverified extra source-revision claims in fixture
observations are rejected on reads and publication. Older native artifacts keep
their existing readers and meanings; there is no automatic migration. The new fixture JSON format requires
canonical UTF-8 JSON plus one newline and a hard 128 KiB cap, independent of a
larger future-source metadata limit.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[Versioned source manifest and data card] --> G[Terms units identity availability gate]
  B[Bounded source bytes and SHA-256] --> G
  G --> F[Typed tiny synthetic fixture]
  F --> O[Independent exact references]
  F --> N[Existing native metric or event replay]
  O --> V[Verified versioned fixture evidence]
  N --> V
  V --> A[Existing immutable artifacts and native manifest]
  M --> P[Bounded local Parquet description]
  B --> P
  P --> D[Source-bound profile and diversity inventory]
  D --> A
  D --> R
  M --> R[Visible blocked sources and missing diversity cells]
  V --> R
```


The next [controlled fault observation adapter](controlled-faults.md) retains
same-test buggy/fixed comparisons, exact elapsed-counter units and negative or
inconclusive outcomes. It verifies producer bytes through the existing source
cache and publishes through the same artifact writer. It does not grant source
admission or convert collection clocks into historical CI chronology. Direct
upstream Java/Python reproductions are documented separately from the owned
synthetic installed example; required diversity cells remain uncovered.



### FILE: docs/code-cost.md

# Code Cost Evaluation

Coleman treats code cost as a **multi-dimensional scorecard**, not a
single number.  This guide explains the tooling and commands available for
evaluating four complementary cost dimensions.

## Dimensions

| Dimension | What it measures | Primary tools |
|-----------|-----------------|---------------|
| **Structural cost** | Maintainability, complexity, and change risk | Radon, Xenon, Wily |
| **Runtime cost** | CPU time, execution hotspots, and memory pressure | Scalene, py-spy |
| **Energy cost** | Estimated energy or carbon impact | CodeCarbon, pyRAPL |
| **Operational cost proxy** | Basis for translating hotspots into infrastructure effort | All of the above |

---

## Quick start

Install all cost evaluation tools together with the rest of the dev
dependencies:

```bash
uv sync --extra dev
```

---

## 1 — Structural cost

### Cyclomatic complexity (Radon CC)

```bash
make cost-complexity
# or
uv run radon cc -s -a coleman/
```

**Example output:**

```text
coleman/runner.py
    F 175:0 get_scenario_provider - C (12)
    F 420:0 run_experiment - B (10)
    F 145:0 create_agents - B (6)
    ...
coleman/bandit.py
    M 110:4 Bandit.add_arms - B (8)
    C 47:0 Bandit - A (3)
    ...

Average complexity: A (2.1)
```

Each entry shows `<type> <line>:<col> <name> - <grade> (<score>)`.  The type
prefix is `M` (method), `C` (class), or `F` (function).  Grades map to
cyclomatic complexity scores: **A** (1–5 — excellent), **B** (6–10 — moderate),
**C** (11–15 — high), **D–F** (≥16 — critical).  The CI gate (Xenon) rejects
anything worse than **C** for a single block.

### Maintainability index (Radon MI)

```bash
make cost-maintainability
# or
uv run radon mi -s coleman/
```

**Example output (all modules pass):**

```text
✅ All modules meet MI ≥ 20
```

The Maintainability Index (MI) is a composite score (0–100) combining
Halstead volume, cyclomatic complexity, and lines of code.  Scores ≥ 20
are considered maintainable; scores below 20 indicate code that is
harder to understand and modify.  The CI gate fails if any module drops
below this threshold.

**Example output (failure case):**

```text
❌ Modules below maintainability threshold (MI < 20):
coleman/legacy.py - C (14.32)
```

### Raw metrics (Radon raw)

```bash
make cost-raw
# or
uv run radon raw coleman/
```

**Example output:**

```text
coleman/runner.py
    LOC: 524
    LLOC: 202
    SLOC: 290
    Comments: 5
    Single comments: 10
    Multi: 143
    Blank: 81
    - Comment Stats
        (C % L): 1%
        (C % S): 2%
        (C + M % L): 28%
```

Key metrics: **LOC** (total lines), **SLOC** (source lines, excluding blanks
and comments), **LLOC** (logical lines — statement count), and **Comment
Stats** showing the ratio of inline comments to code.  Low `C % S` (comments
as a share of source) may indicate under-documented code.

### Xenon complexity gate

Xenon wraps Radon and returns a non-zero exit code when complexity
thresholds are exceeded.  This is the first CI guardrail:

```bash
make cost-xenon
# or
uv run xenon --max-absolute C --max-modules B --max-average A coleman/
```

**Example output (all thresholds met):**

```text
# Exits silently with code 0 — all modules are within threshold
```

**Example output (threshold exceeded):**

```text
/path/to/file.py has a grade of D
```

Xenon exits with a non-zero code when any threshold is breached, which
causes CI to fail.  No output on success (exit code 0).

**Current CI thresholds:**

| Parameter | Threshold | Meaning |
|-----------|-----------|---------|
| `--max-absolute` | **C** | No single block worse than C |
| `--max-modules` | **B** | No module average worse than B |
| `--max-average` | **A** | Project-wide average must be A |

!!! note "Target thresholds"
    The long-term target is `--max-absolute B --max-modules A --max-average A`.
    Current thresholds are relaxed to match the existing codebase and should
    be tightened as complexity hotspots are refactored.

### Run all structural checks at once

```bash
make cost-structural
```

### Trend analysis with Wily

[Wily](https://wily.readthedocs.io/) tracks complexity metrics across
Git history.  It is included as a dev dependency:

```bash
make cost-wily
# custom file:
make cost-wily-file WILY_FILE=coleman/bandit.py

# or individually:
uv run wily build coleman
uv run wily index
uv run wily report coleman/runner.py
uv run wily diff coleman/runner.py -r HEAD^1
```

!!! note
    `wily` with the `git` archiver requires a clean repository. The Makefile
    targets auto-detect a dirty worktree and switch to the `filesystem`
    archiver so reports still work without forcing commit/stash.

**Example output:**

```text
Found 50 revisions from 'git' archiver.
Running operators - raw,cyclomatic,maintainability,halstead
Processing |################################| 200/200
Completed building wily history.

-----------History for coleman/runner.py-----------
╒════════════╤═══════════╤════════╤══════════╤══════╤══════════╕
│ Revision   │ Author    │ Date   │ Lines    │ CC   │ MI       │
╞════════════╪═══════════╪════════╪══════════╪══════╪══════════╡
│ abc1234    │ developer │ 2026-… │ 524      │ 10.2 │ 68.4     │
│ def5678    │ developer │ 2026-… │ 510      │  9.8 │ 69.1     │
╘════════════╧═══════════╧════════╧══════════╧══════╧══════════╛
```

Each row shows how **Lines of Code**, **Cyclomatic Complexity (CC)**, and
**Maintainability Index (MI)** evolved per commit.  Rising CC or falling MI
across revisions signals growing technical debt that should be addressed
before it compounds.

---

## 2 — Runtime cost

### Scalene (CPU + memory profiling)

[Scalene](https://github.com/plasma-umass/scalene) profiles CPU time,
memory allocation, and copy volume line-by-line:

```bash
make cost-profile-scalene
# or
uv run scalene run coleman/cli.py --- --help
```

Replace `--help` with a real workload for meaningful results.  For
example, profile an actual experiment run:

```bash
uv run scalene run coleman/cli.py --- run --config run.yaml
```

!!! note
    For profiling runs with Scalene, prefer sequential execution.
    Multiprocessing and heavy concurrency can produce incomplete attribution
    (for example, what each thread executed) and, on Python 3.14, may trigger
    intermittent spawn-pool serialization errors.

    Use this in your run config:

    ```yaml
    execution:
      parallel_pool_size: 4
      force_sequential_under_scalene: true
    ```
    uv run wily build coleman
    uv run wily index
    uv run wily report coleman/runner.py
    uv run wily diff coleman/runner.py -r HEAD^1
[py-spy](https://github.com/benfred/py-spy) is a sampling profiler that
attaches to a running process with minimal overhead:

```bash
make cost-profile-pyspy
# or
uv python install 3.13
uv venv .venv-pyspy --python 3.13
uv pip install --python .venv-pyspy/bin/python duckdb numpy polars pyarrow scipy scikit-posthocs "pydantic>=2.12.5" "pyyaml>=6.0.3"
PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/py-spy record --rate 20 --subprocesses -o profile.svg -- .venv-pyspy/bin/python -m coleman.cli run --config run.yaml
```

!!! note
    `py-spy` may require elevated privileges (`sudo`) on some systems.
    With Python 3.14 standalone runtimes, `py-spy` may fail with
    "Failed to find python version from target process".
    The workflow above uses a dedicated Python 3.13 profiling venv,
    while your main project environment can remain on Python 3.14.
    For this workload, `--rate 20` avoids severe sampler lag and
    `--subprocesses` captures worker processes spawned by the experiment runner.
    Some `py-spy` runs may still report a teardown error after writing
    `profile.svg`; when the flamegraph is written successfully, the generated
    profile can still be used.

    Prefer `py-spy record` with a real workload. Commands like `--help`
    end too quickly and can fail before samples are collected.
    If you want a live view instead of a saved report, run:

    ```bash
    PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/py-spy top --rate 20 --subprocesses -- .venv-pyspy/bin/python -m coleman.cli run --config run.yaml
    ```

---

## 3 — Energy cost

### CodeCarbon

[CodeCarbon](https://mlco2.github.io/codecarbon/) estimates the carbon
emissions of compute workloads.  A minimal example lives at
`scripts/measure_energy.py`:

```bash
make cost-energy
# or
uv run python scripts/measure_energy.py
```

**Example output:**

```text
[codecarbon INFO] [setup] RAM Tracking...
[codecarbon INFO] [setup] CPU Tracking...
[codecarbon INFO] CPU Model on constant consumption mode: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor
[codecarbon INFO] [setup] GPU Tracking...
[codecarbon INFO] No GPU found.
[codecarbon INFO] The below tracking methods have been set up:
                RAM Tracking Method: RAM power estimation model
                CPU Tracking Method: cpu_load
                GPU Tracking Method: Unspecified
[codecarbon INFO] >> Tracker's metadata:
[codecarbon INFO]   Platform system: Linux-6.8.0-x86_64
[codecarbon INFO]   Python version: 3.12.x
[codecarbon INFO]   Available RAM : 7.758 GB
[codecarbon INFO]   CPU count: 2 thread(s) in 1 physical CPU(s)
[codecarbon INFO]   CPU model: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor
[codecarbon INFO] Emissions data will be saved to emissions.csv
Estimated emissions (kg CO2eq): 0.000012
```

CodeCarbon logs setup details then prints the estimated CO₂-equivalent
emissions after the workload finishes.  Results are also saved to
`emissions.csv` for tracking over time.  On cloud environments (AWS,
Azure, GCP) CodeCarbon will attempt to use region-specific electricity
carbon intensity; when unavailable it falls back to a country average.

You can adapt the script to wrap any representative workload:

```python
from codecarbon import EmissionsTracker

tracker = EmissionsTracker()
tracker.start()
# ... your workload here ...
emissions = tracker.stop()
print(f"Estimated emissions (kg CO2eq): {emissions}")
```

### pyRAPL (Intel hardware only)

[pyRAPL](https://github.com/powerapi-ng/pyRAPL) reads Intel RAPL
counters for direct energy measurement.  It is included as a dev
dependency but only works on supported Intel hardware:

```python
import pyRAPL

pyRAPL.setup()
meter = pyRAPL.Measurement("my_workload")
meter.begin()
# ... your workload here ...
meter.end()
meter.result.export(pyRAPL.outputs.CSVOutput("energy_results.csv"))
```

!!! warning "Platform and Python version limitation"
    pyRAPL requires an Intel CPU with RAPL support **and** read access to
    `/sys/class/powercap/intel-rapl/`.  It does not work on AMD, ARM, or
    virtualised environments without RAPL passthrough.  Additionally, pyRAPL
    is not compatible with Python 3.14 (invalid escape sequences + missing
    `pymongo` dependency cause import errors on startup).  Use CodeCarbon
    (via `make cost-energy`) as the portable fallback on all platforms.

---

## 4 — CI integration

The GitHub Actions workflow **Code Cost — Structural checks**
(`.github/workflows/code-cost.yml`) runs automatically on every pull
request and enforces two gates:

1. **Xenon complexity gate** — fails when cyclomatic complexity exceeds
   the configured thresholds (see above).
2. **Radon maintainability index gate** — fails when any module scores
   below A (MI < 20).

If either gate fails, the PR cannot be merged until the structural
cost is addressed.

Radon cyclomatic complexity is also reported (blocks with rank C or
worse are highlighted) but does not fail the build — Xenon already
covers this dimension.

The heavier tools (Scalene, py-spy, CodeCarbon, pyRAPL) are intended
for **local or manual use** and are not part of the CI pipeline.

---

## Representative workloads

| Purpose | Command |
|---------|---------|
| Structural analysis | `make cost-structural` |
| Raw metrics | `make cost-raw` |
| Trend analysis | `make cost-wily` |
| Runtime profiling (Scalene) | `make cost-profile-scalene` |
| Runtime profiling (py-spy) | `make cost-profile-pyspy` |
| Energy estimation | `make cost-energy` |

For more realistic profiling, replace `--help` with an actual experiment
configuration:

```bash
uv run scalene run coleman/cli.py --- run --config run.yaml
```

---

## Risks and constraints

- Complexity does **not** directly equal energy use.
- Energy must be measured from **runtime execution**, not inferred
  purely from structure.
- Profiling quality depends on how realistic the workload is.
- `pyRAPL` is hardware-dependent and should stay optional.
- Over-enforcement too early may create friction; thresholds should be
  tuned after first real runs.



### FILE: docs/configuration.md

# Configuration

Coleman uses **YAML configuration files** with typed
[Pydantic v2](https://docs.pydantic.dev/) models for validation.  Configs
are loaded via `load_spec()` (library) or `coleman --config` (CLI).

For `coleman sweep`, the same YAML file may also include a top-level
`sweep` section. This section is used only by sweep commands.

## Configuration file format

A configuration file is a YAML document whose top-level keys map directly
to the sections of `RunSpec`:

```yaml
# my-experiment.yaml

execution:
  parallel_pool_size: 4
  independent_executions: 30
  seed: 42                     # optional — deterministic RNG seed
  verbose: false
  force_sequential_under_scalene: true

experiment:
  budget:
    mode: ratio
    values: [0.1, 0.5, 0.8]
  datasets_dir: examples
  datasets:
    - alibaba@druid
  experiment_dir: results/experiments/
  rewards:
    - RNFail
    - TimeRank
  policies:
    - UCB
    - FRRMAB
    - LinUCB

# Note: the list above is an example, not an exhaustive list of available policies.
# See the policy API reference for the complete set.

algorithm:
  ucb:
    rnfail:
      c: 0.5
  frrmab:
    window_sizes: [50, 100, 200]
  linucb:
    rnfail:
      alpha: 0.5

hcs_configuration:
  wts_strategy: false

contextual_information:
  config:
    previous_build: [Duration, NumRan, NumErrors]
  feature_group:
    feature_group_name: time_execution
    feature_group_values: [Duration, NumErrors]

results:
  enabled: true
  sink: parquet               # "parquet" (default), "duckdb" or "clickhouse"
  out_dir: ./runs
  batch_size: 1000
  top_k_prioritization: 0    # 0 = hash only
  manifest_enabled: false    # true = write manifest.json under each run_id
  duckdb:
    file_count: 1
    base_name: results
    shard_key: execution_id

checkpoint:
  enabled: true
  interval: 50000
  base_dir: checkpoints

telemetry:
  enabled: false
  otlp_endpoint: http://localhost:4318
  service_name: coleman
  export_interval_millis: 5000

hooks:
  fail_fast: false
  plugins:
    - my_project.hooks.ForecastHook

extensions:
  my_domain:
    forecast_selection:
      policy: ThompsonSampling
      reward: Binary

sweep:
  axes:
    - mode: grid
      params:
        algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c: [0.1, 0.3, 0.5]
        execution.parallel_pool_size: [1, 4]
  seeds: [0, 1, 2]
```

## RunSpec schema reference

Every configuration file is validated against `RunSpec`, which composes
the following typed sub-specs:

| Section | Model | Key fields |
|---------|-------|------------|
| `execution` | `ExecutionSpec` | `parallel_pool_size`, `independent_executions`, `seed`, `verbose`, `force_sequential_under_scalene` |
| `experiment` | `ExperimentSpec` | `budget`, `datasets_dir`, `datasets`, `experiment_dir`, `rewards`, `policies` |
| `algorithm` | `AlgorithmSpec` | Free-form nested dict — any algorithm can store its own parameters |
| `hcs_configuration` | `HCSConfigurationSpec` | `wts_strategy` |
| `contextual_information` | `ContextualInformationSpec` | `config` (previous build columns), `feature_group` |
| `results` | `ResultsSpec` | `enabled`, `sink`, `out_dir`, `batch_size`, `top_k_prioritization`, `manifest_enabled`, `duckdb`, `clickhouse` |
| `checkpoint` | `CheckpointSpec` | `enabled`, `interval`, `base_dir` |
| `telemetry` | `TelemetrySpec` | `enabled`, `otlp_endpoint`, `service_name`, `export_interval_millis` |
| `hooks` | `HooksSpec` | `fail_fast`, `plugins` |
| `extensions` | `dict[str, Any]` | namespaced custom config passthrough |

`sweep` is not part of `RunSpec`; it is a CLI-level extension consumed by
`coleman sweep`.

## Parallelism model

Coleman supports two independent parallelism layers:

1. **Intra-run process pool** via `execution.parallel_pool_size`.
  This controls how many worker processes execute one run's
  `independent_executions`.
2. **Inter-spec concurrency** via `coleman sweep --workers` (or API
  `run_many(..., max_workers=...)`). This controls how many different
  resolved specs run at the same time.

When Scalene profiling is active, `force_sequential_under_scalene: true`
forces intra-run pool size to `1` for profiling stability.

## Policy and reward name resolution

`experiment.policies` and `experiment.rewards` are resolved case-insensitively.

Supported wildcard aliases:

1. `*`
2. `all`

Unknown names are ignored with warnings and reported before execution starts.

## Runner hooks and extensions

Coleman supports custom domain workflows via two top-level sections:

1. `extensions`: namespaced custom config passed to hook contexts.
2. `hooks`: lifecycle plugins loaded from dotted paths.

### Hook registration

```yaml
hooks:
  fail_fast: false
  plugins:
    - my_project.hooks.ForecastHook
    - my_project.hooks.audit_hook
```

Supported plugin symbols:

1. Class (instantiated with no arguments).
2. Function with signature `(event_name, context, payload=None)`.

### Lifecycle events

Hook methods are optional. Coleman dispatches these events in order:

1. `on_run_start(context)`
2. `on_dataset_start(context)`
3. `on_execution_start(context)`
4. `on_execution_end(context, execution_result)`
5. `on_dataset_end(context, dataset_result)`
6. `on_run_end(context, run_result)`
7. `on_error(context, error)`

`on_error` is also dispatched when execution startup or environment
construction fails, using the most specific available context.

### Execution contract (sequential vs parallel)

1. `on_run_*` and `on_dataset_*` execute in the coordinator process.
2. `on_execution_*` execute in the worker process context.
3. In sequential mode, worker and coordinator are the same process, but the event contract is unchanged.
4. Hook plugin loading in workers is path-based and process-local to keep multiprocessing pickle-safe.

### Error handling (`fail_fast`)

1. `fail_fast: true` (default): hook exceptions stop execution.
2. `fail_fast: false`: hook exceptions are logged with run/dataset/execution identifiers and execution continues.

### Hook context and payloads

`HookContext` includes stable identifiers and execution metadata:

1. `run_id`
2. `dataset_id`
3. `execution_id`
4. `worker_id`
5. `parallel_mode`
6. `iteration`, `trials`, `budget_mode`, `budget_value`
7. `extensions`

Event payloads:

1. `ExecutionResult(status, duration_seconds)`
2. `DatasetResult(status, executions, duration_seconds)`
3. `RunResult(status, datasets, duration_seconds)`

### Lifecycle diagram

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[on_run_start] --> B[on_dataset_start]
    B --> C[on_execution_start]
    C --> D[runner execution]
    D --> E[on_execution_end]
    E --> F[on_dataset_end]
    F --> G{more datasets?}
    G -- yes --> B
    G -- no --> H[on_run_end]
    D -. exception .-> I[on_error]
```

### Minimal end-to-end config

```yaml
packs:
  - execution/default
  - experiment/alibaba_druid
  - algorithm/defaults
  - reward/rnfail
  - results/parquet

execution:
  independent_executions: 10
  parallel_pool_size: 4

hooks:
  fail_fast: false
  plugins:
    - my_project.hooks.ForecastHook

extensions:
  my_domain:
    forecast_selection:
      policy: ThompsonSampling
      reward: Binary
```

For a complete extension guide including custom Policy/Reward and source-level
Environment/EvaluationMetric customization paths, see
[Extensibility & Parallelism](extensibility.md).

All fields have sensible defaults.  A minimal config only needs to specify
the settings you want to override:

```yaml
# minimal.yaml — everything else uses defaults
experiment:
  datasets: ["alibaba@druid"]
  policies: ["UCB"]
  rewards: ["RNFail"]
```

## Config packs

**Config packs** are small, composable YAML fragments stored under
`packs/<category>/<name>.yaml`.  Reference them with the `packs` key:

```yaml
# experiment-with-packs.yaml
packs:
  - policy/linucb
  - reward/rnfail
  - results/parquet
  - telemetry/off

experiment:
  datasets: ["alibaba@druid"]

execution:
  independent_executions: 30
```

### Resolution order

1. Packs are loaded left-to-right and **deep-merged** (nested dicts are
   merged recursively; scalar values from later packs win).
2. Inline keys from the user config are applied **on top** as final
   overrides.
3. The merged dict is validated against `RunSpec`.

### Shipped packs

| Pack | Category | Description |
|------|----------|-------------|
| `policy/linucb` | Policy | LinUCB with default alpha values |
| `reward/rnfail` | Reward | RNFail reward function |
| `runtime/local` | Runtime | Single-process local execution |
| `results/parquet` | Results | Parquet sink with defaults |
| `results/duckdb` | Results | DuckDB sink with consolidated files |
| `telemetry/off` | Telemetry | Telemetry disabled |

### DuckDB sink configuration

Use `results.sink: duckdb` to write results directly into one or more DuckDB files.

```yaml
results:
  enabled: true
  sink: duckdb
  out_dir: ./runs
  batch_size: 1000
  duckdb:
    file_count: 1         # default: single consolidated .duckdb file
    base_name: results    # output: results.duckdb (or results_000.duckdb, ...)
    shard_key: execution_id
```

`file_count` allows partitioning writes across multiple DuckDB files when desired.

### Creating custom packs

Add a YAML file under `packs/<category>/<name>.yaml` with any subset of
`RunSpec` fields.  For example, a custom policy pack:

```yaml
# packs/policy/my-ucb.yaml
experiment:
  policies:
    - UCB

algorithm:
  ucb:
    rnfail:
      c: 0.3
    timerank:
      c: 0.3
```

## Sweep engine

The **sweep engine** generates multiple `RunSpec` instances from a single
base config by expanding parameter ranges.  Two modes are supported:

### Grid mode (Cartesian product)

Every combination of parameter values is generated:

```python
from coleman.spec import RunSpec, SweepSpec, SweepAxis, expand_sweep

base = RunSpec(experiment={"datasets": ["alibaba@druid"], "policies": ["UCB"]})
sweep_spec = SweepSpec(
    axes=[SweepAxis(mode="grid", params={
        "algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c": [0.1, 0.3, 0.5],
        "execution.parallel_pool_size": [1, 4],
    })],
)
specs = expand_sweep(base, sweep_spec)
# 3 × 2 = 6 specs
```

### Zip mode (paired lists)

Parameter lists are paired element-wise.  All lists **must** have equal
length — a `ValueError` is raised otherwise:

```python
sweep_spec = SweepSpec(
    axes=[SweepAxis(mode="zip", params={
        "algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c": [0.1, 0.3, 0.5],
        "algorithm.ucb.timerank.c": [0.2, 0.4, 0.6],
    })],
)
specs = expand_sweep(base, sweep_spec)
# 3 paired specs
```

### Seed replication

Add `seeds` to replicate each generated spec once per seed.  The seed is
stored on `execution.seed` and affects the `run_id`:

```python
sweep_spec = SweepSpec(
    axes=[SweepAxis(mode="grid", params={"algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c": [0.1, 0.5]})],
    seeds=[0, 1, 2],
)
specs = expand_sweep(base, sweep_spec)
# 2 values × 3 seeds = 6 specs, each with a unique run_id
```

### CLI sweep

```bash
# Uses top-level sweep section from base.yaml (if present)
coleman sweep --config base.yaml --workers 4

# Add/override an extra grid dimension from CLI
coleman sweep --config base.yaml \
    --grid algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c=0.1,0.3,0.5 \
    --grid execution.seed=range(0,20) \
    --workers 4

# Dry-run to preview generated specs
coleman sweep --config base.yaml \
    --grid execution.seed=range(0,5) \
    --dry-run
```

If both YAML `sweep.axes` and CLI `--grid` are provided, Coleman merges
them and computes the Cartesian product across all axes.

If both sources define the same dotted key, the sweep is rejected with a
`ValueError` instead of silently creating duplicate combinations.

## Deterministic run_id

Every `RunSpec` produces a **deterministic 12-character identifier**:

```
run_id = sha256(canonical_json(resolved_spec))[:12]
```

The canonical JSON uses sorted keys and compact separators so that the
**same logical config always yields the same `run_id`**, regardless of
field insertion order.

Artifacts are written to `<out_dir>/<run_id>/`:

```
./runs/
  ddd8bbefa143/
    spec.resolved.json     # fully resolved RunSpec
    provenance.json        # git commit, Python version, uv.lock hash
    results/               # experiment results
    checkpoints/           # crash-recovery state
```

## Provenance

Each run persists provenance metadata alongside results:

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `spec.resolved.json` | The fully resolved `RunSpec` as canonical JSON |
| `provenance.json` | Git commit hash, dirty flag, Python version, `uv.lock` hash |

This enables exact experiment reproduction: given the same `spec.resolved.json`,
the same `run_id` and outputs are produced (within documented constraints such
as floating-point non-determinism across platforms).

## Loading and validating configs

### Library API

```python
from coleman.api import load_spec, save_resolved
from coleman.spec.run_id import compute_run_id

# Load with pack resolution
spec = load_spec("my-experiment.yaml", packs_dir="packs")

# Compute run_id
rid = compute_run_id(spec)
print(f"run_id: {rid}")

# Persist resolved config
save_resolved(spec, f"./runs/{rid}/spec.resolved.json")
```

### CLI

```bash
# Validate a config and print the run_id
coleman validate --config my-experiment.yaml

# Validate and write the resolved spec
coleman validate --config my-experiment.yaml --resolve resolved.json
```



### FILE: docs/controlled-faults.md

# Controlled real-fault observations

Controlled buggy/fixed pairs answer a narrow question: does the same selected
assertion fail against one source revision and pass against the corrected revision
under the declared execution conditions? COLEMAN can retain that evidence,
including unexpected and inconclusive results, without presenting a reconstructed
sequence as historical CI.

This source slice of [#261](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/issues/261)
adds an offline typed observation adapter. It does not complete source admission,
fault diversity, baseline comparisons or the cross-corpus benchmark. The registry's
seven required diversity cells remain uncovered. Source assessments for
[RTPTorrent](rtptorrent.md) and [LRTS](lrts.md) remain separate.

The optional [pinned JUnit3 producer](junit-source-capture.md) now provides a
reproducible public Java source recipe, with bounded execution and raw-role recovery.

## Architecture and trust boundary

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    producer[External subject execution] --> report[Pinned producer observation report]
    inputs[Reviewed source / fixture / harness inputs] --> cache[Existing external source cache]
    report --> cache
    context[Frozen controlled context] --> adapter[Offline typed conversion]
    cache --> adapter
    adapter --> pairs[Expected / unexpected / inconclusive pairs]
    adapter --> writer[Existing immutable artifact writer]
    writer --> manifest[Native run artifact manifest]
```

The core reads and verifies cached bytes. It never starts a subject process,
container, compiler, CLI or network transport. A receipt proves byte correspondence,
not that a producer executed those bytes. Runtime and command descriptions remain
producer attestations. Review and execution of external subjects belong outside
this adapter, with their own component terms and resource limits.

`ControlledContext` freezes project, curated fault label, language, fault origin,
source revisions, fixture revision, dependence group, declared test IDs, input
receipts and runtime conditions. Exactly one buggy source, fixed source, common
test fixture and harness input is required. Dependency inputs are separate. Source
versions must match the declared revisions. Input names and test IDs are unique;
permuting those declarations preserves context identity. Opaque source archives
can be cached as raw packages; this adds no TAR or ZIP64 extraction capability.

`ControlledReport` binds observations to the context fingerprint. Each observation
has a trial ID, role, test ID, explicit outcome, capture instants, nullable diagnostic
digest and monotonic elapsed counter. A non-null diagnostic digest must match a
separate regular member of the validated report package; absent references reject.
Diagnostics are not predecision features. Capture instants are collection clocks, not
historical event or feature availability. No observed CI chronology is inferred.

Execution identity hashes the context and `(trial_id, test_id, role)`, excluding
outcomes and capture values. A retry of the same collection retains its trial ID;
a genuinely new execution gets a new trial ID. Both remain in the same declared
dependence group. These IDs do not establish independent bugs or projects.

## Outcomes, units and missingness

| Buggy observation | Fixed observation | Comparison |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assertion failed | Passed | Expected |
| Passed | Passed | Both pass |
| Assertion failed | Assertion failed | Both fail |
| Passed | Assertion failed | Reversed |
| Missing role, test error, skipped, timeout, cancellation, infrastructure error or unavailable | Any | Inconclusive |

The same inconclusive rule applies when the fixed role has a non-assertion outcome.
Only actual test/trial groups are compared. An empty report has no comparisons;
missing observations are never fabricated. Unexpected and inconclusive results
are valid evidence and remain in the dataset.

Elapsed values are strict nonnegative integer **nanoseconds**, at most `2**63-1`,
with meaning `observed-test-harness-monotonic-elapsed-v1`. Zero is observed. Null
requires `unavailable` or `not_applicable`; an observed null or absent-state zero
rejects. Negative, fractional, boolean, nonfinite and incompatible-unit values
reject. Counter resolution establishes no physical measurement accuracy.

Elapsed harness time includes whatever that harness times. It is not independently
removable runner work, shared setup cost, queue delay or developer-visible CI
latency. It must not be substituted for native scheduling costs. This contract
does not claim that all negative numbers are invalid in other result families;
negative signed measurements remain governed by their existing contracts.

## Installed package workflow

Build and install the working branch's wheel in a separate environment. The
released 4.5 wheel predates this adapter. From the checkout:

```bash
wheel_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/coleman-controlled-wheel.XXXXXX)
uv build --wheel --out-dir "$wheel_dir"
uv venv /tmp/coleman-controlled-installed --python 3.14
uv pip install --python /tmp/coleman-controlled-installed/bin/python "$wheel_dir"/*.whl
mkdir -p /tmp/coleman-controlled-workspace
cp examples/controlled_faults/ci.py /tmp/coleman-controlled-workspace/ci.py
cd /tmp/coleman-controlled-workspace
/tmp/coleman-controlled-installed/bin/python ci.py owned-ci /tmp/coleman-controlled-source-cache
```

The example's pairs are **newly authored synthetic schema fixtures**, not external
real faults or measured executions. Their constructed capture instants and
unavailable elapsed counters are explicit. A separate complete owned serial CI
fixture runs real native Random/RNFail with budget 7 seconds, independently checked
NAPFD/APFDc and a second call through the learning checkpoint. No counter from the
controlled observations is projected into that serial fixture's costs.

Re-running the command preserves the controlled artifact and committed native
result. The output includes the frozen `spec`, converted `dataset`, classifications
(`expected`, `inconclusive`), native directory and explicit insufficient-evidence
status. This demonstrates integration and recovery, not external effectiveness.

The following complete SDK example reopens that specification offline. It runs
from the same external workspace and requires no CLI or MCP imports:

```python
from pathlib import Path

from coleman.artifacts import ArtifactWriter
from coleman.corpus import SourceCache
from coleman.corpus.controlled import convert_controlled_source, publish_controlled_dataset
from coleman.corpus.controlled_contracts import ControlledSpec

cache = SourceCache("/tmp/coleman-controlled-source-cache")
spec = ControlledSpec.from_json(Path("owned-ci/controlled-spec.json").read_bytes())
dataset = convert_controlled_source(spec, cache)
assert [pair.classification for pair in dataset.pairs] == ["expected", "inconclusive"]
path = publish_controlled_dataset(dataset, cache, ArtifactWriter("offline-assessment"))
assert dataset.admission == "not_evaluated"
assert dataset.history == "constructed"
print(path)
```

For another cache location, replace the SDK path with the same location supplied
to `ci.py`. Input/report materializations use the existing reviewed-license,
source-digest, bounded-byte and offline validation contracts. Reports have an
8-MiB ceiling and at most 20,000 physical observations; contexts permit at most
10,000 test IDs and 64 input packages. Every report is checked against the bytes
actually parsed, including EOF size/digest, after cache validation.

## Compatibility, duplication and publication

All new interchange models require integer `schema_version: 1`, reject unknown
fields, and reject missing, legacy and future versions. Existing native results,
source manifests, checkpoints and historical artifacts keep their existing
meaning. No migration or automatic reinterpretation occurs. A future converter
must declare any migration separately and preserve original bytes.

Conversion conserves physical rows: `input_rows = observations + duplicates_excluded`.
Identical role/test/trial repeats are counted and excluded; conflicting repetitions
reject. Output observations are sorted by logical key. Permuting physical report
rows preserves normalized observations but changes the pinned source report bytes
and therefore the complete artifact fingerprint. This is deliberate provenance,
not an input-order-dependent policy comparison.

Publication re-converts the actual cache before writing one
`corpus-controlled/<fingerprint>.json` artifact. Identical concurrent publication
is idempotent through the existing immutable writer. Partial work is never a
completed experiment or learning checkpoint. A failed publication can be retried;
recipe-only content must remain local. Artifact metadata alone does not establish
source integrity, execution truth, scientific admission or independence.

## Primary-source investigation and fresh local evidence

The [Defects4J paper](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~mernst/pubs/bug-database-issta2014.pdf)
and [pinned documentation](https://github.com/rjust/defects4j/tree/8c16da8230843cdc918eaf4ddb449637f02b83c6)
describe isolated buggy/fixed subjects, including reconstructed revisions.
The current documentation requires Java 11 and `America/Los_Angeles`; its current
corpus differs from the paper's original snapshot. Framework MIT terms do not
license every subject or dependency. Broad initialization downloads unrelated
repositories and tools; it was not used for the bounded case below.

The [BugsInPy paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.15481v1) describes selected real
source revisions and common exposing tests, with manual isolation review. A later
[independent reproduction study](https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/~marinov/publications/AguilarETAL23ReproducingBugsInPy.pdf)
demonstrates why declared metadata is insufficient: dependency installation and
runtime selection can prevent paired reproduction, and both-pass/both-fail
outcomes must remain visible. Its corpus snapshot and results are that study's
observations, not COLEMAN measurements.

At BugsInPy revision `11c5f1eea954a42132cfd06bf257766a7963e0fd`, no verified
framework license was found. The existing [upstream license question](https://github.com/soarsmu/BugsInPy/issues/94)
remains unresolved. The paper's license and a subject's license do not clear that
framework. No BugsInPy framework code or data is admitted by this increment.

Two **direct upstream** selected-test pairs were freshly executed on 2026-10-16:

| Subject | Buggy revision | Fixed / common test revision | Observed result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Apache Commons CLI, CLI-13 | `8f46f467a33ace44ccd9f394910940b6c48a3827` | `b0e1b80b6d4a10a9c9f46539bc4c7a3cce55886e` | One assertion failure / one pass; zero errors or skips |
| Black, process-pool fallback | `26c9465a22c732ab1e17b0dec578fa3432e9b558` | `c0a7582e3d4cc8bec3b7f5a6c52b36880dcb57d7` | One assertion failure / one pass; zero errors or skips |

Commons CLI used the [official Apache fixed commit](https://github.com/apache/commons-cli/commit/b0e1b80b6d4a10a9c9f46539bc4c7a3cce55886e),
Git-verified source blobs and its Apache-2.0 LICENSE/NOTICE,
common fixed-revision `BugCLI13Test.testCLI13`, Commons Lang 2.1 and JUnit 3.8.1
(Maven Central bytes and checksums). It compiled directly with Java 11.0.32.1,
linux/arm64 Temurin manifest
`sha256:e4b3ff0f1a427efb2deb02b092ff8316d58573480260720d767d6ecdd69999d8`.
This was a direct source-pair experiment, not the complete Defects4J reconstruction
or a full original-suite reproduction. JUnit's component terms are CPL-1.0;
Commons Lang retains its own Apache terms.

Black used the [official upstream fallback fix](https://github.com/psf/black/commit/c0a7582e3d4cc8bec3b7f5a6c52b36880dcb57d7),
MIT source notices, CPython 3.8.3 and 16 pinned offline wheels.
The common fixed-revision
`BlackTestCase.test_works_in_mono_process_only_environment` explicitly injects
`ProcessPoolExecutor` initialization `OSError`. Both roles use the same declared
derived SCM version label `controlled-upstream-source-v1`. The linux/amd64 image
manifest `sha256:13af390c7ababf48b675e151c354de224f2ae6ec17ee08fe04ad3df8d0736501`
was emulated on an arm64 host. Its elapsed counters are not native performance
measurements. This direct upstream experiment does not resolve BugsInPy licensing.

Both used read-only subject/fixture/harness mounts, execution without network,
non-root UID, bounded memory/CPU/processes and per-case timeout. All source/dependency
bytes and raw observations remain outside Git. No third-party test code or rows
are bundled. These are two selected functional reproductions, not a randomized
sample, full corpus admission, fault-localization matrix, historical CI evidence
or an algorithm comparison. The typed reader does not independently certify this
external execution. A distributable pinned producer recipe, component-by-component
admission dossier and broader fresh test/fault matrix remain necessary before
claiming that the Java/non-Java diversity criteria are satisfied.



### FILE: docs/corpus-materialization.md

# Verified source packages for CI benchmarks

COLEMAN **4.4** adds bounded, restartable acquisition and offline integrity
validation for explicitly licensed, pinned raw files and ZIP packages as part of
[#261](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/issues/261). It reuses the existing
immutable artifact writer and native runner/checkpoints. Install the wheel attached
to [COLEMAN 4.9](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/tag/v4.9.0)
in Python 3.14 or newer; 4.3 and earlier wheels retain their previous commands.

A successful materialization means **source integrity only**. It does not admit a
source for evaluation, verify its CI chronology/units/identity semantics, establish
independent observations or demonstrate policy effectiveness. The ten existing
native registrations retain their admission blockers and all seven minimum
corpus diversity regimes remain uncovered. Real-source adapters/conversion,
row-level exclusions and confirmatory studies remain later phases.

## Complete installed library example

Run outside a Git checkout. This uses one tiny repository-authored MIT fixture,
not a third-party archive. No network or optional MCP SDK is required.

```python
import io
from pathlib import Path

from coleman.artifacts import ArtifactWriter
from coleman.corpus import (
    MaterializationSpec, MaterializationReceipt, PackageMember, SourceCache,
    bundled_fixture_bytes, load_registry, materialize_source,
    publish_materialization, validate_cache_separation, validate_fixture_source, validate_materialization,
)

card = load_registry().card("ci-serial-boundary-v1")
payload = bundled_fixture_bytes(card.manifest.benchmark_id)
member = PackageMember(
    name="fixture.json", sha256=card.manifest.source.sha256,
    size_bytes=card.manifest.source.size_bytes,
)
spec = MaterializationSpec(
    schema_version=1, package_id="owned-ci-raw-source-v1", archive="raw",
    source=card.manifest.source, license=card.manifest.license, members=(member,),
)
cache_root = Path("external-source-cache")
writer = ArtifactWriter("integrity-artifacts")
validate_cache_separation(cache_root, writer.run_root)  # Before any cache/source writes.
cache = SourceCache(cache_root)
receipt = materialize_source(spec, cache, lambda: io.BytesIO(payload))
assert receipt.admission == "not_evaluated"
assert materialize_source(spec, cache) == receipt  # Verified cache hit: no source reader.
validate_materialization(receipt, cache)          # Offline, no repair/network.
checked = validate_fixture_source(card.manifest, cache.member_path(receipt, "fixture.json").read_bytes())
assert len(checked.observations) == 2              # Real native metric/oracle checks.
path = publish_materialization(receipt, cache, writer)
assert MaterializationReceipt.from_json(path.read_bytes()) == receipt
Path("owned-package.json").write_text(spec.to_json() + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
Path("owned-source.json").write_bytes(payload)
```

`SourceArtifact` and `LicenseReview` are the same typed metadata contracts used
by the corpus registry. Acquisition requires a digest, exact source byte count,
version/citation, verified data-specific terms and a permitted/recipe-only rule.
Pending, prohibited or incomplete terms fail before opening a source reader.
Source URIs are descriptive; models and the core never follow them or dynamically
import an adapter. Source availability declarations remain frozen; the receipt
records its separate integrity scope.

## Installed commands

The preceding example creates the metadata/source used by these commands:

```bash
python -m coleman.corpus materialization-schema
python -m coleman.corpus fetch owned-package.json \
  --source owned-source.json --cache external-source-cache --output cli-integrity
python -m coleman.corpus fetch owned-package.json \
  --cache external-source-cache --output cli-integrity
python -m coleman.corpus validate-cache \
  cli-integrity/corpus-materializations/RECEIPT_FINGERPRINT.json --cache external-source-cache
```

Use the actual receipt path returned in `artifact`; the fingerprint filename has
no `sha256:` prefix. `fetch` with no source option is cache-only. An explicit
`--source` is always rechecked, even on a cache hit. A changed local source cannot
hide behind previously cached bytes. `validate-cache` rehashes the complete source,
archive-to-member relation and cached members without downloading or repairing.
Exit 0 means integrity verification, never scientific admission; invalid/unknown
metadata, missing/corrupt bytes or I/O/publication failures return 2.

The cache defaults to `~/.cache/coleman/corpus`. The physical root must be outside
Git worktree markers. Supply an explicit external cache for automation/tests.
Spec/receipt JSON paths must resolve within the current workspace, including
symlink targets; SDK callers retain explicit filesystem control. Cache and
published artifact trees cannot overlap, keeping recipe-only source
bytes out of exported artifacts. CLI and native example check this before cache
creation or acquisition. SDK workflows that acquire and publish must call
`validate_cache_separation(cache_root, output_root)` first; publication also
rechecks the roots. The physical materialization-family path must remain within
its output root; a symlink to a sibling cache or other external tree rejects
before acquisition. Output paths/family parents must remain within
the current workspace. These checks assume trusted private parent directories;
concurrent hostile filesystem mutation is outside the local-file contract.

## Frozen ZIP recipe and provenance

A `MaterializationSpec` schema v1 declares:

- source identity/version/citation/SHA-256 and entity byte count;
- specific terms evidence and redistribution policy;
- `archive="raw"` or `archive="zip"` with the fixed `bounded-source-package-v1` recipe;
- every expected regular member's canonical logical name, SHA-256 and decoded bytes;
- source/member/total decoded bytes, archive-entry and ZIP metadata limits.

Member order canonicalizes by name. Duplicates/conflicts reject. Raw recipes must
name exactly the unchanged source hash/size; they cannot silently convert bytes.
ZIP requires exactly the declared regular files; extra or missing members reject.
Directories are checked but never created as output paths. All decoded member
streams are hashed even on cache hits, so an unrelated cached blob cannot certify
that an archive actually contains it.

Defaults are 64 MiB source entity bytes, 128 MiB per member, 256 MiB total decoded
bytes, 128 archive entries and 1 MiB central-directory metadata. Tighter declared
limits apply. Source/member/total limits can be explicitly raised up to 8 GiB;
streaming publication never loads full large bodies for comparison. Source-plus-
members and one member verification temporary file can coexist; existing cached
packages and interrupted-process temporaries consume additional disk. This is a
per-operation bound, not a global cache eviction/quota or measured peak-memory
promise.

Source digest verification precedes ZIP metadata/decoding. End-record bounds are
checked before central-directory allocation. A streaming fixed-header pass also
checks actual record counts, variable-field lengths and every entry's disk reference
before the standard ZIP reader allocates metadata objects; false footer counts
cannot bypass the entry limit. ZIP64 locator auto-detection is rejected even
when the legacy footer has no sentinel, preventing a second metadata interpretation.
V1 supports single-disk, non-ZIP64
stored/deflated ZIP with required extraction version at most 2.0. The
[PKWARE ZIP specification](https://pkware.cachefly.net/webdocs/casestudies/APPNOTE.TXT)
describes these metadata fields; v1 intentionally supports this bounded subset. Encrypted files, links, devices, unsafe/ambiguous paths,
unsupported compression, duplicate names and inconsistent sizes/CRC reject.
Local names, required versions, flags and compression methods must agree with
central entries. Local CRC/compressed/decoded byte counts must match too, except
that descriptor-mode headers may use zero placeholders. Signed and unsigned
32-bit descriptors must match central counts/CRC and fit before the next record.
All local records pass this preflight before any member decoding. Both extra-field
sections are checked for valid framing and prohibited ZIP64 records; legitimate
inert vendor differences are allowed. Encryption and reserved flags reject.
Stored entries require equal compressed/decoded sizes. Deflated entries, including
empty directories, receive a bounded first decode pass that requires exactly one
complete stream consuming all declared compressed bytes, without unused tails.
Regular members then pass through the standard ZIP CRC and frozen hash checks;
this intentionally decodes deflated regular members twice with 64 KiB chunks.
Logical names are conservative portable ASCII relative names. Materialized bytes
are stored under digest filenames; archive names never become filesystem output
paths. Tar, ZIP64 and additional compression/provider formats require separately
reviewed support before those sources can be used.

The standard library documents [ZIP decompression and interruption pitfalls](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/zipfile.html#decompression-pitfalls).
The core avoids `extract()`/`extractall()` and implicit overwrites.

## Explicit public HTTPS transport

`--public-https URL` opts into the separate HTTPS adapter. V1 permits only
`raw.githubusercontent.com`; provider expansion requires reviewed source-specific
integration. Credentials, query/fragment, non-HTTPS origins, redirects, partial
responses, transfer/content compression and inconsistent Content-Length reject.
The adapter uses verified TLS and no ambient proxy/cookie/authentication state.
The frozen digest remains authoritative, regardless of transport.

For example, the owned serial fixture is available at the pinned public source
revision below; its content is checked against the same package metadata:

```bash
python -m coleman.corpus fetch owned-package.json \
  --public-https https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/fd50ef4bc5c13123217d578dcfcf26dcaa7928d6/coleman/corpus/resources/ci-serial-boundary-v1.json \
  --cache external-source-cache --output cli-integrity
```

The reader factory is lazy on a verified cache hit. A cache miss performs the
explicit public request. Socket inactivity defaults to 15 seconds, with elapsed
checks between reads against a 60-second budget. These are not a hard OS deadline
for DNS/header processing or accounting of packet/TLS/header overhead. Automated
tests use local owned bytes and protocol doubles; they make no network calls.
Python's [HTTP client](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/http.client.html) and
[TLS context](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/ssl.html#ssl.create_default_context)
document the underlying transport behavior.

## Recovery, compatibility and native CI

`SourceCache` creates a versioned small format marker and stores immutable SHA-256
blobs. Every accessed blob is size/hash verified; a filename or receipt alone is
never proof. Identical concurrent publications converge. Changed/corrupt bytes
reject rather than silently repairing or relabeling an old artifact. A refresh
verifies supplied input even when cached source bytes already exist.

The existing `ArtifactWriter` now accepts bounded binary streams while preserving
its UTF-8 immutable API. The complete iterator must finish, including its final
checksum check, before hard-link publication. Normal exception unwinding removes
temporaries. SIGKILL/power loss can leave uncommitted temporary files; they never
count as completed blobs. A retry reuses only verified completed source bytes and
repeats member verification. Source/member files can survive an interruption
without a completed package receipt. No learning checkpoint store is duplicated.

`publish_materialization` verifies actual offline source/member bytes before
publishing a deterministic metadata-only receipt under `corpus-materializations/`.
Native manifests discover that family. A manually constructed/deserialized receipt
is metadata, not an assertion that cached files still exist. Missing/future/legacy
schema versions and unknown cache markers reject; old native/card/profile artifacts
retain their original readers/meaning. No implicit migration or source copying
into public artifacts occurs.

Copy [`ci.py`](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/v4.4.0/examples/corpus-materialization/ci.py)
from the reviewed 4.4 release into a workspace outside the checkout:

```bash
python ci.py owned-ci-output /absolute/path/to/external-source-cache
python ci.py owned-ci-output /absolute/path/to/external-source-cache
```

It builds a tiny owned ZIP containing both existing CI correctness fixtures,
materializes them, verifies their actual JSON/native metrics, and feeds two
constructed copies of the serial fixture through native Random/RNFail. It reopens
the real learning checkpoint, checks both persisted rankings against the independent
oracle, and publishes the integrity and correctness receipts via the native
manifest. Repeated invocation keeps exactly two native rows. The two fixtures
share one dependence group; there is no observed CI history, independent sample
or policy superiority claim. All seven required diversity regimes remain uncovered.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Frozen source and member recipe] --> T[Specific terms pins and byte limits]
  T --> R[Explicit local or optional public HTTPS reader]
  R --> H[Streaming source SHA and size]
  H --> C[External immutable content cache]
  C --> Z[ZIP metadata names types and limits]
  Z --> L[Local and central agreement plus bounded descriptors]
  L --> D[Complete stored or deflated stream]
  D --> M[Streaming member SHA and size]
  M --> C
  C --> V[Offline complete package verification]
  V --> A[Metadata-only versioned receipt]
  A --> N[Existing native artifact manifest]
  V --> G[Separate CI schema units identity and temporal gate]
  G --> E[Existing native runner and learning checkpoints]
```



### FILE: docs/decision-benchmarks.md

# Independent CI decision benchmarks

Check a CI decision extension's mathematics before interpreting runtime or test
prioritization benefit. COLEMAN's benchmark profiles compare the native finite
coverage and scenario-allocation services with small independent exhaustive
references, retain complete mathematical artifacts, and measure the cost of each
service invocation.

These are **synthetic finite-model checks**, not evidence that an adaptive policy
generalizes to real CI projects. Repeated seeds do not become independent CI
observations. Use the [protected evaluation](protected-evaluation.md) contracts
for eligible empirical comparisons and keep their observation/group assumptions
separate from these microbenchmarks.

## Run from an installed package

Build a wheel from a checkout containing this module, then execute outside the
source root with only the base installation:

```sh
COLEMAN_BENCH_WORKSPACE="$(mktemp -d)"
uv build --out-dir "$COLEMAN_BENCH_WORKSPACE/dist"
uv venv "$COLEMAN_BENCH_WORKSPACE/venv" --python 3.14
uv pip install --python "$COLEMAN_BENCH_WORKSPACE/venv/bin/python" \
  "$COLEMAN_BENCH_WORKSPACE/dist"/coleman-*.whl
mkdir "$COLEMAN_BENCH_WORKSPACE/work"
cd "$COLEMAN_BENCH_WORKSPACE/work"
"$COLEMAN_BENCH_WORKSPACE/venv/bin/python" -m coleman.benchmarks \
  --profile correctness --output artifacts
```

The command prints JSON with `status`, `reproducibility`, mathematical identity,
observation/failure counts and the exact artifact path. A successful correctness
profile contains 18 invocations. JSON and Markdown reports appear in
`artifacts/benchmark-reports/`. Neither a model, MCP client, credentials nor a
network service is used during execution; installing packages is a separate step.

Output stays within the chosen current workspace. Profiles are known package
resources, not arbitrary plugin names, paths or provider URLs. Exit codes are
0 for a complete checked protocol, 1 for a failed/interrupted attempt with a
report, and 2 for invalid input or publication failure.

## Complete library workflow

```python
from pathlib import Path

from coleman.artifacts import ArtifactWriter
from coleman.benchmarks import (
    BenchmarkExecution,
    BenchmarkReport,
    collect_environment,
    load_suite,
    publish_benchmark_report,
    run_benchmarks,
)

suite = load_suite("correctness")
# Unknown source metadata remains null. When known, supply the actual 40-character
# source commit and whether the code used to build the package had local changes.
environment = collect_environment(source_commit=None, source_dirty=None)
report = run_benchmarks(suite, execution=BenchmarkExecution(environment=environment))
assert report.status == "complete"
assert report.reproducibility == "verified_repeated_labels"

weighted = report.observations[0]
assert weighted.summary.selected_ids == ("A", "C")
assert weighted.summary.objective == 1
assert weighted.summary.absolute_regret == 0
print(weighted.work_used, weighted.work_unit)
print(weighted.elapsed_ns, weighted.python_peak_bytes)

path = publish_benchmark_report(report, ArtifactWriter(Path.cwd() / "artifacts"))
restored = BenchmarkReport.from_json(path.read_bytes())
assert restored.mathematical_identity == report.mathematical_identity
assert restored.to_json() == report.to_json()
print(restored.markdown())
```

Every observation retains canonical native result JSON, including the complete
problem, units, selected IDs, costs/payoffs, constraints, proof/counter fields,
solver status and bounds. Readers recompute independent references and native
proof/forecast checks. They do not invoke a production selector, but their bounded
reference enumeration and replay overhead are real; reading is more than parsing
an unchecked summary.
Every case's declared reference is checked, including cases with no observation
in interrupted or failed reports.

## Frozen manifests and independent answers

The installed `coleman/benchmarks/cases/` resources are self-contained version-1
manifests. A `BenchmarkSuite` declares its cases, methods, work limits and ordered
seed occurrences. `CoverageCase` and `AllocationCase` embed the actual native
problem contracts and an explicit `ReferenceAnswer` with unit/meaning metadata.
Unknown fields are rejected. Inputs and expected values are validated before a
new solver starts.

The concrete `weighted-overlap-3` case contains:

| Candidate | Modeled duration, seconds | Capabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 2 | x, y |
| B | 2 | y, z |
| C | 1 | z |

Weights are x = 0.5, y = 0.3 and z = 0.2; the budget is 3 seconds. The independent
answer is A,C, cost 3 and union objective 1. Coverage weights are capability
weights, not calibrated failure probabilities. Overlapping outcomes count once.
A duplicate membership/outcome identity is rejected; overlapping coverage across
candidates cannot inflate utility.

The correctness profile also declares:

- signed joint payoffs `[0,0]`, `[2,2]`, `[10,-8]` with equal weights: expected
  payoffs 0, 2, 1 and variances 0, 0, 81;
- all-negative alternatives where unchanged allocation is optimal;
- quadratic target utility evaluated on the distribution: the variable plan's
  mean 3 becomes utility 1.2, so the stable plan's utility 2 wins;
- a deliberately work-limited allocation with a feasible no-action incumbent,
  objective 0 and independent regret 2, without a false optimality claim.

The reference code uses `Fraction` arithmetic and combinations. It consumes
validated input contracts, never production search, objective, forecast or
feasibility helpers. Allocation variance uses direct weighted deviations, separate
from the production second-moment formula. Complete signed outcomes, terminal
balances, gross/net/fee accounting, variance, target shortfall and utility are
checked rather than only an argmax or rounded objective.

All primary comparisons have **zero rational tolerance** (`numeric_tolerance:
"0"`). Finite decimal inputs become exact rational quantities; JSON uses rational
strings. Expected numbers reject binary64/boolean coercion and non-finite values.
No display projection or rounded float establishes a passing mathematical gate.

### Evidence and method classes

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `method_class=exact_search` | Finite enumeration/search that can establish an optimum when its completion conditions hold |
| `method_class=heuristic` | A heuristic procedure; reaching the oracle on one case does not make its method exact |
| `evidence=exact` | A checked full-scope optimum or independently confirmed infeasibility |
| `evidence=bounded` | A feasible result with a checked maximizing upper bound dominating the independent optimum |
| `evidence=heuristic` | A feasible partial result without an admitted optimality bound |
| `evidence=unavailable` | No incumbent; objective/regret remain null rather than fabricated zeros |
| `sampled` | A distinct classification, never silently upgraded to exact; current supported finite adapters produce no sampled claims |

Coverage still requires its native certificate for an optimal claim. A case may
require a declared exact method to complete, in which case an incomplete result
fails that protocol even if its incumbent is valid. Performance cases can permit
bounded completion. Benchmark `status=complete` means every declared invocation
ran and passed its applicable gates; inspect each native solver status/evidence.

Scenario probabilities in these mathematical profiles must be **assumed**. Learned
weights require protected evidence and retain the conservative decision behavior
of the [allocation API](scenario-payoffs.md); they are not converted into an
assumed-model optimum for a benchmark table. No learning reward, ranking,
calibration or inferential confidence claim is created.

## Repetition and metamorphic checks

The profiles declare labels `[11,11,29]`. Current finite solvers use no RNG: labels
identify protocol occurrences, not data observations. The two label-11 runs must
match their **entire canonical mathematical artifacts**, including IDs, proofs,
bounds, forecasts, work counters and statuses. Equal rounded objectives are
insufficient. No repeated label means `reproducibility=untested`, even if distinct
labels happen to return the same objective.

`mathematical_identity` hashes the frozen suite and ordered native mathematical
artifacts. Timing, environment, availability and failed-attempt metadata are
excluded. The complete report's content fingerprint includes them. Re-running a
measurement may produce a new report identity while preserving its mathematical
identity; publishing the same complete report object is idempotent.

CI tests include input-order invariance, unique-optimum candidate relabeling,
budget monotonicity and duplicate coverage. A joint payoff/target shift preserves
variance and shortfall while translating expected utility. Those properties are
applied under their stated assumptions; arbitrary renaming of tied optima or
changing a payoff without its relevant risk target is not claimed invariant.
Deliberately faulty solvers prove that invalid bounds, budget overruns, false
optimal status and order-dependent streams fail the gates.

## Timing, memory and compute budgets

`elapsed_ns` measures elapsed `perf_counter_ns` time around the native service,
including its own validation/result construction. Import/setup, independent
reference checks and report serialization are excluded. `python_peak_bytes` is the
process-wide `tracemalloc` peak during that call, not RSS, total native allocation
or an isolated per-thread measurement. Unrelated background allocations can affect
it. Overlapping benchmark instrumentation is rejected; pre-existing tracing is
never reset or stopped by this API.

`work_used` retains its explicit `work_unit`:

- coverage: candidate examination or branch-node pop, sharing the native counter;
- allocation: attempted whole-action evaluation.

Equal counters are not equal CPU budgets across algorithms. Each case fixes its
native limits, methods and problem before comparison. Correctness protocols require
`deadline_seconds=None` and use deterministic work limits so machine speed cannot
change a mathematical assertion. Runtime and memory are reported observations,
not universal performance thresholds or evidence of algorithm superiority.
Deadline termination is rejected in native adapter results, serialized mathematical
observations and interrupted-attempt histories: it contradicts this deadline-free
protocol, even when a case permits a bounded or heuristic outcome.
A `work_limit` stop must have consumed its declared work cap; stopping below that
cap cannot be reported as exhausted computation.
Completed-observation gates also reject native `cancelled` and `interrupted`
artifacts. Live execution retains them as aborted attempts; replay cannot promote
them into successful observations, even for cases permitting nonexact completion.

Local `adapter=` callables execute as trusted Python code. Bundled execution makes
fresh native service calls. Artifact gates verify supplied mathematics and budget
consistency; measurement authenticity and disclosure of external precomputation
remain responsibilities of custom adapter authors.

The `performance` profile adds a 12-candidate overlap instance under a shared
500-work-unit cap and a 32-action/64-joint-state allocation. Run it explicitly:

```sh
python -m coleman.benchmarks --profile performance --output artifacts
```

The `Decision performance observations` workflow runs on manual dispatch. Its
weekly schedule is disabled unless the repository variable
`ENABLE_DECISION_PERFORMANCE` is explicitly `true`. It builds a noneditable wheel,
runs outside the checkout root and preserves JSON/Markdown evidence, including
failed reports. Ordinary correctness CI has no wall-clock pass/fail threshold.
No calibrated hardware-specific regression threshold is supplied in this version.

### Committed observed comparison

The repository includes a [JSON observation](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/3f306af66e6b45984111c5498d78aadeb9c04098/examples/decision-benchmarks/observations/benchmark-reports/b8c35d14627d94f1c871203e5f9ea25083214dd2f611543f8c3c0dbca85c45a4.json)
