and its [human report](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/3f306af66e6b45984111c5498d78aadeb9c04098/examples/decision-benchmarks/observations/benchmark-reports/b8c35d14627d94f1c871203e5f9ea25083214dd2f611543f8c3c0dbca85c45a4.md).
These are actual measurements from a noneditable base wheel built at
`38f94a9d65fe59605e3309a2c0ef2b45a38134e2`, running outside the checkout.
The self-contained suite fixes the weighted-overlap fixture, both coverage methods,
labels `[11,11,29]`, no deadline and a 100,000-unit per-attempt cap. Both methods
choose A,C with objective 1; greedy uses 6 counter units and branch search 13.
The report records individual nanoseconds and Python peak bytes, rather than an
aggregate winner or inferred confidence interval. Six calls on one synthetic
instance and one environment do not establish a general performance advantage.

To repeat the exact protocol, obtain that JSON artifact from the public repository
and run with the installed package from its containing workspace:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from coleman.artifacts import ArtifactWriter
from coleman.benchmarks import (
    BenchmarkExecution, BenchmarkReport, collect_environment,
    publish_benchmark_report, run_benchmarks,
)

source = next(Path(".").glob("b8c35d14627d94f1c871203e5f9ea25083214dd2f611543f8c3c0dbca85c45a4.json"))
previous = BenchmarkReport.from_json(source.read_bytes())
observed = run_benchmarks(
    previous.suite,
    execution=BenchmarkExecution(environment=collect_environment()),
)
assert observed.mathematical_identity == previous.mathematical_identity
publish_benchmark_report(observed, ArtifactWriter(Path("artifacts")))
```

Supply actual source metadata when known. Unknown metadata stays null; copying
the earlier environment onto a new execution would falsely attribute measurements.
The versioned golden test fixtures use explicitly synthetic metadata and zero
placeholder timings; they are serialization fixtures, separate from this measured
observation.

## Interruptions, failed attempts and checkpoints

```python
from coleman.benchmarks import (
    BenchmarkCheckpoint, BenchmarkExecution, collect_environment, load_suite,
    run_benchmarks,
)
from coleman.checkpoint import LocalCheckpointStore
from coleman.checkpoint.state import CheckpointPayload

suite = load_suite()
environment = collect_environment()
partial = run_benchmarks(
    suite, execution=BenchmarkExecution(environment=environment, max_new_invocations=1)
)
store = LocalCheckpointStore("checkpoints")
store.save(CheckpointPayload(
    run_id="ci-benchmark-example", step=1,
    extra={"benchmark_v1": partial.checkpoint().to_json()},
))
saved = store.load("ci-benchmark-example", 0)
if saved is None:
    raise RuntimeError("Expected a saved benchmark checkpoint")
checkpoint = BenchmarkCheckpoint.from_json(saved.extra["benchmark_v1"])
resumed = run_benchmarks(
    suite, checkpoint=checkpoint, execution=BenchmarkExecution(environment=environment)
)
assert resumed.status == "complete"
assert resumed.observations[0] == partial.observations[0]
```

Store JSON in the existing native checkpoint payload; no second checkpoint system
is introduced. The local store uses trusted local pickle state. Complete cached
observations are reverified before new work, including zero-work resumes. Source,
protocol or environment changes reject the checkpoint. Cancellation is still
polled when every invocation is cached.

`BenchmarkRunError` retains a typed failed report and the original exception
cause. Interrupted and failed attempts are distinct from successful mathematical
rows. `report.checkpoint()` carries prior failed/aborted attempts forward, so a
later successful resume cannot silently erase their timing, known work or unknown
costs. Instrumentation rejection records zero solver work and unavailable timing;
a solver exception may have unknown work rather than zero. Histories retain
only null work for solver/verification failures; readers reject invented counters
in both reports and checkpoints. Histories also retain
stable attempt indices and explicit aware availability timestamps. Unavailable
future history is rejected before new work. Any known interrupted-work counter
must fit its matched case's declared work budget, both in current reports and
in resumed histories, including zero-work resumes.
Solver, verification and interrupted failures require their measured runtime and
Python peak bytes on replay; only an instrumentation rejection can leave both
measurements unavailable.
Native `cancelled`/`interrupted` attempts retain a required integer work counter,
including known zero. Exception interruptions such as `KeyboardInterrupt` retain
null work because their interrupted call supplied no trustworthy counter.

An operator interrupt during post-solver verification also returns an interrupted
report: the verified prefix remains intact, and the interrupted attempt retains
its measured solver time and memory. The unverified row is not completed evidence.
Resuming its checkpoint retries that slot and preserves the prior attempt history.
Repeated interrupts while constructing or validating the interrupted report itself
can still abort the call; report publication remains an explicit caller action.

A chunk can be persisted after each complete invocation. Process death before that
checkpoint may require repeating an invocation; cached timings are never called
new independent samples. A native interrupted partial search is a recorded aborted
attempt and restarts with the frozen per-attempt budget. Failed/aborted overhead
remains visible and is not a free warm start. Unexpected cancellation-callback
errors propagate; they are not mathematical insufficiency results.

## Persistence, limits and compatibility

Reports use the existing immutable `ArtifactWriter`. Markdown is written first;
complete JSON is written last and is the publication authority. A Markdown-only
interruption is not a completed JSON report. Identical concurrent publication is
idempotent; conflicting bytes are rejected. Existing manifests add a
`benchmark_report` entry without changing native result or scheduling meanings.

Manifest caps are 16 cases, 16 seed occurrences and 128 declared invocations.
References allow at most 12 coverage candidates, 256 outcomes and 4,096 memberships,
or 32 allocation actions and 64 joint scenarios. Failed-attempt histories are
capped at 128; another retry is refused before solver work once exhausted.
Publication defaults to 32 MiB across JSON and Markdown, with a maximum configurable
limit of 64 MiB. Verification/serialization have bounded but repeated overhead;
these caps are not a hard process-isolation or RSS guarantee.

Schema version 1 is required. Missing, future and unknown versions fail closed,
as do duplicate JSON keys. This is the first benchmark format: there is no legacy
benchmark migration to guess. Existing native, domain, coverage, allocation and
protected-evaluation artifacts retain their versions and interpretation. Versioned
golden report/checkpoint fixtures preserve exact identities and producer metadata.

## Real native TCPCI integration

The existing `examples/finite-coverage/ci.py` now independently benchmarks its real
coverage decision before scheduling the second synthetic CI build. It retains
native agents, first-build shuffle, reward, metrics, sinks and extension callbacks.
The actual scheduled prefix must be A,C before the collector publishes the
coverage and benchmark artifacts. The adapter remains specific to this fully
budget-consuming fixture; it does not implement arbitrary subset scheduling.

Run that script with the installed package as documented in
[finite coverage selection](finite-coverage.md). The installed-wheel test runs it
twice outside the checkout, without mocking the principal runner or solver, and
checks both actual schedules and repeated mathematical artifacts. Modeled coverage
objectives stay separate from measured NAPFD/APFDc and learning rewards. A positive,
negative or inconclusive model result is not a policy promotion.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Manifest[Frozen typed CI benchmark suite] --> Runner[Bounded benchmark service]
    Runner --> Native[Existing coverage / allocation services]
    Manifest --> Oracle[Independent tiny rational references]
    Native --> Gates[Feasibility, bounds, full math and repeat gates]
    Oracle --> Gates
    Gates --> Report[Versioned report and failed-attempt history]
    Report --> Writer[Existing immutable ArtifactWriter]
    Report --> Checkpoint[JSON in existing native checkpoint payload]
    Native --> Extension[Existing native CI extension / collector]
    Extension --> CI[Native scheduling, reward, metrics and sinks]
```



### FILE: docs/decisions/001-point-in-time-observations.md

# ADR 001: point-in-time observations and decision signals

Status: accepted in the 4.2 feature line; implements the boundary requested in
[#258](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/issues/258).

## Context

CI outcomes and durations may arrive late or be corrected. Replacing a stored row
would erase what a policy could know at an earlier decision. The protected
`Timestamp`, `TemporalObservation` and `TemporalPlan` contracts already validate
UTC instants, revisions, groups and temporal eligibility. The native runner already
owns lifecycle, processes, result sinks and checkpoints.

## Decision

Add `coleman.observations` as a transport-independent typed boundary. Immutable
revision histories preserve source availability, first local receipt and explicit
predecessors. As-of selection uses only eligible revisions. Source adapter SDKs,
credentials, collection permissions, clock reconciliation and source-specific
identity rules stay in provider-owned packages implementing `ObservationProvider`.
The base package supplies an offline provider for repository-owned CI fixtures.
No dynamic provider import, network fetch, CLI/MCP dependency or new runner exists.

Reuse protected time/split validation and #251 measurements/provenance. Fit a simple
nonnegative quantity mean only on eligible training observations, frozen before
use. Preserve its evidence and explicit rounding; label outputs as estimates or
priority scores, never calibrated probabilities or inference results. Freshness
uses source event age at the decision and remains an explicit policy parameter.

Use `RunnerExtension.build_environment_fn` for the native example's policy and
monitor integration. Emit typed signals and domain sidecars before the existing
checkpoint advances. Reuse `ArtifactWriter` immutable publication and native
manifest discovery. No second state/checkpoint store is introduced.

## Assumptions and consequences

- The initial source is owned, offline, synthetic CI data. It establishes functional
  behavior, not provider completeness, independence, prospective evidence or value.
- Providers attest identities and complete bounded lineages. First receipt remains
  fixed across duplicate deliveries. UTC source/local clocks must be comparable;
  impossible chronology fails. Existing Python datetime semantics have microsecond
  resolution; providers must declare normalization for finer source clocks.
- Complete single-parent lineages allow out-of-order delivery and timestamp ties.
  Missing parents, forks, conflicting duplicates and changed units/identity fail.
  Truncated histories cannot silently become complete histories.
- Selected input fingerprints exclude future values; whole-source artifact hashes
  remain separate. Later evaluation must still apply the complete protected fold
  grouping protocol; fitting a past view cannot inspect future group memberships.
- Generic signal readers validate metadata/chronology, without executing a producer
  by its name/fingerprint. Mean artifacts rederive training estimates; use the
  frozen model's `verify_signal` when consuming its serialized signals.
- Provider scraping/authentication, signal calibration, sophisticated forecasting,
  streaming retention and external deployment remain outside this issue. Base
  dependencies and native orchestration remain sufficient for the installed demo.

The [human guide](../point-in-time-observations.md) defines the actual v1 API,
limits, compatibility, recovery and complete CI examples.



### FILE: docs/dependency-security.md

# Dependency security maintenance

COLEMAN audits the complete committed `uv.lock`, including development,
documentation, notebook, release, telemetry, ClickHouse and MCP extras, plus packages
that only install on another operating system. The base installation remains
independent of optional tools.

The lock file pins distribution versions and hashes. An advisory audit answers
whether those versions have **known reported vulnerabilities** at the time of the
query. A clean result does not prove that software has no undisclosed defects or
that every possible deployment is secure.

## Reproduce the audit

From a checkout with Python 3.14 and uv:

```sh
python scripts/audit_lock.py > /tmp/coleman-audit-requirements.txt
uv sync --frozen --only-group security --no-build --no-install-project
uv run --frozen --no-sync pip-audit \
  --strict --no-deps --disable-pip \
  --requirement /tmp/coleman-audit-requirements.txt \
  --format json --output /tmp/coleman-audit.json
```

The generated pins are **advisory lookup input**, not installation requirements.
The script reads every registry entry rather than filtering for the current
platform. It skips only COLEMAN's root editable entry; an unknown package source
fails with an actionable error instead of escaping the audit. No project
dependency is installed or executed by this lookup. Install from the hashed
`uv.lock` with `uv sync --frozen` as usual.

The `Locked dependency security audit` GitHub workflow runs on dependency PRs,
main dependency updates, weekly and on manual dispatch. It retains the queried
pins and JSON results as workflow artifacts. Known vulnerabilities, advisory
collection failures and unsupported sources fail the job; there is no blanket
ignore list. Advisory services require network access. Unit tests cover the
inventory and fail-closed source handling offline.

## Updating dependencies

1. Inspect open Dependabot PRs and alerts, including aliases and affected version
   ranges. Counts from different advisory services may differ or contain aliases.
2. Update vulnerable transitive packages in the lock. If a direct pin prevents a
   patched transitive version, update the direct package after checking its
   compatibility and release notes.
3. Re-run the complete audit, native CI tests, installed-package examples, strict
   documentation and the repository quality gates. Notebook/documentation/server
   extras need checks too; they are not exempt because the base API is offline.
4. Merge reviewed corrections before closing superseded bump PRs. Confirm GitHub's
   alert state after its dependency graph refreshes. Explain any actual blocker;
   do not dismiss an alert merely to reduce a counter.

## October 2026 maintenance baseline

The pre-update GitHub inventory contained 106 open Dependabot alerts: 2 critical,
58 high, 42 medium and 4 low, all attached to `uv.lock`. The initial pip-audit
export reported 166 vulnerability occurrences in 17 packages; aliases and
platform/extra representations mean this is not a second count of unique GitHub
alerts.

The update refreshes affected registry packages, including GitPython, Pillow,
Starlette, AnyIO, Authlib, Bleach, Cryptography, IDNA, Mistune, MkDocs Material,
nbconvert, PyMdown Extensions, SoupSieve, Tornado, urllib3 and virtualenv. Zensical
and Marimo direct pins also advance so their supported transitive dependency
ranges admit patched versions. Native numerical dependencies are not upgraded
without a compatibility or security reason.

The all-platform lock audit is the authoritative reproducible check for this
maintenance change; its output is attached to the PR and retained in CI. Future
advisories may change the result and require another update.

## Workflow and documentation boundaries

The same review inventories code-scanning findings separately from dependency
advisories. The October baseline additionally contained 33 SonarCloud alerts,
mostly about installation in GitHub workflows, plus a documentation path warning.

CI pins the setup action and uv version, verifies the Linux archive checksum,
installs registry dependencies from the frozen lock with source builds disabled,
and installs the reviewed local project with the locked build backend. This
explicit local editable build is separate from third-party source distribution
builds; it retains normal development imports. Release/build/audit tools are also
locked. CI checks run without silently synchronizing another dependency set.

Linux CI and DevContainers have a wheel-only installation path. On macOS, the
existing Watchdog 6.0.0 documentation dependency has no wheel: local full-extra
setup may need its hash-pinned source build. The Linux preflight must not be
presented as proof of wheel availability on every platform.

The documentation generator refuses symlink sources and output, checks resolved
source containment, reads the checked path, and atomically replaces complete
output. Tests demonstrate that outside files remain untouched and interruption
preserves the previous complete file. This protects normal repository generation;
it is not an isolation boundary against an adversary concurrently rewriting the
filesystem with the process's own permissions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Lock[All locked registry packages] --> Audit[Known advisory gate]
    Sources[Workflow and filesystem findings] --> Review[Verify and fix findings]
    Audit --> Checks[Tests, install, docs and local review]
    Review --> Checks
    Checks --> Merge[Reviewed security correction on main]
    Merge --> Refresh[Refresh GitHub security findings]
```

## Release distribution inventory

With Syft 1.42.3 installed on PATH, the release SBOM catalogs the wheel's
distribution metadata, requires the expected COLEMAN version, and binds the root to the complete wheel's
SHA-256. The package identifier is bound explicitly to this GitHub repository;
inferred PyPI coordinates and guessed CPEs are removed because the PyPI name
belongs to another project. It does not claim that unbundled dependencies are
installed in the wheel.
The complete lock advisory audit above covers those version pins separately.

```sh
python scripts/release_sbom.py
```

The command accepts no arguments: it reads its checkout's package version and
uses the corresponding wheel and SBOM under that checkout's `dist/`.
The helper reads only the fixed METADATA member; it does not extract archive paths
or execute package code. Empty/mismatched inventories fail before publication.
Host file metadata is excluded, so local extraction paths do not become public
components. Tool timestamps/serial numbers remain observations. Output replaces
atomically after validation; a failed tool or interrupted write retains prior bytes.



### FILE: docs/domain-results.md

# Versioned result records for CI intelligence

COLEMAN keeps its existing TCPCI scheduling output, including NAPFD (`fitness`)
and APFDc (`cost`). Extensions can now add **typed, immutable domain records**
without changing those columns or interpreting a learning reward as an outcome.
A negative or inconclusive outcome remains a valid result. These records supply
metadata for future evaluation methods; they do not establish calibrated
probabilities, independent observations, statistical significance or promotion.

## Contract version 1

Import from `coleman.results.domain`. Constructors validate inputs; models are
frozen, measurements are tuples, and all unknown fields are rejected. Use the
validated constructors or `DomainRecord.from_json`, rather than Pydantic's
unchecked `model_construct`/`model_copy(update=...)` APIs. Local sinks revalidate
records at their persistence boundary.

| Field | Meaning and invariant |
|---|---|
| `schema_version` | Required integer `1`; booleans and strings are rejected. |
| `namespace` | Extension-owned identifier; `coleman` and `coleman.*` are reserved. |
| `run_id` | Logical run identity, normally the existing RunSpec run ID. |
| `execution_id` | Logical independent execution; stable across worker placement and retries. |
| `decision_id` | Logical observation bundle; distinguish build, policy, reward and variant. |
| `data_fingerprint` | `sha256:` plus 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters, over canonical input data. |
| `available_at` | Explicitly zoned ISO datetime, normalized to UTC; numeric epoch strings/numbers and naive dates are rejected. |
| `provenance` | Producer/version, resolved spec fingerprint and evaluation-context fingerprint; optional source revision. |
| `measurements` | Nonempty tuple of unique named `Measurement` objects, serialized as a sorted array. |
| `learning_reward` | Optional separate finite signal with output unit and versioned transformation ID. |

Names, units, meanings and producer identifiers are nonempty, case-sensitive
strings. Unit `s` means seconds in the examples; `1` denotes a dimensionless
scale. Custom unit identifiers are allowed. Producers must document their
interpretation through a versioned `meaning`, such as
`full-suite-serial-duration-v1`. There is no implicit unit registry, currency
conversion or metric inference. For a physically nonnegative quantity, declare
`minimum=0.0` in that same unit. Signed raw outcomes have no implicit lower bound.

Each measurement requires `name`, `value`, `unit`, `meaning`, `direction` and
`status`. Direction is `minimize`, `maximize` or `none`. The value field cannot be
omitted, even when it is null. NaN, infinities, numeric strings and booleans are
rejected, including in rewards and declared minima.

| Representation | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `value=0.0, status="observed"` | A measured zero. |
| `value=-2.0, status="observed"` | A valid signed result, unless below a declared minimum. |
| `value=None, status="unknown"` | Outcome/cost is not known. |
| `value=None, status="unavailable"` | Measurement is unavailable under this protocol. |
| `value=None, status="not_applicable"` | This measurement does not apply. |
| Measurement name omitted from bundle | No declaration about that measurement; querying raises `KeyError`. |

Non-observed states require null; observed states require a finite number.
Optional fields omitted at construction remain absent in JSON; an explicitly
supplied optional null stays null. They therefore have different content digests.
Native column names such as `fitness`, `cost` and `rewards` cannot be measurement
names. Use distinct extension names such as `napfd` and `apfdc`, with their own
explicit meaning. Both outputs can coexist; the legacy table is never overwritten.

## Complete installed-package example

Install the package from the reviewed wheel (`pip install path/to/coleman.whl`).
The following can run from any directory. Its credits are synthetic CI runner
accounting units, with no claim of operational savings.

```python
from datetime import UTC, datetime

from coleman.results.domain import (
    DomainRecord, LearningReward, Measurement, ResultProvenance, fingerprint,
)
from coleman.results.duckdb_sink import DuckDBSink

inputs = {"runner_slots": 2, "jobs": ["unit-tests", "integration-tests"]}
record = DomainRecord(
    schema_version=1,
    namespace="ci.runner_allocation",
    run_id="run-example",
    execution_id="execution-1",
    decision_id="decision-7",
    data_fingerprint=fingerprint(inputs),
    available_at=datetime(2026, 1, 2, 12, tzinfo=UTC),
    provenance=ResultProvenance(
        producer="synthetic-ci-allocation", producer_version="1",
        spec_fingerprint=fingerprint({"allocation": inputs}),
        evaluation_fingerprint=fingerprint({"protocol": "synthetic-runner-credit-v1"}),
    ),
    measurements=(
        Measurement(name="duration", value=3.0, unit="s", direction="minimize",
                    meaning="serial-job-duration-v1", status="observed", minimum=0.0),
        Measurement(name="net_value", value=-2.0, unit="credit", direction="maximize",
                    meaning="synthetic-net-runner-credit-v1", status="observed"),
        Measurement(name="unknown_cost", value=None, unit="credit", direction="minimize",
                    meaning="synthetic-runner-cost-v1", status="unknown"),
    ),
    learning_reward=LearningReward(value=0.25, unit="1", transform_id="bounded-v1"),
)
sink = DuckDBSink(out_dir="./ci-results")
try:
    sink.write_domain_record(record)
    sink.flush()
    restored = sink.read_domain_record(
        "run-example", "execution-1", "decision-7", namespace="ci.runner_allocation",
    )
    assert restored == record
    assert restored.measurement("net_value").value == -2.0
    sink.write_domain_record(record)  # identical replay does not duplicate
    assert len(list(sink.domain_records())) == 1
    print(record.to_json())
finally:
    sink.close()
```

Two standalone examples are maintained and tested against a non-editable wheel:

- [Native TCPCI example](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/main/examples/domain-results/tcpci.py)
  generates a tiny synthetic test dataset, uses `run_with_extension`, the native
  environment, Greedy policy, RNFail reward and NAPFD/APFDc evaluation, then
  queries observations and verifies their fingerprint against `spec.resolved.json`.
- [Runner-slot accounting example](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/main/examples/domain-results/allocation.py)
  persists the signed/null acceptance fixture through DuckDB and queries it.
  This accounts for a declared allocation; it does not implement a solver.

Copy the scripts into a directory outside the repository and execute. The
allocation CLI example requires its output to remain within the current working
directory and rejects traversal outside it; the core sink accepts an explicitly
configured output root:

```bash
python tcpci.py ./tcpci-output
python tcpci.py ./tcpci-parallel-output 2 2  # two logical executions, two workers
python allocation.py ./allocation-output
```

The TCPCI example declares outcome availability from its synthetic build calendar,
not execution time. It reconstructs logical execution identity from scenario,
budget and experiment, and decision identity from build, policy, reward and
variant. Those same native fields provide the join back to scheduling rows;
the physical worker's random execution UUID is not a retry identity. Its
fingerprinted evaluation context includes the budget. Different independent
executions must have different logical execution IDs even with the same seed.

## Integration, commits and recovery

`ParquetSink` and `DuckDBSink` expose the same typed `write_domain_record`,
`read_domain_record` and `domain_records` APIs. Records are additive JSON sidecars
under `<out_dir>/domain-records/<identity-sha256>.json`, shared across native shards.
This deliberately avoids altering Parquet/DuckDB native schemas. Query by logical
key or iterate records and inspect named measurements. Domain sidecars are not
part of the existing native SQL `results` view. ClickHouse, NullSink and existing
third-party sinks raise `NotImplementedError` for unsupported domain operations;
their legacy row interface remains compatible. DuckDB `base_name` must be a single
nonempty filename without directory or drive components; invalid names raise
`ValueError` before filesystem side effects. Unicode basenames remain supported.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Extension[Native runner extension] --> Params[CollectParams with typed records]
    Params --> Monitor[MonitorCollector]
    Monitor --> Commit[Local sink synchronous domain commit]
    Commit --> Writer[ArtifactWriter immutable publication]
    Writer --> JSON[Versioned JSON sidecars]
    Commit --> Native[Existing native row buffer]
    Native --> Flush[Existing flush before checkpoint]
    Flush --> Checkpoint[Existing CheckpointStore]
    JSON --> Query[Typed logical-key query]
    JSON --> Manifest[Existing artifact manifest]
```

Attach a tuple to `CollectParams.domain_records`, or call
`monitor.collect_domain_record(record)` from an extension before the checkpoint
advances. `ResultsWriter.write_domain_record` is also synchronous: it propagates
errors directly instead of leaving failures in a background thread. Its native
queue still needs `stop()` to drain. Domain commits do not increment the native
row counter. A bundle with several records is not a multi-record transaction.

The logical key is `(namespace, run_id, execution_id, decision_id)` and excludes
schema version. An identical canonical replay succeeds; any different content at
that key raises `ValueError`. A change to measurements or provenance requires an
explicit new decision/revision identity; schema changes cannot bypass conflicts.
Version 1 records are immutable rather than updated in place.

The writer fsyncs a unique temporary file, atomically hard-links it to the final
name without overwriting, then fsyncs the containing directory. Threads and
processes compete on the same publication operation. Readers and manifests ignore
`.tmp` files, including leftovers after process termination. A crash before
publication exposes no complete record; a crash after publication recovers through
identical replay. A successful synchronous write precedes checkpoint publication.
A resumed execution can encounter records ahead of its checkpoint without creating
duplicates. Failures are propagated, and an uncertain post-publication I/O failure
must be retried. This requires local hard-link/directory-fsync support; unsupported
filesystems raise `OSError`. Full power-loss durability of newly created parent
directories, network filesystems and object stores is outside this contract.

Domain records and native rows are **not jointly atomic**. Legacy native rows
remain append-only and may repeat on a resumed execution; this feature guarantees
idempotence for domain records only. The existing checkpoint/runner is reused.
Exactly-once native output, RNG-state recovery and global snapshot isolation are
not added here. Iteration scans a filename snapshot and concurrent new records may
appear on the next scan. One JSON file per decision favors auditability over
large-scale analytical throughput; a future indexed backend can implement the same
contract without weakening conflict rules.

## Comparisons, fingerprints and evolution

`record.require_comparable(other, "duration")` validates namespace, schema,
unit, meaning, objective direction, declared lower bound, dataset fingerprint and
evaluation fingerprint, and requires observed values. Incompatibility raises
`ValueError`; an undeclared name raises `KeyError`. It performs no statistical
analysis. `require_compatible` checks the same metadata while permitting unknown
values, for explicit insufficient-evidence reporting. Different candidate specs may
share an evaluation context; the producer
must fingerprint all relevant protocol definitions, grouping, data interpretation
and comparison semantics. Seeds alone do not supply independent evidence.

`fingerprint` accepts JSON values with string object keys. COLEMAN JSON v1 uses
sorted object keys, compact separators, UTF-8, finite numbers and significant
array order. Measurement declaration order is normalized by name; timestamps are
normalized to UTC. There is no rounding, automatic `str()` coercion, Unicode
normalization or promise of RFC 8785 cross-language canonicalization.
`identity_digest` hashes the logical key; `digest` hashes serialized content.
Native RunSpec run-ID derivation is unchanged. Fingerprint the actual public
resolved spec used for audit, not a private configuration or credentials. Producers
choose input observations explicitly; this API does not collect or redact secrets.

Readers dispatch strictly on `schema_version`; currently only integer 1 is
supported. Missing, older, future and unknown versions fail closed. Duplicate JSON
keys and unknown fields also fail. A legacy native file is read through its existing
Parquet/DuckDB APIs, unchanged; missing domain sidecars return `None`/empty iteration.
There is no automatic legacy-to-v1 migration because old data does not establish
units, availability, objective meaning or provenance. To annotate legacy output,
explicitly declare these from verified external metadata and write new sidecars
with an auditable producer/version, leaving the source artifact intact. If this
metadata is unavailable, keep the legacy result without inventing a v1 record.
A future schema must add an explicit reader and migration with versioned fixtures;
rewriting v1 files at the same logical key is never an implicit migration.

::: coleman.results.domain



### FILE: docs/extensibility.md

# Extensibility & Parallelism

This page is a complete implementation guide for extending Coleman while keeping
its native orchestration model.

## What You Can Extend

| Component | Typical goal | Current support |
|---|---|---|
| Policy | New action-selection strategy | Fully supported (source extension + config) |
| Reward | New credit assignment signal | Fully supported (source extension + config) |
| Hooks | Domain lifecycle logic and custom artifacts | Fully supported via `hooks.plugins` |
| Extensions | Namespaced custom domain config | Fully supported via `extensions` |
| EvaluationMetric | Alternate quality/cost metric logic | Supported via source extension (runner wiring) |
| Environment | Alternate orchestration/runtime behavior | Supported via source extension (runner wiring) |

## Public Runner Extension API

Coleman now provides a public extension layer that keeps orchestration in core
while allowing custom environment and metric wiring.

```python
from coleman.api import run_with_extension
from coleman.runner import RunnerExtension

extension = RunnerExtension(
  build_environment_fn=my_build_environment,
  build_metric_fn=my_build_metric,            # optional
  post_execution_fn=my_post_execution_hook,   # optional
)

result = run_with_extension(spec, extension)
```

Concrete example entrypoint:

1. [examples/custom-environment-template/advanced/my_project/extension_entrypoint.py](examples/custom-environment-template/advanced/my_project/extension_entrypoint.py)

Core-owned responsibilities remain unchanged:

1. execution plan generation
2. process-pool orchestration
3. hook event ordering
4. run_id and folder layout

Extension-owned responsibilities:

1. environment instantiation (`build_environment_fn`)
2. optional metric substitution (`build_metric_fn`)
3. optional per-execution post-processing (`post_execution_fn`)

## Parallelism Model (Complete)

Coleman has two independent parallel layers:

1. Intra-run process parallelism
   - Controlled by `execution.parallel_pool_size`.
   - Executes one run's `independent_executions` in worker processes.

2. Inter-spec sweep parallelism
   - Controlled by `coleman sweep --workers` or API `run_many(..., max_workers=...)`.
   - Executes multiple specs concurrently.

### Operational contract

1. Coordinator process events
   - `on_run_start`, `on_dataset_start`, `on_dataset_end`, `on_run_end`.
2. Worker process events
   - `on_execution_start`, `on_execution_end`.
3. Error event
   - `on_error` can be triggered in both contexts.
4. Profiling safety
   - `force_sequential_under_scalene: true` forces sequential worker mode under Scalene.

## Namespaced Custom Config (`extensions`)

Use `extensions` to pass domain-specific settings without relaxing strict RunSpec validation:

```yaml
extensions:
  my_domain:
    forecast_selection:
      policy: ThompsonSampling
      reward: Binary
      risk_budget: 0.15
```

Guidelines:

1. Keep keys namespaced (`my_domain`, `my_team`, etc.).
2. Keep values JSON-serializable.
3. Consume values from hook context (`context.extensions`).

## Hook Plugins (`hooks`)

Register plugins only in configuration:

```yaml
hooks:
  fail_fast: false
  plugins:
    - my_project.hooks.ForecastHook
    - my_project.hooks.audit_hook
```

Supported plugin forms:

1. Class plugin
   - Instantiated with no arguments.
   - Implement any lifecycle methods needed.
2. Function plugin
   - Signature: `(event_name, context, payload=None)`.

### Hook lifecycle

1. `on_run_start(context)`
2. `on_dataset_start(context)`
3. `on_execution_start(context)`
4. `on_execution_end(context, execution_result)`
5. `on_dataset_end(context, dataset_result)`
6. `on_run_end(context, run_result)`
7. `on_error(context, error)`

`on_error` is dispatched for startup failures as well, so hook-based cleanup
and telemetry can observe broken execution setup paths.

### Hook context fields

- `run_id`
- `dataset_id`
- `execution_id`
- `worker_id`
- `parallel_mode`
- `iteration`
- `trials`
- `budget_mode`
- `budget_value`
- `extensions`

## Typed Domain Results

Use [versioned domain records](domain-results.md) for observations that need units,
raw outcomes, explicit availability, provenance and retry-safe identity. The local
Parquet and DuckDB sinks commit these records as immutable JSON sidecars without
changing TCPCI columns. Pass `CollectParams.domain_records` or use
`monitor.collect_domain_record(record)` before the existing checkpoint advances.
The guide includes installed-package examples using the native runner extension
and synthetic CI runner-slot accounting.

## Deterministic Hook Artifacts

Use `ArtifactWriter` to create deterministic, collision-safe paths and atomic
JSON/CSV files for hook artifacts.

```python
from coleman.artifacts import ArtifactWriter

writer = ArtifactWriter("./runs")
path = writer.path_for(
  run_id=context.run_id or "unknown",
  dataset_id=context.dataset_id,
  budget_mode=context.budget_mode.value if context.budget_mode else None,
  budget_value=context.budget_value,
  execution_id=context.execution_id,
  artifact_type="forecast",
  ext="json",
)
writer.write_json_atomic(path, payload)
```

Concrete plugin example (class + function hooks):

1. [examples/custom-environment-template/advanced/my_project/hooks.py](examples/custom-environment-template/advanced/my_project/hooks.py)

Default artifact layout:

`<runs>/<run_id>/artifacts/<artifact_type>/<budget_segment>/<dataset_id>/<execution_id>/<stem>.<ext>`

## Public Scalene Compatibility Helper

For custom entrypoints, use `effective_parallel_pool_size(...)` from
`coleman.runner` to mirror the same Scalene safeguard behavior as the core runner.

## Adding a New Policy

Current loading contract:

1. Runner reads policy names from `experiment.policies`.
2. For each policy `X`, runner loads class `XPolicy` from `coleman.policy` module exports.

### Implementation steps

1. Create your policy class in `coleman/policy/...` extending base behavior from existing policy patterns.
2. Expose the class in `coleman/policy/__init__.py`.
3. Add algorithm hyperparameters under `algorithm.<policy_name_lower>` in YAML.
4. Add policy name (without suffix) in `experiment.policies`.
5. Add tests for deterministic behavior and credit-assignment updates.

Example config:

```yaml
experiment:
  policies: [MyPolicy]
  rewards: [RNFail]

algorithm:
  mypolicy:
    rnfail:
      temperature: 0.2
```

## Adding a New Reward

Current loading contract:

1. Runner reads reward names from `experiment.rewards`.
2. For each reward `Y`, runner loads class `YReward` from `coleman.reward` module exports.

### Implementation steps

1. Create your reward class in `coleman/reward/...` inheriting reward base contract.
2. Expose the class in `coleman/reward/__init__.py`.
3. Add reward name (without suffix) in `experiment.rewards`.
4. Add tests validating `evaluate(...)` against expected metric scenarios.

Example config:

```yaml
experiment:
  policies: [UCB]
  rewards: [MyReward]

algorithm:
  ucb:
    myreward:
      c: 0.4
```

## Custom EvaluationMetric (Source Extension)

Current default wiring uses `NAPFDVerdictMetric` in runner environment construction.

If you need a custom metric class today:

1. Implement metric class in `coleman/evaluation/...` extending evaluation base behavior.
2. Expose it in `coleman/evaluation/__init__.py`.
3. Wire it in runner environment construction where evaluation metric instance is created.
4. Add tests for metric math invariants and edge cases (no failures, full failures, partial budget).

## Custom Environment (Source Extension)

Current default wiring uses `Environment` in runner environment construction.

If you need a custom environment today:

1. Implement class inheriting `AbstractEnvironment`.
2. Preserve compatibility with monitor/checkpoint/telemetry contracts.
3. Wire your class in runner environment creation.
4. Add integration tests for sequential and parallel execution consistency.

## Recommended Strategy for Large Domain Workflows

1. Prefer `hooks + extensions` first.
2. Keep core runner orchestration untouched whenever possible.
3. Use source-level Environment/EvaluationMetric customization only when behavior cannot be expressed via hooks.
4. Persist custom artifacts with run/execution identifiers for later joins in analysis.

## Official Starter Template

An in-repo starter template is available under:

1. `examples/custom-environment-template/minimal/`
2. `examples/custom-environment-template/advanced/`

The advanced track includes hooks, extension-style wiring, and manifest-ready
artifact layout for parallel runs.

Quickstart for advanced track:

```bash
cd examples/custom-environment-template/advanced
python -m my_project.extension_entrypoint
```

## End-to-End Example (Parallel + Extensions + Hooks)

```yaml
packs:
  - execution/default
  - experiment/alibaba_druid
  - algorithm/defaults
  - reward/rnfail
  - results/parquet

execution:
  independent_executions: 20
  parallel_pool_size: 4
  force_sequential_under_scalene: true

experiment:
  policies: [UCB, MyPolicy]
  rewards: [RNFail, MyReward]

algorithm:
  ucb:
    rnfail:
      c: 0.3
  mypolicy:
    rnfail:
      temperature: 0.15

hooks:
  fail_fast: false
  plugins:
    - my_project.hooks.ForecastHook
    - my_project.hooks.audit_hook

extensions:
  my_domain:
    forecast_selection:
      policy: ThompsonSampling
      reward: Binary
      risk_budget: 0.15
```

CLI sweep with inter-spec parallelism:

```bash
coleman sweep --config run.yaml \
  --grid execution.seed=range(0,10) \
  --grid algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c=0.1,0.3,0.5 \
  --workers 4
```

## Testing Checklist for Extensions

1. Sequential and parallel should produce expected hook side effects.
2. Hook errors should obey `fail_fast` policy.
3. Custom artifacts should carry `run_id` and `execution_id`.
4. New policies/rewards should be covered by deterministic unit tests.
5. Any Environment/Metric source customization should include integration tests.



### FILE: docs/finite-coverage.md

# Finite coverage selection for CI

COLEMAN can select a finite set of overlapping test capabilities under an explicit
budget. This library API is separate from bandit learning: it optimizes declared
nonnegative coverage weights, without inventing a learning reward, a calibrated
probability or evidence that a policy improves production CI.

Existing ratio, fixed-time and subset-size scheduling behavior is unchanged. The
API reuses [versioned domain results](domain-results.md), `ArtifactWriter`, local
sinks, manifests and the existing checkpoint store. It has no CLI/MCP dependency.

## Complete small CI example

```python
from decimal import Decimal

from coleman.results.domain import fingerprint
from coleman.selection import (
    CoverageCandidate, CoverageConstraints, CoverageOutcome, CoverageProblem,
    CoverageResult, Quantity, SearchLimits, UnitSemantics, solve_coverage,
)

duration = UnitSemantics(unit="s", meaning="modeled-serial-test-duration-v1")
capability = UnitSemantics(unit="1", meaning="weighted-test-capability-v1")

def amount(value, semantics):
    return Quantity(value=Decimal(value), semantics=semantics)

definitions = [
    {"id": "A", "duration": "2", "covers": ["x", "y"]},
    {"id": "B", "duration": "2", "covers": ["y", "z"]},
    {"id": "C", "duration": "1", "covers": ["z"]},
]
weights = {"x": "0.5", "y": "0.3", "z": "0.2"}
problem = CoverageProblem(
    schema_version=1,
    data_fingerprint=fingerprint({"candidates": definitions, "weights": weights}),
    objective_semantics=capability,
    candidates=tuple(
        CoverageCandidate(
            candidate_id=item["id"],
            cost=amount(item["duration"], duration),
            covers=tuple(item["covers"]),
        )
        for item in definitions
    ),
    outcomes=tuple(
        CoverageOutcome(outcome_id=name, weight=amount(weight, capability))
        for name, weight in weights.items()
    ),
    constraints=CoverageConstraints(budget=amount("3", duration)),
)
result = solve_coverage(
    problem, method="branch_bound_v1",
    limits=SearchLimits(deadline_seconds=None),
)
assert result.status == "optimal"
assert result.selected_ids == ("A", "C")
assert result.cost.value == Decimal("3")
assert result.objective.value == result.upper_bound.value == Decimal("1")
assert result.absolute_gap.value == Decimal("0")
assert CoverageResult.from_json(result.to_json()) == result
```

`x/y/z` denote synthetic test capabilities. A capability contributes its weight
once to the union, even when multiple tests cover it. With budget 2 the proven
selection is `("A",)`, objective 0.8. No external dataset/service is needed.

## Inputs, units and exact arithmetic

Every cost, budget and weight is a `Quantity(value, semantics)` with an explicit
unit and versioned meaning. Costs must match budget semantics exactly; weights
must match `objective_semantics`. Seconds/milliseconds or different meanings are
rejected, including for zero values. No implicit conversion is performed.

The objective is additive nonnegative union coverage. Negative costs/weights,
nonfinite numbers, null/unknown quantities, duplicate IDs/memberships, and unknown
candidate/outcome references fail validation. A missing cost requires an explicit
upstream modeling/exclusion decision; it never becomes a free test. An empty
universe/outcome set is valid. Budget zero permits genuinely zero-cost candidates.

Use `Decimal` or decimal strings at the input boundary. At most twelve fractional
places are accepted, with each input cost/weight/budget at most `10^12`. Computation
uses integral `10^-12` ticks, exact sums and rational density comparisons,
independently of the process Decimal precision. **Decision tolerance is zero.**
A floating expression already containing rounding error can therefore fail the
precision check; it is never silently rounded into a feasible budget.

JSON quantities use canonical decimal strings (`"0"`, `"0.3"`), preserving finite
values and normalized equivalent spellings. Signed zero normalizes before hashing
and binary64 projection. Aggregate quantities allow up to
`10^24` and 37 decimal digits; accepted problem dimensions keep actual aggregate
weights below that ceiling. Cost/coverage declarations are modeled inputs, not
automatically measured performance, unique faults or calibrated probabilities.

`CoverageConstraints` adds `required_ids` and optional `maximum_selected` to the
inclusive budget. Mandatory costs/cardinality exceeding their ceiling prove
infeasibility. Cardinality zero permits the empty selection when nothing is
mandatory. No arbitrary nonlinear/group constraint is implied by this v1 API.

## Full and restricted scope

`CoverageProblem.candidates` is the complete declared universe. `search_ids=None`
resolves canonically to every candidate; an explicit subset produces a restricted
scope. Candidate/outcome/membership/constraint ordering does not change identity.
The full problem and normalized search IDs determine `scope_fingerprint`.

An optimum in a restricted scope makes no optimality claim about excluded
candidates. A mandatory candidate excluded from search makes that **scope**
infeasible, even when the full universe could work. Input fingerprints and scope
proofs cannot certify completeness of an undisclosed external universe. Producers
must retain the full source definitions, availability and selection/exclusion rules.

## Solvers and verifiable certificates

`greedy_density_v1` repeatedly selects positive marginal coverage per unit cost,
prioritizing free positive coverage. Exact density ties use ascending candidate
IDs; zero-gain optional candidates are omitted. A resumed feasible hint is never
worsened. This implementation declares **no approximation guarantee** under its
budget/cardinality/mandatory constraints and never labels greedy completion optimal.

`branch_bound_v1` shares the same overall work budget with its greedy warm start,
then explores binary include/exclude prefixes in sorted optional-ID order.
Nonnegative union coverage bounds the remaining objective. Equal bounds are not
pruned, preserving the globally smallest selected-ID tuple among equal objectives;
cost is a constraint, not an undeclared tie-break objective.

A completed search retains a bounded prefix certificate. Each prefix represents a
subtree: `0` excludes an optional candidate and `1` includes it. On reading a result,
the independent verifier checks that prefix intervals are disjoint and cover the
entire binary search cube, then verifies that each subtree is infeasible, strictly
dominated by a union bound, or a complete assignment no better under the objective
and lexicographic tie rule. It does not run the optimizer or the test-only
combinations oracle. A missing, overlapping, incomplete or unjustified certificate
cannot establish optimality.

Version 1 exact verification is deliberately small: at most **20 scoped candidates,
256 touched outcomes, 4096 scoped memberships and 1024 certificate prefixes**.
These caps cannot be increased by a request. If a complete proof cannot be retained,
the feasible incumbent remains visible with `certificate_limit`, not `optimal`.
The independent exhaustive test oracle is capped at ten candidates and is not
imported by production code. No local-improvement algorithm or unmeasured
performance superiority is claimed.

## Results and stopping behavior

`CoverageResult` embeds the complete problem, method/version, limits, preflight
counts/estimated bytes, scope/fingerprint, selected IDs, exact cost/objective,
feasibility, status, termination reason, work used, upper bound, absolute gap and
optional completed proof. Reading/serialization revalidates quantities and evidence.

| Status | Meaning | Selection and bound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `optimal` | Complete verified scoped proof | Feasible selection; bound=objective; gap=0 |
| `feasible` | Greedy completed or search stopped with an incumbent | Feasible selection; entire scoped coverage union bounds the objective |
| `infeasible` | Mandatory budget/cardinality/scope proof | Null selection, quantities, bound and gap |
| `limited` | Resource preflight refused search | Null incumbent; no claim of mathematical infeasibility |

An empty selected tuple is a real feasible choice with zero cost/coverage. Null
selected IDs mean no incumbent was produced. Bounds/gaps are null when unavailable.
A feasible result can have gap zero without a completed tie-aware search proof;
this does not silently change its status to optimal.

`SearchLimits` bounds candidate/outcome/membership dimensions, estimated additional
working bytes, `max_work`, `deadline_seconds` and proof size. One search-work unit
is one examined greedy candidate or popped branch node. Warm start and exact
search share the counter and the timer; no phase resets a budget. The timer starts
at API entry, including setup. Cancellation/deadline polls occur between bounded
search operations; `KeyboardInterrupt` during search returns the last complete
incumbent. Unexpected callback/validation errors propagate.

The deadline is cooperative, **not a hard real-time process limit**. Initialization,
validated output, serialization and bounded certificate verification add overhead;
these phases cannot be interrupted into a falsely completed artifact. Memory
preflight is a conservative sparse-working-allocation estimate, not measured RSS;
it excludes the already supplied input, interpreter and artifact payload. No dense
candidate/outcome matrix is allocated. Input tuples themselves are capped at
10,000 candidates/outcomes and 10,000 memberships per candidate. Apply byte-level
request limits at an external transport boundary when exposing this library.

## Checkpoints, artifacts and installed examples

`result.checkpoint()` produces versioned JSON containing a feasible incumbent and
the full problem fingerprint. Persist it using existing infrastructure:

```python
from coleman.checkpoint import LocalCheckpointStore
from coleman.checkpoint.state import CheckpointPayload
from coleman.selection import CoverageCheckpoint

partial = solve_coverage(problem, method="branch_bound_v1", limits=SearchLimits(max_work=3))
store = LocalCheckpointStore("./trusted-local-checkpoints")
store.save(CheckpointPayload(
    run_id="coverage-ci", step=partial.work_used,
    extra={"coverage_v1": partial.checkpoint().to_json()},
))
saved = store.load("coverage-ci", 0)
checkpoint = CoverageCheckpoint.from_json(saved.extra["coverage_v1"])
resumed = solve_coverage(problem, method="branch_bound_v1", checkpoint=checkpoint)
```

Checkpoint identity and selection feasibility are checked even when preflight
would refuse work or the problem is infeasible. Resume restarts search at the root
with the verified incumbent. It does not trust a discarded frontier, saved bound
or prior completion flag. This favors a small auditable contract over preserving all search work;
repeated tiny budgets may repeat work. Existing pickle-based checkpoints are for
trusted local state. Preflight rejection never modifies a supplied checkpoint.

`publish_coverage_result(result, ArtifactWriter(root))` stores deterministic exact
JSON under `coverage-results/<content-digest>.json`. Existing atomic immutable
publication makes identical retries/concurrent publication idempotent and rejects
conflicts; incomplete temporary files are not completed artifacts. Manifests list
these results. Local hard-link/fsync and power-loss limitations are unchanged.

`coverage_record(result, run_id=..., available_at=...)` creates #251 measurements
for existing sinks. Exact decimal JSON remains authoritative. The scalar adapter
explicitly projects to binary64, names measurements `selection_cost`,
`coverage_objective`, `coverage_upper_bound`, `coverage_absolute_gap`, and suffixes
their meanings with `binary64-projection-v1`. It neither replaces native `cost`
(APFDc) nor feeds projected values back into verification. No learning reward is
fabricated. Supply actual zoned availability after calculation and retain that
timestamp on retries; null incumbent quantities become unavailable measurements.

The standalone installed-package examples need only base dependencies:

```bash
pip install path/to/coleman.whl
python ci.py ./ci-output
python resources.py ./resource-output
```

Copy [ci.py](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/main/examples/finite-coverage/ci.py)
or [resources.py](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/main/examples/finite-coverage/resources.py)
outside the repository before running. Example output stays within the invocation
directory. The CI example runs both solvers through
the actual runner, agent, RNFail reward, metric and Parquet sink. Build 1 retains
the native initial shuffle; build 2 exercises selection. Its fixture-only ranking
adapter verifies that the selected prefix consumes the entire modeled fixed-time
budget and that native scheduling matches. It does not claim arbitrary subset
constraints can be enforced by any full ranking. The resolved RunSpec records
the complete typed inputs, method and adapter version in `extensions`. On an
identical rerun, it reuses a committed domain record's availability timestamp and
revalidates its content, keeping the pure result and sidecar publication idempotent.
Legacy native row retry semantics are unchanged. The resource
example reserves synthetic CI runner slots for overlapping capabilities; it is not
a measurement of financial return or an argument for a new learning algorithm.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Inputs[Typed CI capabilities, units, costs and constraints] --> Scope[Complete universe and declared search scope]
    Scope --> Guard[Dimension and memory preflight]
    Guard --> Greedy[Deterministic greedy incumbent]
    Greedy --> Search[Bounded small branch-and-bound]
    Search --> Proof[Complete prefix proof or explicit limited search]
    Proof --> Result[Versioned exact decimal result and verified bounds]
    Result --> Writer[Existing ArtifactWriter and manifests]
    Result --> Projection[Explicit binary64 domain record adapter]
    Projection --> Sinks[Existing local result sinks]
    Result --> Hint[Verified incumbent JSON in existing checkpoint store]
    Hint --> Greedy
    Scope --> Native[Existing native runner extension example]
    Native --> Sinks
```

## Compatibility and limits

Problem/result/checkpoint artifacts require integer `schema_version=1` and
`coverage-v1` solver semantics. Missing/old/future versions, duplicate JSON keys,
unknown fields and invalid certificates fail closed. No migration invents missing
units, source data, constraints or proof coverage. Legacy native results and
protected-evaluation artifact bytes retain their existing contracts; their strict
JSON base is shared without changing serialization.

Independent mathematical/performance benchmarks remain #255 work. Temporal claims
about learned cost/coverage models need the [protected evaluation](protected-evaluation.md)
protocol, justified independent observations and conservative insufficient-evidence
handling. Passing the finite fixture proves its declared mathematical decision,
not effectiveness on a broad CI corpus or commercial value.

::: coleman.selection



### FILE: docs/getting-started.md

# Getting Started

## Installation

### Option A: DevContainer (recommended)

The fastest way to start is with a [DevContainer](https://containers.dev/).
Open the repo in **VS Code** (or any DevContainer-compatible editor) and
select **"Reopen in Container"** — **everything works out of the box**,
including the full observability stack.

**What happens automatically:**

1. Python 3.14 + uv + all dependencies (including telemetry & ClickHouse extras) are installed
2. Pre-commit hooks are configured
3. The **observability stack** (OTel Collector + Grafana) starts via Docker-in-Docker
4. **Telemetry** can be enabled via the `telemetry/local` pack in `run.yaml`

After the container builds, just run your experiment:

```bash
coleman run --config run.yaml
# Open http://localhost:3000 → Grafana shows metrics in real-time
```

No manual steps required — skip to [Running Experiments](#running-experiments).

**What's included:**

| What | Why |
|------|-----|
| **Python 3.14 + uv** | Project package manager |
| **Docker-in-Docker** | Runs the observability stack automatically |
| **VS Code extensions** | Ruff, Pylance, Pyright, Copilot, TOML, Jupyter, and more |
| **Telemetry + ClickHouse extras** | Pre-installed — no extra `pip install` needed |
| **OTel Collector + Grafana** | Started automatically on container start |
| **Port forwarding** | All service ports mapped to your host browser |

### Option B: Local setup

#### Prerequisites

- Python 3.14+
- [UV](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

#### Install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman.git
cd coleman
uv sync
uv pip install -e .
```

#### Development Setup

```bash
# Install all development dependencies
make install

# Install pre-commit hooks
make pre-commit-install
```

## Configuration

Coleman uses YAML configuration files with typed Pydantic v2 models.
You can compose configs with **config packs** and override specific settings
inline.

### Quick config (YAML + packs)

Create a YAML config file:

```yaml
# my-experiment.yaml
packs:
  - policy/linucb
  - reward/rnfail
  - results/parquet
  - telemetry/off

experiment:
  datasets: ["alibaba@druid"]

execution:
  independent_executions: 30
```

Run with the `coleman` CLI:

```bash
coleman run --config my-experiment.yaml
```

Or use the library API:

```python
from coleman.api import run, load_spec

spec = load_spec("my-experiment.yaml")
result = run(spec)
print(result.run_id, result.artifacts_dir)
```

See the [Configuration guide](configuration.md) for the full schema
reference, config packs, sweep engine, and determinism contract.

## Running Experiments

### Using the `coleman` CLI (recommended)

```bash
# Single run
coleman run --config my-experiment.yaml

# Parameter sweep
coleman sweep --config my-experiment.yaml \
    --grid algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c=0.1,0.3,0.5 \
    --grid execution.seed=range(0,10) \
    --workers 4

# Parameter sweep declared in my-experiment.yaml (top-level sweep:)
coleman sweep --config my-experiment.yaml --workers 4

# Dry-run (preview specs without executing)
coleman sweep --config my-experiment.yaml \
    --grid execution.seed=range(0,5) \
    --dry-run
```

When both YAML `sweep` and CLI `--grid` are present, they are merged.

If the same dotted key appears in both places, Coleman raises an error
instead of generating duplicate sweep combinations.

Results are written to `./runs/<run_id>/` with `spec.resolved.json` and
`provenance.json` alongside the experiment data.

### DevContainer: just run it

If you're in the DevContainer, the observability stack is already running and
telemetry is enabled.  Just run:

```bash
coleman run --config my-experiment.yaml
# Results    → ./runs/       (Parquet)
# Checkpoints → ./checkpoints/
# Metrics    → http://localhost:3000 (Grafana, live)
```

## Checking Final Results

Grafana is for live execution behavior: throughput, latency, CPU, memory, and
run separation while the experiment is still running.

The final experiment facts are stored separately:

* Parquet, by default: `./runs/`
* Checkpoint progress for resume/recovery: `./checkpoints/`
* ClickHouse, when enabled: table `coleman_results`

### What happens if you run experiments again?

By default, Coleman **appends** new final results instead of replacing the
old ones.

For the default Parquet sink this means:

* new files are created under `./runs/`
* previous files are preserved
* old and new executions coexist in the same dataset
* the new `execution_id` lets you separate one run from another analytically

For the ClickHouse sink this means:

* new rows are inserted into `coleman_results`
* previous rows are preserved unless you explicitly delete them

Checkpoint behavior is different: for the same run and experiment, the latest
checkpoint progress is updated so recovery can continue from the most recent
durable step.

If you want a completely fresh analysis space, choose one of these options
before running again:

```bash
# Option 1: start from a clean Parquet directory
rm -rf ./runs

# Option 2: keep old runs, but write new ones elsewhere
# Set results.out_dir: "./runs-new" in your run.yaml

# Option 3: clean checkpoints too, if you do not want recovery state reused
rm -rf ./checkpoints
```

### Default Parquet output

After `coleman run --config run.yaml`, inspect the partitioned Parquet dataset:

```bash
find ./runs -name '*.parquet' | head
```

Prepare a reusable view in DuckDB, then query it directly:

```python
import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect("analysis.duckdb")
con.execute("""
    CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW experiment_results AS
    SELECT *
    FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
""")

con.sql("""
    SELECT scenario,
           execution_id,
           policy,
           reward_function,
           AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
           AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc,
           AVG(process_memory_rss_mib) AS avg_rss_mib,
           AVG(process_cpu_utilization_percent) AS avg_cpu_pct
    FROM experiment_results
    GROUP BY scenario, execution_id, policy, reward_function
    ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC
""")
```

### DuckDB, in practice

DuckDB is the easiest way to inspect final results deeply without moving data
out of the Parquet dataset.

#### Start an interactive session

```bash
uv run ipython
```

Then initialize once and reuse the same view across the remaining examples:

```python
import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect("analysis.duckdb")
con.execute("""
    CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW experiment_results AS
    SELECT *
    FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
""")
```

#### Inspect available columns

```python
con.sql("""
    DESCRIBE
    SELECT *
    FROM experiment_results
""").df()
```

#### See which executions are available

```python
con.sql("""
    SELECT scenario,
           execution_id,
           COUNT(*) AS rows,
           MIN(step) AS first_step,
           MAX(step) AS last_step
    FROM experiment_results
    GROUP BY scenario, execution_id
    ORDER BY scenario, execution_id
""").df()
```

#### Compare policies by final quality and resource cost

```python
con.sql("""
    SELECT scenario,
           policy,
           reward_function,
           AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
           AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc,
           AVG(prioritization_time) AS avg_prioritization_time,
           AVG(process_memory_rss_mib) AS avg_rss_mib,
           AVG(process_cpu_utilization_percent) AS avg_cpu_pct,
           MAX(wall_time_seconds) AS wall_time_seconds
    FROM experiment_results
    GROUP BY scenario, policy, reward_function
    ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC, avg_apfdc DESC
""").df()
```

#### Slice one specific execution

```python
execution_id = 'replace-with-real-execution-id'
con.sql(f"""
    SELECT experiment,
           step,
           policy,
           reward_function,
           fitness,
           cost,
           process_memory_rss_mib,
           process_cpu_utilization_percent
    FROM experiment_results
    WHERE execution_id = '{execution_id}'
    ORDER BY experiment, step, policy
""").df()
```

#### Export a filtered report

Before executte the following command, create the `analysis` directory first under the `runs/` directory.

```python
con.sql("""
    COPY (
        SELECT scenario,
               execution_id,
               policy,
               reward_function,
               AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
               AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc
        FROM experiment_results
        GROUP BY scenario, execution_id, policy, reward_function
    ) TO './runs/analysis/final-summary.csv' (HEADER, DELIMITER ',')
""")
print('exported ./runs/analysis/final-summary.csv')
```

### ClickHouse, in practice

If you want a long-lived analytical store instead of Parquet files, switch the
 results sink to ClickHouse.

#### Enable it

```yaml
# In your run.yaml, override the results section:
results:
  enabled: true
  sink: clickhouse
```

Run the service locally:

```bash
cd examples/observability
docker compose --profile clickhouse up -d
```

#### Initialize once and reuse

Start a Python session and connect once — then reuse `client` across all the
examples below:

```python
import clickhouse_connect

client = clickhouse_connect.get_client(host='localhost', port=8123, database='default')
```

#### Inspect stored schema

```python
print(client.query('DESCRIBE TABLE coleman_results').result_rows)
```

#### See which executions are available

```python
rows = client.query('''
    SELECT scenario,
           execution_id,
           COUNT(*) AS rows,
           MIN(step)  AS first_step,
           MAX(step)  AS last_step
    FROM coleman_results
    GROUP BY scenario, execution_id
    ORDER BY scenario, execution_id
''')
print(rows.result_rows)
```

#### Compare policies by final quality and resource cost

```python
rows = client.query('''
    SELECT scenario,
           policy,
           reward_function,
           AVG(fitness)                      AS avg_napfd,
           AVG(cost)                         AS avg_apfdc,
           AVG(prioritization_time)          AS avg_prioritization_time,
           AVG(process_memory_rss_mib)       AS avg_rss_mib,
           AVG(process_cpu_utilization_percent) AS avg_cpu_pct,
           MAX(wall_time_seconds)            AS wall_time_seconds
    FROM coleman_results
    GROUP BY scenario, policy, reward_function
    ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC, avg_apfdc DESC
''')
print(rows.result_rows)
```

#### Query a summary across all executions

```python
rows = client.query('''
    SELECT scenario,
           execution_id,
           policy,
           reward_function,
           AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
           AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc,
           AVG(process_memory_rss_mib) AS avg_rss_mib,
           AVG(process_cpu_utilization_percent) AS avg_cpu_pct
    FROM coleman_results
    GROUP BY scenario, execution_id, policy, reward_function
    ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC
''')
print(rows.result_rows)
```

#### Slice one specific execution

```python
execution_id = 'replace-with-real-execution-id'
rows = client.query(f'''
    SELECT experiment,
           step,
           policy,
           reward_function,
           fitness,
           cost,
           process_memory_rss_mib,
           process_cpu_utilization_percent
    FROM coleman_results
    WHERE execution_id = '{execution_id}'
    ORDER BY experiment, step, policy
''')
print(rows.result_rows)
```

#### Export a filtered report to CSV

```python
import csv

rows = client.query('''
    SELECT scenario,
           execution_id,
           policy,
           reward_function,
           AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
           AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc
    FROM coleman_results
    GROUP BY scenario, execution_id, policy, reward_function
''')

with open('./runs/analysis/final-summary.csv', 'w', newline='') as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(rows.column_names)
    writer.writerows(rows.result_rows)

print('exported ./runs/analysis/final-summary.csv')
```

#### Clean old data when needed

ClickHouse also accumulates results by default. If you need a fresh table:

```python
client.command('TRUNCATE TABLE coleman_results')
print('coleman_results truncated')
```

### Resume and recovery

If checkpoints are enabled, Coleman writes one directory per run under
`./checkpoints/`. Each experiment keeps a `progress_ex<N>.json` file pointing
to the last durable checkpoint.

To inspect recovery state:

```bash
find ./checkpoints -name 'progress_*.json' -maxdepth 3 -print
```

When `coleman run --config run.yaml` is started again with the same configuration,
the framework loads the last saved checkpoint and resumes from the next step
instead of replaying completed builds.

### Notebook workflow

For a guided end-to-end workflow covering configuration, observability,
checkpoints, export, and analysis, open the marimo notebook example in
[docs/workflow.py](docs/workflow.py).

| Port | Service | URL |
|------|---------|-----|
| **3000** | Grafana | [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000) |
| **4317** | OTel Collector (gRPC) | — (used by the framework) |
| **4318** | OTel Collector (HTTP) | — (used by the framework) |
| **8889** | Prometheus metrics | [http://localhost:8889/metrics](http://localhost:8889/metrics) |
| **8123** | ClickHouse (HTTP) | [http://localhost:8123](http://localhost:8123) *(profile: clickhouse)* |
| **9000** | ClickHouse (native) | — *(profile: clickhouse)* |

!!! note "DevContainer vs. local"
    In the DevContainer, the OTel Collector + Grafana start automatically
    and telemetry is enabled.  Locally, you start them manually with
    `docker compose up -d` and use the `telemetry/local` pack in your `run.yaml`.

### FILE: docs/index.md

# Coleman

**Multi-Armed Bandit based Test Case Prioritization for Continuous Integration**

Coleman is a framework that applies Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) algorithms to
solve the Test Case Prioritization problem in Continuous Integration (CI)
environments.

## Features

- Adaptive learning from test execution feedback
- Multiple MAB policies: baseline, Bayesian/stochastic, adversarial, and non-stationary variants
- Contextual bandits: LinUCB/SWLinUCB plus LinTS and contextual epsilon-greedy variants
- HCS support with WTS and VTS strategies
- Cost-effective prioritization under time budgets
- **Typed configuration** — Pydantic v2 models with YAML configs and composable config packs
- **Library-first API** — `run()`, `run_many()`, `sweep()`, `load_spec()`
- **`coleman` CLI** — thin wrapper: `coleman run`, `coleman sweep`, `coleman validate`
- **Sweep engine** — grid (Cartesian) and zip (paired) parameter expansion with seed replication
- **Deterministic `run_id`** — `sha256(canonical_json(spec))[:12]` for exact replication
- **Provenance tracking** — `spec.resolved.json` + `provenance.json` per run

## New in 4.10

[Collect a controlled Java fault matrix](java-fault-matrix.md) with the published
wheel: three curated upstream fixes across Apache Commons CLI and Codec, frozen
source/runtime recipes, typed indices and offline recovery. Source/context/raw
validation keeps every selected outcome inspectable. The initial qualification
retained **714 role observations / 357 same-test pairs**, including both-fail and
inconclusive results. Incomplete collection never acquires a completion marker.

The complete guide includes the verified wheel, explicit native arm64 Docker
preparation, collection, offline validation and recovery. Controlled observations
retain their admission and generalization limits. See the
[4.10 release notes](releases/4.10.0.md) for compatibility and scientific limits.

## LRTS stage views

[Run larger LRTS histories with explicit stage views](lrts-stage-views.md).
The published wheel preserves **18,901 ActiveMQ method observations** and
**30,066 Log4j observations**, with separate Ubuntu/Windows native views.
Exact source-context/node bindings keep stages distinct; all raw methods and
processed stages remain analytical evidence. Each four-build view produces
eight Random/UCB result rows and resumes committed checkpoints.

The Log4j views share source project/build groups. Missing executor, outcome and
feature clocks, expected test universe, verified continuity and concurrency
remain explicit blockers. The workflow is a post-hoc serial simulation, and
broader corpus admission and confirmation remain open.
See the [4.9 release notes](releases/4.9.0.md).

## Existing real-data workflows

[Turn real RTPTorrent CI history into Parquet and native TCPCI replays](rtptorrent-parquet-etl.md).
The published wheel verifies the complete ZIP64 source, preserves **46,995 class
executions / 1,662 source jobs**, and projects 18 executions from eight declared
jobs into Random/UCB replay with the existing checkpoints. All exclusions, units
and source/producer/file identities remain inspectable.

The [LRTS download-to-Parquet workflow](lrts-parquet-etl.md) remains available in
the same wheel: eight Karaf builds, 6,876 method observations, 6,567 compatible
native executions and 309 not-run exclusions. Each workflow produces 16 result
rows and resumes without duplicating committed rounds. Their post-hoc serial
and budget-censored feedback assumptions do not establish observed chronology,
policy efficacy or prospective savings. Source admission and confirmation remain open.

The 4.8 release also corrected Linux worker memory accounting while retaining its
limits and historical general telemetry. See the [4.8 release notes](releases/4.8.0.md).

[Controlled observations](controlled-faults.md), the
[pinned JUnit3 source recipe](junit-source-capture.md),
[RTPTorrent](rtptorrent.md) and [LRTS](lrts.md) readers,
[corpus profiles](benchmark-corpus.md) and [source cache](corpus-materialization.md)
retain their workflows. All seven required diversity regimes remain uncovered.

[Exact resource accounting](resource-replay.md) and [frozen shadow evaluation](prospective-shadow.md)
retain their 4.3 behavior. The included synthetic shadow fixture remains inconclusive.

[Point-in-time observations](point-in-time-observations.md) preserve what each
decision knew, including late/corrected outcomes and conservative freshness.
The [corpus foundation](benchmark-corpus.md) retains two known-answer fixtures and
visible source-admission gaps; all seven diversity regimes remain uncovered.
Use the [operational CI pilot](operational-pilot.md), [application API](application-api.md)
and [independent benchmarks](decision-benchmarks.md) for complete experiments and
correctness checks. See the [4.10 release notes](releases/4.10.0.md) for examples,
compatibility and limits.

## Quick Start

With Python 3.14 or later in an activated environment, install the GitHub release wheel.
For SHA-256 verification before installation, use the [complete setup command](setup.md#default-run-no-docker-required):

```bash
python -m pip install "https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"
coleman run --config my-experiment.yaml
```

Or use the library API:

```python
from coleman.api import run, load_spec

spec = load_spec("my-experiment.yaml")
result = run(spec)
```

See the [Getting Started](getting-started.md) guide for full instructions
and the [Configuration](configuration.md) guide for the YAML schema,
config packs, sweep engine, and determinism contract.
For deep post-run analytics, see the [Analysis Playbook](analysis-playbook.md).
For advanced customization and parallel extension contracts, see
[Extensibility & Parallelism](extensibility.md).



### FILE: docs/java-fault-matrix.md

# Run a controlled Java fault matrix

Collect three curated upstream fixes across Apache Commons CLI and Codec with
one frozen plan. Each cell runs buggy and fixed source against the same declared
fixed-tree fixture, retaining every observed pass, failure, test error and
incomplete collection. This is controlled functional evidence for TCPCI research;
it is separate from historical CI and policy comparisons.

The published **4.10 wheel** includes the matrix transport. It reuses the existing
single-pair producer and the generic [controlled-observation
domain](controlled-faults.md). It does not introduce a learning runner or change
existing source recipes, results, checkpoints or raw-capture semantics.

## Install and collect outside checkout

Use Python 3.14+, uv, POSIX and a native Linux arm64 Docker engine. These frozen
recipes pin Temurin `11.0.32.1`, the arm64 image digest and
`America/Los_Angeles`. A different architecture needs a separately reviewed
recipe; changing its label does not validate another runtime.

Install the verified published wheel into a fresh external environment; no checkout
is required:

```bash
uv venv /tmp/coleman-matrix-env --python 3.14
uv pip install --python /tmp/coleman-matrix-env/bin/python "https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.10.0/coleman-4.10.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=b85b6d94fdb48d7f31d580583dfe1be96de2c63f07341b7159d2fbf777639d29"

# Explicit operator preparation; COLEMAN never pulls an image.
docker pull --platform linux/arm64 eclipse-temurin@sha256:e4b3ff0f1a427efb2deb02b092ff8316d58573480260720d767d6ecdd69999d8

mkdir -p /tmp/coleman-matrix-workspace
cd /tmp/coleman-matrix-workspace
/tmp/coleman-matrix-env/bin/python -m coleman.transports.junit_matrix \
  --cache /tmp/coleman-java-source-cache \
  --output /tmp/coleman-java-observations --fetch > matrix-summary.json

# Same plan/trials: validate committed evidence rather than collect it again.
/tmp/coleman-matrix-env/bin/python -m coleman.transports.junit_matrix \
  --cache /tmp/coleman-java-source-cache \
  --output /tmp/coleman-java-observations
```
